INPUTS: You have three pieces of data: first, an integer n; second, a list called lst where every item is a triple of integers (x0, y0, val0); and third, another integer m. Everything you need lives in those three variables. 

LOGICS: First, what you do is build an adjacency structure called A. Make A a list with n+1 empty sublists in it. That way you can use indices 1 through n directly. Next, go through each triple in lst one at a time. Unpack the triple into x0, y0, val0. Then hop over to A[x0] and append the pair (y0, val0). Also hop to A[y0] and append (x0, val0). At this point, A holds every connection twice, once in each direction.

Now you set up a small dictionary mp with three counters inside: 'bs_steps' at 0, 'dfs_calls' at 0, and 'max_cuts' at 0. These will track key statistics as you go.

Next, you need a helper check routine we’ll call can_do. You’ll pass it a candidate number val, and it will return True or False depending on whether you can satisfy a certain condition with that threshold. Inside can_do, start by creating a local counter named c and set it to 0. This c will count how many times you exceed the threshold in various spots.  

Then define a nested procedure called dfs that takes two inputs: u (the current node index) and p (the parent node index). Every time you enter dfs, add 1 to mp['dfs_calls']. Then create an empty list L. Now look at every pair in A[u] – call each pair (v0, val1). If v0 equals p, just skip it, because that would send you right back where you came from. Otherwise, call dfs(v0, u) recursively, take whatever number that call gives you back, and add val1. Call that sum up. If up is strictly greater than the threshold val, add 1 to c. If up is less than or equal to val, append up into L.

When you’ve tried all neighbors, check if L is empty. If it is, return 0 immediately. If it isn’t, sort L in ascending order. Then, as long as there are at least two items in L and the sum of the two largest items is over val, do this: remove the largest item from L (pop it off the end) and add 1 to c. Keep doing that until the sum of the two biggest numbers left is no longer above val or you have fewer than two items. Finally, return the last item in L (the biggest remaining value).

After you’ve defined dfs, call it with u = 1 and p = -1, and let its return value be x. If that x is greater than val, add 1 more to c. Now compare c to mp['max_cuts']; if c is larger, overwrite mp['max_cuts'] with c. In the end, can_do hands you back True if c is less than or equal to m, otherwise False.

With that helper in place, you perform a binary search to find the smallest val that makes can_do return True. So set a low bound x to 0 and a high bound y to twice the sum of all the val0 values in your original lst. Then start a loop: while x is less than y, do these steps:
1. Add 1 to mp['bs_steps'].  
2. Compute mid as the integer division of (x + y) by 2.  
3. Call can_do(mid).  
4. If it returns True, set y = mid. Otherwise, set x = mid + 1.  
Keep looping until x is no longer less than y. When that loop ends, x is your final answer. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things back. First is the integer x, which is the smallest threshold found by the binary search. Second is the mp dictionary, where 'bs_steps' tells you how many times you adjusted your binary search bounds, 'dfs_calls' tells you how many times you entered the dfs routine in total, and 'max_cuts' tells you the largest value of c you ever recorded in any single can_do call.

Next, go through each triple in lst one at a time. Unpack the triple into x0, y0, val0. Then hop over to A[x0] and append the pair (y0, val0). Also hop to A[y0] and append (x0, val0). At this point, A holds every connection twice, once in each direction.

Now you set up a small dictionary mp with three counters inside: 'bs_steps' at 0, 'dfs_calls' at 0, and 'max_cuts' at 0. These will track key statistics as you go.

Next, you need a helper check routine we’ll call can_do. You’ll pass it a candidate number val, and it will return True or False depending on whether you can satisfy a certain condition with that threshold. Inside can_do, start by creating a local counter named c and set it to 0. This c will count how many times you exceed the threshold in various spots.  

Then define a nested procedure called dfs that takes two inputs: u (the current node index) and p (the parent node index). Every time you enter dfs, add 1 to mp['dfs_calls']. Then create an empty list L. Now look at every pair in A[u] – call each pair (v0, val1). If v0 equals p, just skip it, because that would send you right back where you came from. Otherwise, call dfs(v0, u) recursively, take whatever number that call gives you back, and add val1. Call that sum up. If up is strictly greater than the threshold val, add 1 to c. If up is less than or equal to val, append up into L.

When you’ve tried all neighbors, check if L is empty. If it is, return 0 immediately. If it isn’t, sort L in ascending order. Then, as long as there are at least two items in L and the sum of the two largest items is over val, do this: remove the largest item from L (pop it off the end) and add 1 to c. Keep doing that until the sum of the two biggest numbers left is no longer above val or you have fewer than two items. Finally, return the last item in L (the biggest remaining value).

After you’ve defined dfs, call it with u = 1 and p = -1, and let its return value be x. If that x is greater than val, add 1 more to c. Now compare c to mp['max_cuts']; if c is larger, overwrite mp['max_cuts'] with c. In the end, can_do hands you back True if c is less than or equal to m, otherwise False.

With that helper in place, you perform a binary search to find the smallest val that makes can_do return True. So set a low bound x to 0 and a high bound y to twice the sum of all the val0 values in your original lst. Then start a loop: while x is less than y, do these steps:
1. Add 1 to mp['bs_steps'].  
2. Compute mid as the integer division of (x + y) by 2.  
3. Call can_do(mid).  
4. If it returns True, set y = mid. Otherwise, set x = mid + 1.  
Keep looping until x is no longer less than y. When that loop ends, x is your final answer. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things back. First is the integer x, which is the smallest threshold found by the binary search. Second is the mp dictionary, where 'bs_steps' tells you how many times you adjusted your binary search bounds, 'dfs_calls' tells you how many times you entered the dfs routine in total, and 'max_cuts' tells you the largest value of c you ever recorded in any single can_do call.

def f(n, A):
    import heapq
    from collections import Counter
    stats = {'pop_ops': 0, 'push_ops': 0, 'alt_selections': 0}
    mp = Counter(A)
    lst = [(-c, v) for v, c in mp.items()]
    heapq.heapify(lst)
    last = None
    res = 0
    while lst:
        stats['pop_ops'] += 1
        c1, v1 = heapq.heappop(lst)
        c1 = -c1
        if v1 != last:
            last = v1
            c1 -= 1
            if c1 > 0:
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
        else:
            if not lst:
                res += 1
                last = v1
                c1 -= 1
                if c1 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
            else:
                stats['alt_selections'] += 1
                stats['pop_ops'] += 1
                c2, v2 = heapq.heappop(lst)
                c2 = -c2
                last = v2
                c2 -= 1
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
                if c2 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c2, v2))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
    return res, stats

LOGICS: Start by creating a dictionary called stats with three entries: 'pop_ops' set to 0, 'push_ops' set to 0, and 'alt_selections' set to 0. Next, build a dictionary called mp by going through each item in A; for each value v, if it is not yet a key in mp then set mp[v] to 1, otherwise add 1 to mp[v]. After you have mp, make a list called lst by taking every (v, c) pair in mp and turning it into a tuple (-c, v). Once lst holds those tuples, call heapq.heapify(lst) to arrange it so you can pop the smallest first element. Then set last = None and res = 0. Now you go into a loop that runs while lst is not empty. In each cycle of the loop: first, add 1 to stats['pop_ops'], then pop out the top tuple from lst with heapq.heappop and call that (c1, v1). Immediately do c1 = -c1 to restore the positive count. Next, check if v1 is different from last. If it is different: set last = v1, subtract 1 from c1, and if c1 is now greater than 0, push (-c1, v1) back into lst with heapq.heappush and add 1 to stats['push_ops']. If v1 is the same as last, then check if lst is empty now. If lst is empty: add 1 to res, set last = v1, subtract 1 from c1, and if c1 > 0 push (-c1, v1) back and add 1 to stats['push_ops']. If lst is not empty: add 1 to stats['alt_selections'], then add another 1 to stats['pop_ops'] and pop the next tuple from lst calling it (c2, v2), then do c2 = -c2. Set last = v2, subtract 1 from c2, then push the original pair (-c1, v1) back into lst and add 1 to stats['push_ops'], and if c2 > 0 push (-c2, v2) back into lst and add 1 to stats['push_ops']. After handling those cases, go back to the top of the loop. Once lst is empty, you exit the loop and you are done. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you will have two results: res and the stats dictionary. The variable res is a count of how many times you ended up in a situation where v1 equaled last and there was no other item to pick, so you incremented res.     import heapq
    from collections import Counter
    stats = {'pop_ops': 0, 'push_ops': 0, 'alt_selections': 0}
    mp = Counter(A)
    lst = [(-c, v) for v, c in mp.items()]
    heapq.heapify(lst)
    last = None
    res = 0
    while lst:
        stats['pop_ops'] += 1
        c1, v1 = heapq.heappop(lst)
        c1 = -c1
        if v1 != last:
            last = v1
            c1 -= 1
            if c1 > 0:
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
        else:
            if not lst:
                res += 1
                last = v1
                c1 -= 1
                if c1 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
            else:
                stats['alt_selections'] += 1
                stats['pop_ops'] += 1
                c2, v2 = heapq.heappop(lst)

def f(n, A):
    import heapq
    from collections import Counter
    stats = {'pop_ops': 0, 'push_ops': 0, 'alt_selections': 0}
    mp = Counter(A)
    lst = [(-c, v) for v, c in mp.items()]
    heapq.heapify(lst)
    last = None
    res = 0
    while lst:
        stats['pop_ops'] += 1
        c1, v1 = heapq.heappop(lst)
        c1 = -c1
        if v1 != last:
            last = v1
            c1 -= 1
            if c1 > 0:
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
        else:
            if not lst:
                res += 1
                last = v1
                c1 -= 1
                if c1 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
            else:
                stats['alt_selections'] += 1
                stats['pop_ops'] += 1
                c2, v2 = heapq.heappop(lst)
                c2 = -c2
                last = v2
                c2 -= 1
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
                if c2 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c2, v2))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
    return res, stats

def f(n, A):
    import heapq
    from collections import Counter
    stats = {'pop_ops': 0, 'push_ops': 0, 'alt_selections': 0}
    mp = Counter(A)
    lst = [(-c, v) for v, c in mp.items()]
    heapq.heapify(lst)
    last = None
    res = 0
    while lst:
        stats['pop_ops'] += 1
        c1, v1 = heapq.heappop(lst)
        c1 = -c1
        if v1 != last:
            last = v1
            c1 -= 1
            if c1 > 0:
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
        else:
            if not lst:
                res += 1
                last = v1
                c1 -= 1
                if c1 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
            else:
                stats['alt_selections'] += 1
                stats['pop_ops'] += 1
                c2, v2 = heapq.heappop(lst)
                c2 = -c2
                last = v2
                c2 -= 1
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
                if c2 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c2, v2))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
    return res, stats

def f(n, A):
    import heapq
    from collections import Counter
    stats = {'pop_ops': 0, 'push_ops': 0, 'alt_selections': 0}
    mp = Counter(A)
    lst = [(-c, v) for v, c in mp.items()]
    heapq.heapify(lst)
    last = None
    res = 0
    while lst:
        stats['pop_ops'] += 1
        c1, v1 = heapq.heappop(lst)
        c1 = -c1
        if v1 != last:
            last = v1
            c1 -= 1
            if c1 > 0:
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
        else:
            if not lst:
                res += 1
                last = v1
                c1 -= 1
                if c1 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
            else:
                stats['alt_selections'] += 1
                stats['pop_ops'] += 1
                c2, v2 = heapq.heappop(lst)
                c2 = -c2
                last = v2
                c2 -= 1
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
                if c2 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c2, v2))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
    return res, stats

def f(n, A):
    import heapq
    from collections import Counter
    stats = {'pop_ops': 0, 'push_ops': 0, 'alt_selections': 0}
    mp = Counter(A)
    lst = [(-c, v) for v, c in mp.items()]
    heapq.heapify(lst)
    last = None
    res = 0
    while lst:
        stats['pop_ops'] += 1
        c1, v1 = heapq.heappop(lst)
        c1 = -c1
        if v1 != last:
            last = v1
            c1 -= 1
            if c1 > 0:
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
        else:
            if not lst:
                res += 1
                last = v1
                c1 -= 1
                if c1 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
            else:
                stats['alt_selections'] += 1
                stats['pop_ops'] += 1
                c2, v2 = heapq.heappop(lst)
                c2 = -c2
                last = v2
                c2 -= 1
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
                if c2 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c2, v2))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
    return res, stats

INPUTS: A is a list of numbers; B is a list of numbers; C is a list of numbers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is walk through these three lists and build up a running table of scores. First, sort A so the biggest number is first and the smallest is last. Do exactly the same thing with B, and then do it again with C. Next, note down two lengths: call the number of items in A “n” and the number of items in B “m.”

Now set up three counters called rg_ops, rb_ops, and gb_ops, and give each of them a starting value of zero. After that, draw a grid on your paper that has n+1 rows (label them 0 through n) and m+1 columns (label them 0 through m). Fill every cell in that grid with a zero; that whole thing is your dp_prev table.

Here comes the loop over C: take each value x in your sorted C, one at a time, in the order they appear. For each x, you’re going to make a brand-new grid of the same size (n+1 by m+1), fill every cell with zero, and call it dp_curr.

Now the way this works is you will visit every cell in dp_curr by going row by row and column by column. So start with i = 0, then j = 0, then j = 1, all the way up to j = m, then go back to i = 1 and repeat until you reach i = n and j = m. For each pair (i, j), do this:

1.  Set a local variable best to zero.  
2.  If i > 0 and j > 0, then add 1 to your rg_ops counter. Look at dp_curr at row i−1, column j−1, take that number and add A’s i-th item (that’s A[i−1]) times B’s j-th item (that’s B[j−1]); call the result v1. If v1 is bigger than best, then replace best with v1.  
3.  If i > 0, then add 1 to your rb_ops counter. Look at dp_prev at row i−1, column j, take that number and add A’s i-th item (A[i−1]) times x; call it v2. If v2 is bigger than best, replace best with v2.  
4.  If j > 0, then add 1 to your gb_ops counter. Look at dp_prev at row i, column j−1, take that and add B’s j-th item (B[j−1]) times x; call it v3. If v3 is bigger than best, replace best with v3.  
5.  Write best into dp_curr at row i, column j.

Once you’ve done all (i, j) in that dp_curr grid, copy dp_curr over so it becomes the new dp_prev. Then move on to the next x in C and repeat: draw a fresh dp_curr, fill zeros, loop i and j, compute best three ways, update counters, write best, then replace dp_prev.

When you finish the last value in C, dp_prev will be your final grid. The number sitting in row n, column m of that grid is your final output value, and your three counters—rg_ops, rb_ops, and gb_ops—have the totals of how many times you went into each of those three branches during the whole process. 

OUTPUTS: You will end up with two things. First, a single number taken from the final grid at position [n][m]—that’s your main result. Second, a dictionary of three counts: “rg_ops” tells you how many times you combined an A-item and a B-item; “rb_ops” tells you how many times you combined an A-item and the current C-item; and “gb_ops” tells you how many times you combined a B-item and the current C-item.

description:
INPUTS: A is a list of numbers; B is a list of numbers; C is a list of numbers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is walk through these three lists and build up a running table of scores. First, sort A so the biggest number is first and the smallest is last. Do exactly the same thing with B, and then do it again with C. Next, note down two lengths: call the number of items in A “n” and the number of items in B “m.”

Now set up three counters called rg_ops, rb_ops, and gb_ops, and give each of them a starting value of zero. After that, draw a grid on your paper that has n+1 rows (label them 0 through n) and m+1 columns (label them 0 through m). Fill every cell in that grid with a zero; that whole thing is your dp_prev table.

Here comes the loop over C: take each value x in your sorted C, one at a time, in the order they appear. For each x, you’re going to make a brand-new grid of the same size (n+1 by m+1), fill every cell with zero, and call it dp_curr.

Now the way this works is you will visit every cell in dp_curr by going row by row and column by column. So start with i = 0, then j = 0, then j = 1, all the way up to j = m, then go back to i = 1 and repeat until you reach i = n and j = m. For each pair (i, j), do this:

1.  Set a local variable best to zero.  
2.  If i > 0 and j > 0, then add 1 to your rg_ops counter. Look at dp_curr at row i−1, column j−1, take that number and add A’s i-th item (that’s A[i−1]) times B’s j-th item (that’s B[j−1]); call the result v1. If v1 is bigger than best, then replace best with v1.  
3.  If i > 0, then add 1 to your rb_ops counter. Look at dp_prev at row i−1, column j, take that number and add A’s i-th item (A[i−1]) times x; call it v2. If v2 is bigger than best, replace best with v2.  
4.  If j > 0, then add 1 to your gb_ops counter. Look at dp_prev at row i, column j−1, take that and add B’s j-th item (B[j−1]) times x; call it v3. If v3 is bigger than best, replace best with v3.  
5.  Write best into dp_curr at row i, column j.

Once you’ve done all (i, j) in that dp_curr grid, copy dp_curr over so it becomes the new dp_prev. Then move on to the next x in C and repeat: draw a fresh dp_curr, fill zeros, loop i and j, compute best three ways, update counters, write best, then replace dp_prev.

When you finish the last value in C, dp_prev will be your final grid. The number sitting in row n, column m of that grid is your final output value, and your three counters—rg_ops, rb_ops, and gb_ops—have the totals of how many times you went into each of those three branches during the whole process. 

OUTPUTS: You will end up with two things. First, a single number taken from the final grid at position [n][m]—that’s your main result. Second, a dictionary of three counts: “rg_ops” tells you how many times you combined an A-item and a B-item; “rb_ops” tells you how many times you combined an A-item and the current C-item; and “gb_ops” tells you how many times you combined a B-item and the current C-item.

INPUTS: A is a list of numbers; B is a list of numbers; C is a list of numbers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is walk through these three lists and build up a running table of scores. First, sort A so the biggest number is first and the smallest is last. Do exactly the same thing with B, and then do it again with C. Next, note down two lengths: call the number of items in A “n” and the number of items in B “m.”

Now set up three counters called rg_ops, rb_ops, and gb_ops, and give each of them a starting value of zero. After that, draw a grid on your paper that has n+1 rows (label them 0 through n) and m+1 columns (label them 0 through m). Fill every cell in that grid with a zero; that whole thing is your dp_prev table.

Here comes the loop over C: take each value x in your sorted C, one at a time, in the order they appear. For each x, you’re going to make a brand-new grid of the same size (n+1 by m+1), fill every cell with zero, and call it dp_curr.

Now the way this works is you will visit every cell in dp_curr by going row by row and column by column. So start with i = 0, then j = 0, then j = 1, all the way up to j = m, then go back to i = 1 and repeat until you reach i = n and j = m. For each pair (i, j), do this:

1.  Set a local variable best to zero.  
2.  If i > 0 and j > 0, then add 1 to your rg_ops counter. Look at dp_curr at row i−1, column j−1, take that number and add A’s i-th item (that’s A[i−1]) times B’s j-th item (that’s B[j−1]); call the result v1. If v1 is bigger than best, then replace best with v1.  
3.  If i > 0, then add 1 to your rb_ops counter. Look at dp_prev at row i−1, column j, take that number and add A’s i-th item (A[i−1]) times x; call it v2. If v2 is bigger than best, replace best with v2.  
4.  If j > 0, then add 1 to your gb_ops counter. Look at dp_prev at row i, column j−1, take that and add B’s j-th item (B[j−1]) times x; call it v3. If v3 is bigger than best, replace best with v3.  
5.  Write best into dp_curr at row i, column j.

Once you’ve done all (i, j) in that dp_curr grid, copy dp_curr over so it becomes the new dp_prev. Then move on to the next x in C and repeat: draw a fresh dp_curr, fill zeros, loop i and j, compute best three ways, update counters, write best, then replace dp_prev.

When you finish the last value in C, dp_prev will be your final grid. The number sitting in row n, column m of that grid is your final output value, and your three counters—rg_ops, rb_ops, and gb_ops—have the totals of how many times you went into each of those three branches during the whole process. 

OUTPUTS: You will end up with two things. First, a single number taken from the final grid at position [n][m]—that’s your main result. Second, a dictionary of three counts: “rg_ops” tells you how many times you combined an A-item and a B-item; “rb_ops” tells you how many times you combined an A-item and the current C-item; and “gb_ops” tells you how many times you combined a B-item and the current C-item.

1. Start by setting two counters:
   - m = 0   (this will count how many times you join things together)

   - If n is 0, then you have no items.  In that case your final value val is 0, and both counters m and y stay at 0.  You’re done.
   - If n is 1, then you have exactly one number in arr (that’s arr[0]).  To get val:
       a. Figure out min(k, 0):  if k is negative, min(k, 0) = k; otherwise it’s 0.
       b. Take arr[0], add that min(k, 0), then add k again.  That sum is your val.
     In this n=1 situation you still return m=0 and y=0.  And you stop right there.
   - If n is greater than 1, keep going.

3. Build a helper list L of length n–1.  Write down n–1 zeros to start.
   Now for each index i from 0 up through n–2:
     a. Compute a temporary number x = arr[i] – arr[i+1] + 1.
     b. If x is greater than 0, set L[i] = x; otherwise leave L[i] = 0.
   After you do that, L holds either positive gaps or zeros.

4. Make a bucket structure B of size (k + 2).  In practice you write down k+2 empty lists: B[0], B[1], …, B[k+1].
   Then for each position p from 0 to n–2:
     a. Look at L[p], add 1 to it, call that value x = L[p] + 1.
     b. If x is at least 1 and at most k, go to the list B[x] and append p.
   All the other buckets (B[0], and anything beyond B[k]) stay empty.

5. Set up your union–find structure.  You need two parallel lists of length n:
     A = [0, 1, 2, …, n–1]
     lst = [0, 1, 2, …, n–1]
   A will track parent pointers, and lst will track the smallest original index in each set.

6. Define your find operation.  To find the root of an index x (where x is between 0 and n–1):
     a. While A[x] is not equal to x, do:
          i.   Set A[x] = A[A[x]]   (this flattens the chain)
          ii.  Then set x = A[x]
     b. When you exit the loop, A[x] == x, so return x as the root.

7. Define your union operation on two neighbors u and v:
     a. Let ru = find(u) and rv = find(v).
     b. If ru and rv are the same, do nothing (they’re already joined).
     c. Otherwise:
          i.   Set A[rv] = ru   (attach the second root under the first)
          ii.  If lst[rv] < lst[ru], then set lst[ru] = lst[rv].
          iii. Increment m by 1 (you just made a merge).

8. Prepare a DP list dp1 of length n+1, filled with zeros at indexes 0 through n.

     b. Next, make a fresh list dp2 of length n+1, all zeros.
     c. Then for each i from 1 to n (inclusive), do these steps in order:
          i.   Compute root = find(i–1).  That gives you the representative for index i–1.
          ii.  Compute val = i – lst[root].
          iii. Compute x = dp1[i] + val.
          iv.  Compare dp2[i–1] and x.  If dp2[i–1] is larger, set dp2[i] = dp2[i–1]; otherwise set dp2[i] = x.
          v.   Add 1 to your counter y (that’s one DP step).
     d. After finishing i = 1..n, replace dp1 with dp2 so the next stroke uses the new values.

     a. Add up every number in your original list arr to get a sumArr.
     b. Take sumArr and add dp1[n] to it.  That total is your final val.

         – 'dp_steps': the final value of y (how many DP updates you made)

  • 'dp_steps' tells you how many individual DP calculation steps you performed (that’s counter y).

LOGICS: Okay, what you’re going to do is follow these steps exactly:

1. Start by setting two counters:
   - m = 0   (this will count how many times you join things together)
   - y = 0   (this will count how many little DP decisions you make)

2. Handle the tiny‐n case.  Look at n:
   - If n is 0, then you have no items.  In that case your final value val is 0, and both counters m and y stay at 0.  You’re done.
   - If n is 1, then you have exactly one number in arr (that’s arr[0]).  To get val:
       a. Figure out min(k, 0):  if k is negative, min(k, 0) = k; otherwise it’s 0.
       b. Take arr[0], add that min(k, 0), then add k again.  That sum is your val.
     In this n=1 situation you still return m=0 and y=0.  And you stop right there.
   - If n is greater than 1, keep going.

3. Build a helper list L of length n–1.  Write down n–1 zeros to start.
   Now for each index i from 0 up through n–2:
     a. Compute a temporary number x = arr[i] – arr[i+1] + 1.
     b. If x is greater than 0, set L[i] = x; otherwise leave L[i] = 0.
   After you do that, L holds either positive gaps or zeros.

4. Make a bucket structure B of size (k + 2).  In practice you write down k+2 empty lists: B[0], B[1], …, B[k+1].
   Then for each position p from 0 to n–2:
     a. Look at L[p], add 1 to it, call that value x = L[p] + 1.
     b. If x is at least 1 and at most k, go to the list B[x] and append p.
   All the other buckets (B[0], and anything beyond B[k]) stay empty.

5. Set up your union–find structure.  You need two parallel lists of length n:
     A = [0, 1, 2, …, n–1]
     lst = [0, 1, 2, …, n–1]
   A will track parent pointers, and lst will track the smallest original index in each set.

6. Define your find operation.  To find the root of an index x (where x is between 0 and n–1):
     a. While A[x] is not equal to x, do:
          i.   Set A[x] = A[A[x]]   (this flattens the chain)
          ii.  Then set x = A[x]
     b. When you exit the loop, A[x] == x, so return x as the root.

7. Define your union operation on two neighbors u and v:
     a. Let ru = find(u) and rv = find(v).
     b. If ru and rv are the same, do nothing (they’re already joined).
     c. Otherwise:
          i.   Set A[rv] = ru   (attach the second root under the first)
          ii.  If lst[rv] < lst[ru], then set lst[ru] = lst[rv].
          iii. Increment m by 1 (you just made a merge).

8. Prepare a DP list dp1 of length n+1, filled with zeros at indexes 0 through n.

9. Now you do your main loop for stroke from 1 up to k (inclusive).
   For each stroke:
     a. First, look at bucket B[stroke].  For each position p stored in that bucket, call union(p, p+1).  That may update A, lst, and bump up m.
     b. Next, make a fresh list dp2 of length n+1, all zeros.
     c. Then for each i from 1 to n (inclusive), do these steps in order:
          i.   Compute root = find(i–1).  That gives you the representative for index i–1.
          ii.  Compute val = i – lst[root].
          iii. Compute x = dp1[i] + val.
          iv.  Compare dp2[i–1] and x.  If dp2[i–1] is larger, set dp2[i] = dp2[i–1]; otherwise set dp2[i] = x.
          v.   Add 1 to your counter y (that’s one DP step).
     d. After finishing i = 1..n, replace dp1 with dp2 so the next stroke uses the new values.

10. After finishing all strokes from 1 to k, compute your final val.  To do that:
     a. Add up every number in your original list arr to get a sumArr.
     b. Take sumArr and add dp1[n] to it.  That total is your final val.

11. You’re done.  Return two things:
     • val  (the number you just computed in step 10)
     • A dictionary with two entries:
         – 'merges': the final value of m  (how many times you joined two sets)
         – 'dp_steps': the final value of y (how many DP updates you made)
 

OUTPUTS: You end up with a single number val, which is the sum of all elements in arr plus the DP adjustment dp1[n].  Alongside that you get a small dictionary of statistics:

  • 'merges' tells you how many times two items were joined in the union–find process (that’s counter m).
  • 'dp_steps' tells you how many individual DP calculation steps you performed (that’s counter y).

1. Start by setting two counters:

       b. Take arr[0], add that min(k, 0), then add k again.  That sum is your val.
     In this n=1 situation you still return m=0 and y=0.  And you stop right there.
   - If n is greater than 1, keep going.

3. Build a helper list L of length n–1.  Write down n–1 zeros to start.
   Now for each index i from 0 up through n–2:
     a. Compute a temporary number x = arr[i] – arr[i+1] + 1.
     b. If x is greater than 0, set L[i] = x; otherwise leave L[i] = 0.
   After you do that, L holds either positive gaps or zeros.

4. Make a bucket structure B of size (k + 2).  In practice you write down k+2 empty lists: B[0], B[1], …, B[k+1].
   Then for each position p from 0 to n–2:
     a. Look at L[p], add 1 to it, call that value x = L[p] + 1.
     b. If x is at least 1 and at most k, go to the list B[x] and append p.
   All the other buckets (B[0], and anything beyond B[k]) stay empty.

5. Set up your union–find structure.  You need two parallel lists of length n:

     lst = [0, 1, 2, …, n–1]
   A will track parent pointers, and lst will track the smallest original index in each set.

6. Define your find operation.  To find the root of an index x (where x is between 0 and n–1):
     a. While A[x] is not equal to x, do:
          i.   Set A[x] = A[A[x]]   (this flattens the chain)
          ii.  Then set x = A[x]
     b. When you exit the loop, A[x] == x, so return x as the root.

7. Define your union operation on two neighbors u and v:
     a. Let ru = find(u) and rv = find(v).

def f(n,k,A):
    MAXB=61
    B=[0]*MAXB
    for x in A:
        B[x]+=1
    total=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x
    if total<k:
        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1
                D(x+1,-1)
        c=curr//2
    return (ret, {"bit_updates": p, "bit_queries": q, "bit_searches": r})

Otherwise, keep going. At this point set size to MAXB (so size is 61) and build another array C of length size+1 (so 62 entries) all zeros. Also set three counters p, q, and r each to 0; these will track how many times you do different operations. Now you need to think of three helper routines, although you’ll actually execute them by hand in this order: D, E, and G. Here’s how each one works:  • D(idx, delta): first add 1 to p. Then, while idx is at most size, do this: add delta to C[idx], then figure out the lowbit of idx (that is, the largest power of two that divides idx) and add that lowbit to idx. Repeat until idx exceeds size.  • E(idx): first add 1 to q. Then set a local sum m to 0. While idx is greater than 0, add C[idx] to m, then subtract the lowbit of idx from idx. When idx reaches 0, return m.  • G(target): first add 1 to r. Then set pos to 0, and pick an initial bitMask by starting at 1 and doubling it until it becomes strictly greater than size. Now, while bitMask is at least 1, do: let nxt be pos + bitMask. If nxt is at most size and C[nxt] is less than target, then subtract C[nxt] from target and set pos = nxt. In any case, halve bitMask (drop any fraction). When that loop finishes, return pos + 1. With those in mind, you next load your counts from B into the C structure: for each x from 0 up to 60, if B[x] is positive call D(x+1, B[x]). That seeds your structure and advances p accordingly. Now set ret to 0 and c to 0. These two track how many splits you do and what carry you have as you move up. Then you loop x from 0 to 60 again. Inside that loop, first compute curr = B[x] + c. Then check whether the x-th bit of k is 1 by taking (k >> x) & 1. If that bit is 1, you need to consume one unit at this position. If curr is already positive, just subtract 1 from curr. If curr is zero or negative, you must borrow from a higher position: start by asking used = E(x+1) (that tells how many total units you have in positions 0 through x), then do pos = G(used + 1) to find the first position above that in your structure. Let y = pos - 1. Now you have a single unit sitting at y. You need to split it down to x one level at a time. So for each z from y down to x+1 (that means z = y, y-1, …, x+1), do: subtract 1 from B[z], call D(z+1, -1), then add 2 to B[z-1], call D(z, 2), and add 1 to ret. That effectively breaks one unit at level z into two at level z-1. After doing that loop you will have new counts at B[x], so recompute curr = B[x] + c, subtract 1 from curr to consume the one you needed, then do B[x] -= 1 and call D(x+1, -1). After handling that bit requirement (whether you had enough or borrowed and split), set c = floor(curr / 2) (that carries any leftover pairs up to the next x). Then continue to the next x. When x reaches 60 and you finish that loop, you stop. Finally return ret along with a dictionary showing how many times you ran each helper routine: p for D calls, q for E calls, and r for G calls.

def f(n,k,A):
    MAXB=61
    B=[0]*MAXB
    for x in A:
        B[x]+=1
    total=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x
    if total<k:
        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1
                D(x+1,-1)
        c=curr//2
    return (ret, {"bit_updates": p, "bit_queries": q, "bit_searches": r})

def f(n,k,A):
    MAXB=61
    B=[0]*MAXB
    for x in A:
        B[x]+=1
    total=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x
    if total<k:
        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1
                D(x+1,-1)
        c=curr//2
    return (ret, {"bit_updates": p, "bit_queries": q, "bit_searches": r})

def f(n,k,A):
    MAXB=61
    B=[0]*MAXB
    for x in A:
        B[x]+=1
    total=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x
    if total<k:
        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1

def f(n,k,A):

    for x in A:
        B[x]+=1

    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x
    if total<k:
        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1
                D(x+1,-1)
        c=curr//2
    return (ret, {"bit_updates": p, "bit_queries": q, "bit_searches": r})

def f(n,k,A):
    MAXB=61
    B=[0]*MAXB
    for x in A:
        B[x]+=1
    total=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x
    if total<k:
        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1
                D(x+1,-1)
        c=curr//2
    return (ret, {"bit_updates": p, "bit_queries": q, "bit_searches": r})

def f(n,k,A):
    MAXB=61
    B=[0]*MAXB
    for x in A:
        B[x]+=1
    total=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x
    if total<k:
        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1
                D(x+1,-1)
        c=curr//2
    return (ret, {"bit_updates": p, "bit_queries": q, "bit_searches": r})

def f(n,k,A):
    MAXB=61
    B=[0]*MAXB
    for x in A:
        B[x]+=1
    total=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x
    if total<k:
        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1
                D(x+1,-1)
        c=curr//2
    return (ret, {"bit_updates": p, "bit_queries": q, "bit_searches": r})

Now check: if x is zero (meaning s was empty), then you're done. Your final value is 0, and each of your three counters (which we'll call num_blocks, dp_states, and merge_checks) is also 0. If x is not zero, set up a grid called M with x rows and x columns. Fill every cell in M with the number 0 to start. Then for each position i from 0 up to x minus 1, go to cell M[i][i] on the main diagonal and set it to 1. After that, create two counters y and z and initialize them both to 0. You'll use y to count how many dp states you process, and z to count how many times you check for a possible merge. Now build a mapping called mp: for each index idx from 0 to x minus 1, look at the character ch at lst[idx]. In mp you keep a list of indices for each character. So if ch isn't already a key in mp, start an empty list there; then add idx to the list for ch. Once mp is done, you're ready for the main loops. You'll consider every interval length from 2 up to x. So start a loop where length goes from 2 to x inclusive. Inside that, start another loop where i goes from 0 up to x minus length, inclusive. Compute j as i plus length minus 1. What you do now is set M[i][j] to M[i+1][j] plus 1. Then add 1 to y because you just computed a new dp state. After that, you want to see if you can do better by merging blocks that match lst[i]. So look up the list mp[lst[i]] and go through each k in that list in order. Before each check, add 1 to z. Then as you examine k, if k is less than or equal to i, skip ahead to the next k. If k is greater than j, break out of this inner k loop since everything beyond j is irrelevant. Otherwise, you compute a temporary value called val: if k equals i plus 1, set val to M[k][j]; otherwise set val to M[i+1][k-1] plus M[k][j]. Now compare val to the current M[i][j]. If val is smaller, update M[i][j] to val. That finishes your k loop. Once you've done that for all k, you're done with this pair i,j and move on. Keep going until all intervals have been processed. At that point, the number in the cell M[0][x-1] is your final result.

INPUTS: You have a single input called arr, which is just a list of positive whole numbers.  There are no other inputs or settings. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is walk through arr step by step and keep track of three little counters along the way.  Here’s how:

1.  Start by figuring out how many items are in arr.  Call that n.  Then create three counters named c1, c2, and c3, and set each one to zero.  These will record your "sieve operations," "factor extractions," and "dp updates" respectively.

2.  Right after that, check if n is 0 or 1.  If it is, you don’t need to do any heavy lifting.  Just stop here and you’ll end up returning 0 plus a dictionary showing c1 = 0, c2 = 0, c3 = 0.

3.  If n is bigger than 1, the next thing is to find the largest number in arr; call it m.  Now build an array called spf of length m + 1 (so its indexes go from 0 up to m), and fill every position with 0.  Think of spf[i] as a place where you’ll store the first prime-like factor you discover for i.

4.  Next you run a loop where i goes from 2 all the way up to m.  For each i:
   - Check spf[i].  If it’s already nonzero, skip it—someone already marked it.
   - If it’s zero, that means i hasn’t been marked yet.  So now start another loop with j = i, then j = i + i, then j = i + 2·i, and so on, as long as j ≤ m.
     * For each of those j values, look at spf[j].  If spf[j] is still zero, set spf[j] = i and add 1 to c1.  If it’s nonzero, leave it alone.  This inner stepping marks every multiple of i exactly once at the moment you first see it.

5.  By the time both loops finish, c1 holds your total "sieve operations."

6.  Now you’re ready to process each number in arr one at a time.  Create an empty map called mp (it starts with no entries) and also set a variable res = 0.

7.  For each item x in arr:
   a. Copy x into a work variable y.  Also make a fresh empty list called L.
   b. While y is bigger than 1:
      – Look up p = spf[y].  That p is your next factor.  Append p onto L, and add 1 to c2 (that’s one more "factor extraction").
      – Now reduce y by dividing out p as many times as you can: while y % p == 0, do y = y // p.  When that inner division loop finishes, go back to the outer while and see if y is still above 1.
   c. At this point L holds a sequence of prime-like factors (with repeats).  Turn L into a set—call it st—so you have each distinct factor just once.
   d. Now figure out where to place x in your hidden sequence by looking at mp.  Set a temporary best = 0, then for each factor p in st:
      – Check mp[p].  If there’s no entry, pretend it’s 0.  If mp[p] is bigger than best, copy mp[p] into best.
   e. Once you’ve scanned all p in st, define dp = best + 1.  If dp is larger than your running res, then update res = dp.
   f. Finally, you update mp for every p in st: if dp is bigger than the current mp[p] (or 0 if none), set mp[p] = dp and add 1 to c3 (that’s one more "dp update").
   g. Move on to the next x in arr and repeat.

8.  When you’ve handled every single x in arr, you’re done.  The number res represents the length of the longest chain you built; the value you actually return is n – res.  Meanwhile c1, c2, c3 hold the counts you collected along the way.
 

OUTPUTS: You come away with two things:

1.  A single number equal to n minus res.  That’s the first part of what you return.
2.  A dictionary with three entries:
   – "sieve_ops": the final value of c1 (how many times you set a new spf entry),
   – "factor_extractions": the final value of c2 (how many times you pulled out a factor p),
   – "dp_updates": the final value of c3 (how many times you updated mp[p]).

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is set up your workspace with a few counters and an empty list. Start by making a counter called div_ops and set it to zero, another called dp_updates set to zero, and one more called pair_evals set to zero. Then create an empty list called lst.

Next, you need to go through each item in your list A one by one. For each item, which we’ll call val, you’ll figure out two numbers: x and y.

 1. To get x: start by copying val into a temporary variable (let’s call it temp) and set x to zero. Then, while temp is divisible by 2, divide temp by 2 and add 1 to x. Keep doing that until temp is odd. If at any point x becomes greater than m, set x to m and stop dividing by 2 immediately. When you finish, x holds the number of times you divided by 2 (but never more than m).

 2. To get y: start y at zero and copy val into another variable named val2. While val2 is divisible by 5, divide val2 by 5, add 1 to y, and also add 1 to your counter div_ops. Keep going until val2 is no longer divisible by 5 or until y exceeds m. If y goes above m, set y to m and break out of this loop. That way you count every division you actually performed, up to m.

After you’ve determined both x and y for this val, append the pair (x,y) to your list lst. Repeat this process for every element in A—by the end you’ll have lst filled with one (x,y) pair for each original number.

Now you’ll build a two-dimensional tally table M with m+1 rows and m+1 columns, all initialized to zero. You can imagine a grid labeled from row 0 to row m and column 0 to column m, each cell starting at zero. Then go through your list lst again: for each pair (x,y), go to row x, column y in M and add 1 to whatever number is already there. That builds up counts of how many times each combination happened.

Once M is ready, build another table called grid that has one extra row and one extra column—that is, (m+2) by (m+2)—and fill it all with zeros too.

Now comes a filling trick: you’ll traverse grid from bottom-right back to top-left. Concretely, let i go from m down to 0, and inside that let j go from m down to 0. At each cell (i,j), calculate a value by taking M[i][j], adding grid[i+1][j], adding grid[i][j+1], then subtracting grid[i+1][j+1]. Write that result into grid[i][j], and every time you do that add 1 to dp_updates. When you finish all i and j in that reverse order, grid[i][j] tells you how many entries in M lie in the rectangle from (i,j) down to (m,m).

At this point it’s time to compute the final sum. Set a running total res to zero. Then loop i from 0 up to m, and inside that loop j from 0 up to m. For each (i,j) pair:

 - Add 1 to pair_evals.
 - Look at cnt = M[i][j]. If cnt is zero, skip to the next j (nothing to add).
 - Otherwise, compute ri = m - i; if m - i is negative, set ri to 0. Compute rj = m - j; if that is negative, set rj to 0.

 - Multiply cnt by total_ge and add that to res.
 - Then, if i ≥ ri and j ≥ rj, subtract cnt from res to correct for counting self-pairs twice.

After both loops finish, you’ve counted each pair twice, so divide your running total res by 2. That final quotient is your primary output number.

INPUTS: You’re working with three things: an integer n, an integer m, and a list A of integers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is set up your workspace with a few counters and an empty list. Start by making a counter called div_ops and set it to zero, another called dp_updates set to zero, and one more called pair_evals set to zero. Then create an empty list called lst.

Next, you need to go through each item in your list A one by one. For each item, which we’ll call val, you’ll figure out two numbers: x and y.

 1. To get x: start by copying val into a temporary variable (let’s call it temp) and set x to zero. Then, while temp is divisible by 2, divide temp by 2 and add 1 to x. Keep doing that until temp is odd. If at any point x becomes greater than m, set x to m and stop dividing by 2 immediately. When you finish, x holds the number of times you divided by 2 (but never more than m).

 2. To get y: start y at zero and copy val into another variable named val2. While val2 is divisible by 5, divide val2 by 5, add 1 to y, and also add 1 to your counter div_ops. Keep going until val2 is no longer divisible by 5 or until y exceeds m. If y goes above m, set y to m and break out of this loop. That way you count every division you actually performed, up to m.

After you’ve determined both x and y for this val, append the pair (x,y) to your list lst. Repeat this process for every element in A—by the end you’ll have lst filled with one (x,y) pair for each original number.

Now you’ll build a two-dimensional tally table M with m+1 rows and m+1 columns, all initialized to zero. You can imagine a grid labeled from row 0 to row m and column 0 to column m, each cell starting at zero. Then go through your list lst again: for each pair (x,y), go to row x, column y in M and add 1 to whatever number is already there. That builds up counts of how many times each combination happened.

Once M is ready, build another table called grid that has one extra row and one extra column—that is, (m+2) by (m+2)—and fill it all with zeros too.

Now comes a filling trick: you’ll traverse grid from bottom-right back to top-left. Concretely, let i go from m down to 0, and inside that let j go from m down to 0. At each cell (i,j), calculate a value by taking M[i][j], adding grid[i+1][j], adding grid[i][j+1], then subtracting grid[i+1][j+1]. Write that result into grid[i][j], and every time you do that add 1 to dp_updates. When you finish all i and j in that reverse order, grid[i][j] tells you how many entries in M lie in the rectangle from (i,j) down to (m,m).

At this point it’s time to compute the final sum. Set a running total res to zero. Then loop i from 0 up to m, and inside that loop j from 0 up to m. For each (i,j) pair:

 - Add 1 to pair_evals.
 - Look at cnt = M[i][j]. If cnt is zero, skip to the next j (nothing to add).
 - Otherwise, compute ri = m - i; if m - i is negative, set ri to 0. Compute rj = m - j; if that is negative, set rj to 0.
 - Look up total_ge = grid[ri][rj]. That number tells you how many (x,y) pairs in M meet or exceed (i,j).
 - Multiply cnt by total_ge and add that to res.
 - Then, if i ≥ ri and j ≥ rj, subtract cnt from res to correct for counting self-pairs twice.

After both loops finish, you’ve counted each pair twice, so divide your running total res by 2. That final quotient is your primary output number.

At the very end, you’ll return two things: first that halved number, and second a small dictionary containing your three counters—div_ops, dp_updates, and pair_evals—so you know how many divisions by 5 you did, how many grid updates you performed, and how many (i,j) pairs you considered in the last step. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with a pair: 1) an integer which is the final summed result divided by two, and 2) a statistics dictionary with three entries: 'div_ops' is the total count of times you divided by 5, 'dp_updates' is the number of times you filled a cell in the reverse-order grid step, and 'pair_evals' is how many (i,j) positions you evaluated in the final nested loops.

INPUTS: You’re working with three things: an integer n, an integer m, and a list A of integers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is set up your workspace with a few counters and an empty list. Start by making a counter called div_ops and set it to zero, another called dp_updates set to zero, and one more called pair_evals set to zero. Then create an empty list called lst.

Next, you need to go through each item in your list A one by one. For each item, which we’ll call val, you’ll figure out two numbers: x and y.

 1. To get x: start by copying val into a temporary variable (let’s call it temp) and set x to zero. Then, while temp is divisible by 2, divide temp by 2 and add 1 to x. Keep doing that until temp is odd. If at any point x becomes greater than m, set x to m and stop dividing by 2 immediately. When you finish, x holds the number of times you divided by 2 (but never more than m).

 2. To get y: start y at zero and copy val into another variable named val2. While val2 is divisible by 5, divide val2 by 5, add 1 to y, and also add 1 to your counter div_ops. Keep going until val2 is no longer divisible by 5 or until y exceeds m. If y goes above m, set y to m and break out of this loop. That way you count every division you actually performed, up to m.

After you’ve determined both x and y for this val, append the pair (x,y) to your list lst. Repeat this process for every element in A—by the end you’ll have lst filled with one (x,y) pair for each original number.

Now you’ll build a two-dimensional tally table M with m+1 rows and m+1 columns, all initialized to zero. You can imagine a grid labeled from row 0 to row m and column 0 to column m, each cell starting at zero. Then go through your list lst again: for each pair (x,y), go to row x, column y in M and add 1 to whatever number is already there. That builds up counts of how many times each combination happened.

Once M is ready, build another table called grid that has one extra row and one extra column—that is, (m+2) by (m+2)—and fill it all with zeros too.

Now comes a filling trick: you’ll traverse grid from bottom-right back to top-left. Concretely, let i go from m down to 0, and inside that let j go from m down to 0. At each cell (i,j), calculate a value by taking M[i][j], adding grid[i+1][j], adding grid[i][j+1], then subtracting grid[i+1][j+1]. Write that result into grid[i][j], and every time you do that add 1 to dp_updates. When you finish all i and j in that reverse order, grid[i][j] tells you how many entries in M lie in the rectangle from (i,j) down to (m,m).

At this point it’s time to compute the final sum. Set a running total res to zero. Then loop i from 0 up to m, and inside that loop j from 0 up to m. For each (i,j) pair:

 - Add 1 to pair_evals.
 - Look at cnt = M[i][j]. If cnt is zero, skip to the next j (nothing to add).
 - Otherwise, compute ri = m - i; if m - i is negative, set ri to 0. Compute rj = m - j; if that is negative, set rj to 0.
 - Look up total_ge = grid[ri][rj]. That number tells you how many (x,y) pairs in M meet or exceed (i,j).
 - Multiply cnt by total_ge and add that to res.
 - Then, if i ≥ ri and j ≥ rj, subtract cnt from res to correct for counting self-pairs twice.

After both loops finish, you’ve counted each pair twice, so divide your running total res by 2. That final quotient is your primary output number.

At the very end, you’ll return two things: first that halved number, and second a small dictionary containing your three counters—div_ops, dp_updates, and pair_evals—so you know how many divisions by 5 you did, how many grid updates you performed, and how many (i,j) pairs you considered in the last step. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with a pair: 1) an integer which is the final summed result divided by two, and 2) a statistics dictionary with three entries: 'div_ops' is the total count of times you divided by 5, 'dp_updates' is the number of times you filled a cell in the reverse-order grid step, and 'pair_evals' is how many (i,j) positions you evaluated in the final nested loops.

 2. To get y: start y at zero and copy val into another variable named val2. While val2 is divisible by 5, divide val2 by 5, add 1 to y, and also add 1 to your counter div_ops. Keep going until val2 is no longer divisible by 5 or until y exceeds m. If y goes above m, set y to m and break out of this loop. That way you count every division you actually performed, up to m.

After you’ve determined both x and y for this val, append the pair (x,y) to your list lst. Repeat this process for every element in A—by the end you’ll have lst filled with one (x,y) pair for each original number.

Now you’ll build a two-dimensional tally table M with m+1 rows and m+1 columns, all initialized to zero. You can imagine a grid labeled from row 0 to row m and column 0 to column m, each cell starting at zero. Then go through your list lst again: for each pair (x,y), go to row x, column y in M and add 1 to whatever number is already there. That builds up counts of how many times each combination happened.

Once M is ready, build another table called grid that has one extra row and one extra column—that is, (m+2) by (m+2)—and fill it all with zeros too.

Now comes a filling trick: you’ll traverse grid from bottom-right back to top-left. Concretely, let i go from m down to 0, and inside that let j go from m down to 0. At each cell (i,j), calculate a value by taking M[i][j], adding grid[i+1][j], adding grid[i][j+1], then subtracting grid[i+1][j+1]. Write that result into grid[i][j], and every time you do that add 1 to dp_updates. When you finish all i and j in that reverse order, grid[i][j] tells you how many entries in M lie in the rectangle from (i,j) down to (m,m).

INPUTS: You’re working with three things: an integer n, an integer m, and a list A of integers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is set up your workspace with a few counters and an empty list. Start by making a counter called div_ops and set it to zero, another called dp_updates set to zero, and one more called pair_evals set to zero. Then create an empty list called lst.

Next, you need to go through each item in your list A one by one. For each item, which we’ll call val, you’ll figure out two numbers: x and y.

 1. To get x: start by copying val into a temporary variable (let’s call it temp) and set x to zero. Then, while temp is divisible by 2, divide temp by 2 and add 1 to x. Keep doing that until temp is odd. If at any point x becomes greater than m, set x to m and stop dividing by 2 immediately. When you finish, x holds the number of times you divided by 2 (but never more than m).

 2. To get y: start y at zero and copy val into another variable named val2. While val2 is divisible by 5, divide val2 by 5, add 1 to y, and also add 1 to your counter div_ops. Keep going until val2 is no longer divisible by 5 or until y exceeds m. If y goes above m, set y to m and break out of this loop. That way you count every division you actually performed, up to m.

After you’ve determined both x and y for this val, append the pair (x,y) to your list lst. Repeat this process for every element in A—by the end you’ll have lst filled with one (x,y) pair for each original number.

Now you’ll build a two-dimensional tally table M with m+1 rows and m+1 columns, all initialized to zero. You can imagine a grid labeled from row 0 to row m and column 0 to column m, each cell starting at zero. Then go through your list lst again: for each pair (x,y), go to row x, column y in M and add 1 to whatever number is already there. That builds up counts of how many times each combination happened.

Once M is ready, build another table called grid that has one extra row and one extra column—that is, (m+2) by (m+2)—and fill it all with zeros too.

Now comes a filling trick: you’ll traverse grid from bottom-right back to top-left. Concretely, let i go from m down to 0, and inside that let j go from m down to 0. At each cell (i,j), calculate a value by taking M[i][j], adding grid[i+1][j], adding grid[i][j+1], then subtracting grid[i+1][j+1]. Write that result into grid[i][j], and every time you do that add 1 to dp_updates. When you finish all i and j in that reverse order, grid[i][j] tells you how many entries in M lie in the rectangle from (i,j) down to (m,m).

At this point it’s time to compute the final sum. Set a running total res to zero. Then loop i from 0 up to m, and inside that loop j from 0 up to m. For each (i,j) pair:

 - Add 1 to pair_evals.
 - Look at cnt = M[i][j]. If cnt is zero, skip to the next j (nothing to add).
 - Otherwise, compute ri = m - i; if m - i is negative, set ri to 0. Compute rj = m - j; if that is negative, set rj to 0.
 - Look up total_ge = grid[ri][rj]. That number tells you how many (x,y) pairs in M meet or exceed (i,j).
 - Multiply cnt by total_ge and add that to res.
 - Then, if i ≥ ri and j ≥ rj, subtract cnt from res to correct for counting self-pairs twice.

After both loops finish, you’ve counted each pair twice, so divide your running total res by 2. That final quotient is your primary output number.

At the very end, you’ll return two things: first that halved number, and second a small dictionary containing your three counters—div_ops, dp_updates, and pair_evals—so you know how many divisions by 5 you did, how many grid updates you performed, and how many (i,j) pairs you considered in the last step. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with a pair: 1) an integer which is the final summed result divided by two, and 2) a statistics dictionary with three entries: 'div_ops' is the total count of times you divided by 5, 'dp_updates' is the number of times you filled a cell in the reverse-order grid step, and 'pair_evals' is how many (i,j) positions you evaluated in the final nested loops.

INPUTS: You’re working with three things: an integer n, an integer m, and a list A of integers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is set up your workspace with a few counters and an empty list. Start by making a counter called div_ops and set it to zero, another called dp_updates set to zero, and one more called pair_evals set to zero. Then create an empty list called lst.

Next, you need to go through each item in your list A one by one. For each item, which we’ll call val, you’ll figure out two numbers: x and y.

 1. To get x: start by copying val into a temporary variable (let’s call it temp) and set x to zero. Then, while temp is divisible by 2, divide temp by 2 and add 1 to x. Keep doing that until temp is odd. If at any point x becomes greater than m, set x to m and stop dividing by 2 immediately. When you finish, x holds the number of times you divided by 2 (but never more than m).

 2. To get y: start y at zero and copy val into another variable named val2. While val2 is divisible by 5, divide val2 by 5, add 1 to y, and also add 1 to your counter div_ops. Keep going until val2 is no longer divisible by 5 or until y exceeds m. If y goes above m, set y to m and break out of this loop. That way you count every division you actually performed, up to m.

After you’ve determined both x and y for this val, append the pair (x,y) to your list lst. Repeat this process for every element in A—by the end you’ll have lst filled with one (x,y) pair for each original number.

Now you’ll build a two-dimensional tally table M with m+1 rows and m+1 columns, all initialized to zero. You can imagine a grid labeled from row 0 to row m and column 0 to column m, each cell starting at zero. def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    build(1, 1, n)
    res = []
    for t, i, j in B:
        if t == 1:
            update(1, 1, n, i, j)
        elif t == 2:
            _, _, _, ans = query(1, 1, n, i, j)
            res.append(ans)
    stats = {"build_calls": cnt_build, "query_calls": cnt_query, "update_calls": cnt_update}
    return res, stats

def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    build(1, 1, n)
    res = []
    for t, i, j in B:
        if t == 1:
            update(1, 1, n, i, j)
        elif t == 2:
            _, _, _, ans = query(1, 1, n, i, j)
            res.append(ans)
    stats = {"build_calls": cnt_build, "query_calls": cnt_query, "update_calls": cnt_update}
    return res, stats
