def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    build(1, 1, n)
    res = []
    for t, i, j in B:
        if t == 1:
            update(1, 1, n, i, j)
        elif t == 2:
            _, _, _, ans = query(1, 1, n, i, j)
            res.append(ans)
    stats = {"build_calls": cnt_build, "query_calls": cnt_query, "update_calls": cnt_update}
    return res, stats

def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    build(1, 1, n)
    res = []
    for t, i, j in B:
        if t == 1:
            update(1, 1, n, i, j)
        elif t == 2:
            _, _, _, ans = query(1, 1, n, i, j)
            res.append(ans)
    stats = {"build_calls": cnt_build, "query_calls": cnt_query, "update_calls": cnt_update}
    return res, stats

def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    build(1, 1, n)
    res = []
    for t, i, j in B:
        if t == 1:
            update(1, 1, n, i, j)
        elif t == 2:
            _, _, _, ans = query(1, 1, n, i, j)
            res.append(ans)
    stats = {"build_calls": cnt_build, "query_calls": cnt_query, "update_calls": cnt_update}
    return res, stats

LOGICS: Start by creating four lists of length four times n, each filled with zeros and call them tree_s, tree_p, tree_su, and tree_m. Also make three counters named cnt_build, cnt_query, and cnt_update and set them all to zero. First you run a build procedure on the entire range from l equal to 1 to r equal to n using a pointer p equal to 1. Each time you enter build you add 1 to cnt_build. Inside build you check if l and r are the same. If they are, you’re at a leaf: grab the value from A at index (l minus one), call it v, and store v into tree_s at p, tree_p at p, tree_su at p, and tree_m at p, then return. If l is not r, compute the midpoint m as floor((l+r)/2), set lc to p times 2 and rc to lc plus 1, then call build on the left child (lc, l, m) and on the right child (rc, m+1, r). When both return, let Ls=tree_s[lc] and Rs=tree_s[rc], then set tree_s[p]=Ls+Rs; set tree_p[p] to the larger of tree_p[lc] and (Ls+tree_p[rc]); set tree_su[p] to the larger of tree_su[rc] and (Rs+tree_su[lc]); to set tree_m[p], first compare tree_m[lc] and tree_m[rc] choose the larger as t1, then choose the larger of t1 and (tree_su[lc]+tree_p[rc]). Return from build. Once that initial sweep is done, create an empty list named res. Now go through each operation triple in B in order: let t be the first number, i the second, j the third. If t equals 1, call an update routine with p=1, l=1, r=n, pos=i, val=j. Inside update add 1 to cnt_update, check if l equals r; if so, overwrite tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p] with j and return; otherwise compute m, lc, rc as before, decide if pos≤m then recurse left else recurse right, then after that recursion finishes recombine tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p] exactly as you did in build, and return. If t equals 2, call a query routine with p=1, l=1, r=n, i, j; inside query add 1 to cnt_query, then check if the segment [l,r] is fully inside [i,j] (i≤l and r≤j) and if so immediately return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]. If not, compute m, lc, rc; if j≤m recurse left and return; if i>m recurse right and return; otherwise recurse both: get Ls,Lp,Lsu,Lmx from the left call and Rs,Rp,Rsu,Rmx from the right call, then combine them by setting tot=Ls+Rs, pre=max(Lp, Ls+Rp), suf=max(Rsu, Rs+Lsu), t1=max(Lmx, Rmx), mx=max(t1, Lsu+Rp), and return tot, pre, suf, mx. Back in the main flow for a query, take the fourth returned number, call it ans, and append ans to res. Continue until you process every triple in B. At that point cnt_build tells you how many times you ran build, cnt_query how many times you ran query, and cnt_update how many times you ran update. You then package those three counters into a stats map under keys build_calls, query_calls, and update_calls, and return both res and stats. 

OUTPUTS: You will end up with res, a list of numbers giving each result for the t equals 2 operations in B in order, and a stats map with three entries: build_calls (how many times build ran), query_calls (how many times query ran), and update_calls (how many times update ran).

def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    build(1, 1, n)
    res = []
    for t, i, j in B:
        if t == 1:
            update(1, 1, n, i, j)
        elif t == 2:
            _, _, _, ans = query(1, 1, n, i, j)
            res.append(ans)
    stats = {"build_calls": cnt_build, "query_calls": cnt_query, "update_calls": cnt_update}
    return res, stats

description:
INPUTS: You have three things to start with:

1. n: a single integer. It tells you how many numbered slots you have, from 1 up to n.

2. A: a list of pairs (x, y). Each pair contains two numbers between 1 and n. Think of each pair as a connection from x down to y.

3. B: another list of pairs (x, y). These are the queries you'll process later. Each query involves two numbers between 1 and n, and you’ll keep track of an index for each one. 

LOGICS: Alright, let’s walk through exactly what you’d do by hand. Imagine you’ve got a big sheet of paper and you’re jotting down lists and boxes for each variable.

1. Build L (a list of lists):
   - Write down n + 1 blank lines labeled 0, 1, 2, …, n. You’ll ignore line 0 in practice, but it’s there for convenience.
   - Now go through each pair (x, y) in your list A. For each one, find line x in L and write y on that line. So if A has (3, 5), you go to L[3] and append 5 at the end of whatever’s already there.

2. Build st (a boolean marker list):
   - Make another list of length n+1, fill every entry with the word FALSE.
   - Again go through each pair (x, y) in A. This time, for each y you see, go to st[y] and change it to TRUE. That way you mark every y that ever appears as a second element.

3. Find the root:
   - Look from index 1 up to n in your st list. The very first index i you hit that’s still FALSE is called root. Write down that number as root.

4. Set up your union-find scaffolding:
   - parent: write down numbers 0 through n again. Then put a tick next to each so parent[i] = i for every i from 0 to n.
   - ancestor: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with 0.
   - vis: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with FALSE.

5. Build d (a dictionary of adjacency for queries):
   - For each i from 1 to n, start with an empty list d[i].
   - Now go through each query pair in B in order, keeping track of its position idx starting at 0.
     * Suppose the idx-th pair is (x, y). Go to d[x] and append the tuple (y, idx). Then go to d[y] and append the tuple (x, idx).

6. Prepare result and stats containers:
   - res: make a list of length equal to the number of queries in B, and fill it with zeros.
   - stats: make a little table or box with three counters, all starting at 0:
        find_calls = 0
        union_calls = 0
        answered_queries = 0

7. Define your find operation (you won’t really write code, but you’ll follow this logic every time):
   - To "find" u:
     a. Add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     b. Look at parent[u]. If parent[u] is exactly u, you’re done and you return u.
     c. If parent[u] is some other number, say w, then you go and "find(w)" by repeating these steps, and when you get an answer r, you overwrite parent[u] with r. Then you return r.

8. Define your union operation:
   - To "union" u and v:
     a. Add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     b. Find the ultimate parent of v by using your find steps. Call that Pv.
     c. Find the ultimate parent of u by using your find steps. Call that Pu.
     d. Set parent[ Pv ] = Pu. (You attach v’s root under u’s root.)

9. Now do the depth-first sweep starting from root:
   - You’ll write a little note that you’re calling dfs(root).
   - In dfs(u):
     a. First, find the current representative of u by doing find(u). Then go to ancestor[ that representative ] and write down u. In other words, ancestor[ find(u) ] = u.
     b. Next, look at your list L[u]. For each child v in that list, you do:
        i. Call dfs(v) — you repeat all these steps from (a) down for v.
       ii. After dfs(v) finishes, do union(u, v). That merges v’s set into u’s set.
      iii. Right after that union, do ancestor[ find(u) ] = u again, so that the representative for the merged set points to u.
     c. When you’ve done all of u’s children, set vis[u] = TRUE.
     d. Now look at the list d[u]. For every tuple (v, idx) in that list:
        i. Check vis[v]. If vis[v] is still FALSE, skip it and move on.
       ii. If vis[v] is TRUE, then you know you can answer that query now.
           - Add 1 to answered_queries.
           - Find the representative of v by doing find(v), let’s call it Rv.
           - Look up ancestor[Rv], and write that value into res at position idx.
   - That completes dfs(u). When you finish the last line of dfs(root), you’re done with all nodes.

10. Once dfs(root) is fully done, you stop. You haven’t missed any child or any query, because at the moment both vis[u] and vis[v] are TRUE you answered every relevant query exactly once. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things:

1. res – a list of the same length as B. Each entry in res corresponds to one query pair from B (in the same order). The number you see at position idx is exactly the value you wrote into res[idx] during the dfs step when that query was answered.

2. stats – a small dictionary with three numbers:
   • "find_calls": how many times you ran the find operation altogether.  
   • "union_calls": how many times you ran the union operation.  
   • "answered_queries": how many queries from B you actually answered (each time you wrote into res you bumped this by 1).

INPUTS: You have three things to start with:

1. n: a single integer. It tells you how many numbered slots you have, from 1 up to n.

2. A: a list of pairs (x, y). Each pair contains two numbers between 1 and n. Think of each pair as a connection from x down to y.

3. B: another list of pairs (x, y). These are the queries you'll process later. Each query involves two numbers between 1 and n, and you’ll keep track of an index for each one. 

LOGICS: Alright, let’s walk through exactly what you’d do by hand. Imagine you’ve got a big sheet of paper and you’re jotting down lists and boxes for each variable.

1. Build L (a list of lists):
   - Write down n + 1 blank lines labeled 0, 1, 2, …, n. You’ll ignore line 0 in practice, but it’s there for convenience.
   - Now go through each pair (x, y) in your list A. For each one, find line x in L and write y on that line. So if A has (3, 5), you go to L[3] and append 5 at the end of whatever’s already there.

2. Build st (a boolean marker list):
   - Make another list of length n+1, fill every entry with the word FALSE.
   - Again go through each pair (x, y) in A. This time, for each y you see, go to st[y] and change it to TRUE. That way you mark every y that ever appears as a second element.

3. Find the root:
   - Look from index 1 up to n in your st list. The very first index i you hit that’s still FALSE is called root. Write down that number as root.

4. Set up your union-find scaffolding:
   - parent: write down numbers 0 through n again. Then put a tick next to each so parent[i] = i for every i from 0 to n.
   - ancestor: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with 0.
   - vis: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with FALSE.

5. Build d (a dictionary of adjacency for queries):
   - For each i from 1 to n, start with an empty list d[i].
   - Now go through each query pair in B in order, keeping track of its position idx starting at 0.
     * Suppose the idx-th pair is (x, y). Go to d[x] and append the tuple (y, idx). Then go to d[y] and append the tuple (x, idx).

6. Prepare result and stats containers:
   - res: make a list of length equal to the number of queries in B, and fill it with zeros.
   - stats: make a little table or box with three counters, all starting at 0:
        find_calls = 0
        union_calls = 0
        answered_queries = 0

7. Define your find operation (you won’t really write code, but you’ll follow this logic every time):
   - To "find" u:
     a. Add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     b. Look at parent[u]. If parent[u] is exactly u, you’re done and you return u.
     c. If parent[u] is some other number, say w, then you go and "find(w)" by repeating these steps, and when you get an answer r, you overwrite parent[u] with r. Then you return r.

8. Define your union operation:
   - To "union" u and v:
     a. Add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     b. Find the ultimate parent of v by using your find steps. Call that Pv.
     c. Find the ultimate parent of u by using your find steps. Call that Pu.
     d. Set parent[ Pv ] = Pu. (You attach v’s root under u’s root.)

9. Now do the depth-first sweep starting from root:
   - You’ll write a little note that you’re calling dfs(root).
   - In dfs(u):
     a. First, find the current representative of u by doing find(u). Then go to ancestor[ that representative ] and write down u. In other words, ancestor[ find(u) ] = u.
     b. Next, look at your list L[u]. For each child v in that list, you do:
        i. Call dfs(v) — you repeat all these steps from (a) down for v.
       ii. After dfs(v) finishes, do union(u, v). That merges v’s set into u’s set.
      iii. Right after that union, do ancestor[ find(u) ] = u again, so that the representative for the merged set points to u.
     c. When you’ve done all of u’s children, set vis[u] = TRUE.
     d. Now look at the list d[u]. For every tuple (v, idx) in that list:
        i. Check vis[v]. If vis[v] is still FALSE, skip it and move on.
       ii. If vis[v] is TRUE, then you know you can answer that query now.
           - Add 1 to answered_queries.
           - Find the representative of v by doing find(v), let’s call it Rv.
           - Look up ancestor[Rv], and write that value into res at position idx.
   - That completes dfs(u). When you finish the last line of dfs(root), you’re done with all nodes.

10. Once dfs(root) is fully done, you stop. You haven’t missed any child or any query, because at the moment both vis[u] and vis[v] are TRUE you answered every relevant query exactly once. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things:

1. res – a list of the same length as B. Each entry in res corresponds to one query pair from B (in the same order). The number you see at position idx is exactly the value you wrote into res[idx] during the dfs step when that query was answered.

2. stats – a small dictionary with three numbers:
   • "find_calls": how many times you ran the find operation altogether.  
   • "union_calls": how many times you ran the union operation.  
   • "answered_queries": how many queries from B you actually answered (each time you wrote into res you bumped this by 1).

2. A: a list of pairs (x, y). Each pair contains two numbers between 1 and n. Think of each pair as a connection from x down to y.

3. B: another list of pairs (x, y). These are the queries you'll process later. Each query involves two numbers between 1 and n, and you’ll keep track of an index for each one. 

LOGICS: Alright, let’s walk through exactly what you’d do by hand. Imagine you’ve got a big sheet of paper and you’re jotting down lists and boxes for each variable.

1. Build L (a list of lists):
   - Write down n + 1 blank lines labeled 0, 1, 2, …, n. You’ll ignore line 0 in practice, but it’s there for convenience.
   - Now go through each pair (x, y) in your list A. For each one, find line x in L and write y on that line. So if A has (3, 5), you go to L[3] and append 5 at the end of whatever’s already there.

2. Build st (a boolean marker list):
   - Make another list of length n+1, fill every entry with the word FALSE.
   - Again go through each pair (x, y) in A. This time, for each y you see, go to st[y] and change it to TRUE. That way you mark every y that ever appears as a second element.

3. Find the root:
   - Look from index 1 up to n in your st list. The very first index i you hit that’s still FALSE is called root. Write down that number as root.

4. Set up your union-find scaffolding:
   - parent: write down numbers 0 through n again. Then put a tick next to each so parent[i] = i for every i from 0 to n.
   - ancestor: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with 0.
   - vis: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with FALSE.

5. Build d (a dictionary of adjacency for queries):
   - For each i from 1 to n, start with an empty list d[i].
   - Now go through each query pair in B in order, keeping track of its position idx starting at 0.
     * Suppose the idx-th pair is (x, y). Go to d[x] and append the tuple (y, idx). Then go to d[y] and append the tuple (x, idx).

6. Prepare result and stats containers:
   - res: make a list of length equal to the number of queries in B, and fill it with zeros.
   - stats: make a little table or box with three counters, all starting at 0:
        find_calls = 0
        union_calls = 0
        answered_queries = 0

7. Define your find operation (you won’t really write code, but you’ll follow this logic every time):
   - To "find" u:
     a. Add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     b. Look at parent[u]. If parent[u] is exactly u, you’re done and you return u.
     c. If parent[u] is some other number, say w, then you go and "find(w)" by repeating these steps, and when you get an answer r, you overwrite parent[u] with r. Then you return r.

8. Define your union operation:
   - To "union" u and v:
     a. Add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     b. Find the ultimate parent of v by using your find steps. Call that Pv.
     c. Find the ultimate parent of u by using your find steps. Call that Pu.
     d. Set parent[ Pv ] = Pu. (You attach v’s root under u’s root.)

9. Now do the depth-first sweep starting from root:
   - You’ll write a little note that you’re calling dfs(root).
   - In dfs(u):
     a. First, find the current representative of u by doing find(u). Then go to ancestor[ that representative ] and write down u. In other words, ancestor[ find(u) ] = u.
     b. Next, look at your list L[u]. For each child v in that list, you do:
        i. Call dfs(v) — you repeat all these steps from (a) down for v.
       ii. After dfs(v) finishes, do union(u, v). That merges v’s set into u’s set.
      iii. Right after that union, do ancestor[ find(u) ] = u again, so that the representative for the merged set points to u.
     c. When you’ve done all of u’s children, set vis[u] = TRUE.
     d. Now look at the list d[u]. For every tuple (v, idx) in that list:
        i. Check vis[v]. If vis[v] is still FALSE, skip it and move on.
       ii. If vis[v] is TRUE, then you know you can answer that query now.
           - Add 1 to answered_queries.
           - Find the representative of v by doing find(v), let’s call it Rv.
           - Look up ancestor[Rv], and write that value into res at position idx.
   - That completes dfs(u). When you finish the last line of dfs(root), you’re done with all nodes.

10. Once dfs(root) is fully done, you stop. You haven’t missed any child or any query, because at the moment both vis[u] and vis[v] are TRUE you answered every relevant query exactly once.

1. res – a list of the same length as B. Each entry in res corresponds to one query pair from B (in the same order). The number you see at position idx is exactly the value you wrote into res[idx] during the dfs step when that query was answered.

2. stats – a small dictionary with three numbers:
   • "find_calls": how many times you ran the find operation altogether.  
   • "union_calls": how many times you ran the union operation.  
   • "answered_queries": how many queries from B you actually answered (each time you wrote into res you bumped this by 1).

description:
INPUTS: You have three things to start with:

1. n: a single integer. It tells you how many numbered slots you have, from 1 up to n.

2. A: a list of pairs (x, y). Each pair contains two numbers between 1 and n. Think of each pair as a connection from x down to y.

3. B: another list of pairs (x, y). These are the queries you'll process later. Each query involves two numbers between 1 and n, and you’ll keep track of an index for each one. 

LOGICS: Alright, let’s walk through exactly what you’d do by hand. Imagine you’ve got a big sheet of paper and you’re jotting down lists and boxes for each variable.

1. Build L (a list of lists):
   - Write down n + 1 blank lines labeled 0, 1, 2, …, n. You’ll ignore line 0 in practice, but it’s there for convenience.
   - Now go through each pair (x, y) in your list A. For each one, find line x in L and write y on that line. So if A has (3, 5), you go to L[3] and append 5 at the end of whatever’s already there.

2. Build st (a boolean marker list):
   - Make another list of length n+1, fill every entry with the word FALSE.
   - Again go through each pair (x, y) in A. This time, for each y you see, go to st[y] and change it to TRUE. That way you mark every y that ever appears as a second element.

3. Find the root:
   - Look from index 1 up to n in your st list. The very first index i you hit that’s still FALSE is called root. Write down that number as root.

4. Set up your union-find scaffolding:
   - parent: write down numbers 0 through n again. Then put a tick next to each so parent[i] = i for every i from 0 to n.
   - ancestor: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with 0.
   - vis: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with FALSE.

5. Build d (a dictionary of adjacency for queries):
   - For each i from 1 to n, start with an empty list d[i].
   - Now go through each query pair in B in order, keeping track of its position idx starting at 0.
     * Suppose the idx-th pair is (x, y). Go to d[x] and append the tuple (y, idx). Then go to d[y] and append the tuple (x, idx).

6. Prepare result and stats containers:
   - res: make a list of length equal to the number of queries in B, and fill it with zeros.
   - stats: make a little table or box with three counters, all starting at 0:
        find_calls = 0
        union_calls = 0
        answered_queries = 0

7. Define your find operation (you won’t really write code, but you’ll follow this logic every time):
   - To "find" u:
     a. Add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     b. Look at parent[u]. If parent[u] is exactly u, you’re done and you return u.
     c. If parent[u] is some other number, say w, then you go and "find(w)" by repeating these steps, and when you get an answer r, you overwrite parent[u] with r. Then you return r.

8. Define your union operation:
   - To "union" u and v:
     a. Add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     b. Find the ultimate parent of v by using your find steps. Call that Pv.
     c. Find the ultimate parent of u by using your find steps. Call that Pu.
     d. Set parent[ Pv ] = Pu. (You attach v’s root under u’s root.)

9. Now do the depth-first sweep starting from root:
   - You’ll write a little note that you’re calling dfs(root).
   - In dfs(u):
     a. First, find the current representative of u by doing find(u). Then go to ancestor[ that representative ] and write down u. In other words, ancestor[ find(u) ] = u.
     b. Next, look at your list L[u]. For each child v in that list, you do:
        i. Call dfs(v) — you repeat all these steps from (a) down for v.
       ii. After dfs(v) finishes, do union(u, v). That merges v’s set into u’s set.
      iii. Right after that union, do ancestor[ find(u) ] = u again, so that the representative for the merged set points to u.
     c. When you’ve done all of u’s children, set vis[u] = TRUE.
     d. Now look at the list d[u]. For every tuple (v, idx) in that list:
        i. Check vis[v]. If vis[v] is still FALSE, skip it and move on.
       ii. If vis[v] is TRUE, then you know you can answer that query now.
           - Add 1 to answered_queries.
           - Find the representative of v by doing find(v), let’s call it Rv.
           - Look up ancestor[Rv], and write that value into res at position idx.
   - That completes dfs(u). When you finish the last line of dfs(root), you’re done with all nodes.

10. Once dfs(root) is fully done, you stop. You haven’t missed any child or any query, because at the moment both vis[u] and vis[v] are TRUE you answered every relevant query exactly once. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things:

1. res – a list of the same length as B. Each entry in res corresponds to one query pair from B (in the same order). The number you see at position idx is exactly the value you wrote into res[idx] during the dfs step when that query was answered.

2. stats – a small dictionary with three numbers:
   • "find_calls": how many times you ran the find operation altogether.  
   • "union_calls": how many times you ran the union operation.  
   • "answered_queries": how many queries from B you actually answered (each time you wrote into res you bumped this by 1).

INPUTS: You have three things to start with:

1. n: a single integer. It tells you how many numbered slots you have, from 1 up to n.

2. A: a list of pairs (x, y). Each pair contains two numbers between 1 and n. Think of each pair as a connection from x down to y.

3. B: another list of pairs (x, y). These are the queries you'll process later. Each query involves two numbers between 1 and n, and you’ll keep track of an index for each one. 

LOGICS: Alright, let’s walk through exactly what you’d do by hand. Imagine you’ve got a big sheet of paper and you’re jotting down lists and boxes for each variable.

1. Build L (a list of lists):
   - Write down n + 1 blank lines labeled 0, 1, 2, …, n. You’ll ignore line 0 in practice, but it’s there for convenience.
   - Now go through each pair (x, y) in your list A. For each one, find line x in L and write y on that line. So if A has (3, 5), you go to L[3] and append 5 at the end of whatever’s already there.

2. Build st (a boolean marker list):
   - Make another list of length n+1, fill every entry with the word FALSE.
   - Again go through each pair (x, y) in A. This time, for each y you see, go to st[y] and change it to TRUE. That way you mark every y that ever appears as a second element.

3. Find the root:
   - Look from index 1 up to n in your st list. The very first index i you hit that’s still FALSE is called root. Write down that number as root.

4. Set up your union-find scaffolding:
   - parent: write down numbers 0 through n again. Then put a tick next to each so parent[i] = i for every i from 0 to n.
   - ancestor: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with 0.
   - vis: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with FALSE.

5. Build d (a dictionary of adjacency for queries):
   - For each i from 1 to n, start with an empty list d[i].
   - Now go through each query pair in B in order, keeping track of its position idx starting at 0.
     * Suppose the idx-th pair is (x, y). Go to d[x] and append the tuple (y, idx). Then go to d[y] and append the tuple (x, idx).

6. Prepare result and stats containers:
   - res: make a list of length equal to the number of queries in B, and fill it with zeros.
   - stats: make a little table or box with three counters, all starting at 0:
        find_calls = 0
        union_calls = 0
        answered_queries = 0

7. Define your find operation (you won’t really write code, but you’ll follow this logic every time):
   - To "find" u:
     a. Add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     b. Look at parent[u]. If parent[u] is exactly u, you’re done and you return u.
     c. If parent[u] is some other number, say w, then you go and "find(w)" by repeating these steps, and when you get an answer r, you overwrite parent[u] with r. Then you return r.

8. Define your union operation:
   - To "union" u and v:
     a. Add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     b. Find the ultimate parent of v by using your find steps. Call that Pv.
     c. Find the ultimate parent of u by using your find steps. Call that Pu.
     d. Set parent[ Pv ] = Pu. (You attach v’s root under u’s root.)

9. Now do the depth-first sweep starting from root:
   - You’ll write a little note that you’re calling dfs(root).
   - In dfs(u):
     a. First, find the current representative of u by doing find(u). Then go to ancestor[ that representative ] and write down u. In other words, ancestor[ find(u) ] = u.
     b. Next, look at your list L[u]. For each child v in that list, you do:
        i. Call dfs(v) — you repeat all these steps from (a) down for v.
       ii. After dfs(v) finishes, do union(u, v). That merges v’s set into u’s set.
      iii. Right after that union, do ancestor[ find(u) ] = u again, so that the representative for the merged set points to u.
     c. When you’ve done all of u’s children, set vis[u] = TRUE.
     d. Now look at the list d[u]. For every tuple (v, idx) in that list:
        i. Check vis[v]. If vis[v] is still FALSE, skip it and move on.
       ii. If vis[v] is TRUE, then you know you can answer that query now.
           - Add 1 to answered_queries.
           - Find the representative of v by doing find(v), let’s call it Rv.
           - Look up ancestor[Rv], and write that value into res at position idx.
   - That completes dfs(u). When you finish the last line of dfs(root), you’re done with all nodes.

10. Once dfs(root) is fully done, you stop. You haven’t missed any child or any query, because at the moment both vis[u] and vis[v] are TRUE you answered every relevant query exactly once. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things:

1. res – a list of the same length as B. Each entry in res corresponds to one query pair from B (in the same order). The number you see at position idx is exactly the value you wrote into res[idx] during the dfs step when that query was answered.

2. stats – a small dictionary with three numbers:
   • "find_calls": how many times you ran the find operation altogether.  
   • "union_calls": how many times you ran the union operation.  
   • "answered_queries": how many queries from B you actually answered (each time you wrote into res you bumped this by 1).

description:
INPUTS: You have three things to start with:

1. n: a single integer. It tells you how many numbered slots you have, from 1 up to n.

2. A: a list of pairs (x, y). Each pair contains two numbers between 1 and n. Think of each pair as a connection from x down to y.

3. B: another list of pairs (x, y). These are the queries you'll process later. Each query involves two numbers between 1 and n, and you’ll keep track of an index for each one. 

LOGICS: Alright, let’s walk through exactly what you’d do by hand. Imagine you’ve got a big sheet of paper and you’re jotting down lists and boxes for each variable.

1. Build L (a list of lists):
   - Write down n + 1 blank lines labeled 0, 1, 2, …, n. You’ll ignore line 0 in practice, but it’s there for convenience.
   - Now go through each pair (x, y) in your list A. For each one, find line x in L and write y on that line. So if A has (3, 5), you go to L[3] and append 5 at the end of whatever’s already there.

2. Build st (a boolean marker list):
   - Make another list of length n+1, fill every entry with the word FALSE.
   - Again go through each pair (x, y) in A. This time, for each y you see, go to st[y] and change it to TRUE. That way you mark every y that ever appears as a second element.

3. Find the root:
   - Look from index 1 up to n in your st list. The very first index i you hit that’s still FALSE is called root. Write down that number as root.

4. Set up your union-find scaffolding:
   - parent: write down numbers 0 through n again. Then put a tick next to each so parent[i] = i for every i from 0 to n.
   - ancestor: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with 0.
   - vis: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with FALSE.

5. Build d (a dictionary of adjacency for queries):
   - For each i from 1 to n, start with an empty list d[i].
   - Now go through each query pair in B in order, keeping track of its position idx starting at 0.
     * Suppose the idx-th pair is (x, y). Go to d[x] and append the tuple (y, idx). Then go to d[y] and append the tuple (x, idx).

6. Prepare result and stats containers:
   - res: make a list of length equal to the number of queries in B, and fill it with zeros.
   - stats: make a little table or box with three counters, all starting at 0:
        find_calls = 0
        union_calls = 0
        answered_queries = 0

7. Define your find operation (you won’t really write code, but you’ll follow this logic every time):
   - To "find" u:
     a. Add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     b. Look at parent[u]. If parent[u] is exactly u, you’re done and you return u.
     c. If parent[u] is some other number, say w, then you go and "find(w)" by repeating these steps, and when you get an answer r, you overwrite parent[u] with r. Then you return r.

8. Define your union operation:
   - To "union" u and v:
     a. Add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     b. Find the ultimate parent of v by using your find steps. Call that Pv.
     c. Find the ultimate parent of u by using your find steps. Call that Pu.
     d. Set parent[ Pv ] = Pu. (You attach v’s root under u’s root.)

9. Now do the depth-first sweep starting from root:
   - You’ll write a little note that you’re calling dfs(root).
   - In dfs(u):
     a. First, find the current representative of u by doing find(u). Then go to ancestor[ that representative ] and write down u. In other words, ancestor[ find(u) ] = u.
     b. Next, look at your list L[u]. For each child v in that list, you do:
        i. Call dfs(v) — you repeat all these steps from (a) down for v.
       ii. After dfs(v) finishes, do union(u, v). That merges v’s set into u’s set.
      iii. Right after that union, do ancestor[ find(u) ] = u again, so that the representative for the merged set points to u.
     c. When you’ve done all of u’s children, set vis[u] = TRUE.
     d. Now look at the list d[u]. For every tuple (v, idx) in that list:
        i. Check vis[v]. If vis[v] is still FALSE, skip it and move on.
       ii. If vis[v] is TRUE, then you know you can answer that query now.
           - Add 1 to answered_queries.
           - Find the representative of v by doing find(v), let’s call it Rv.
           - Look up ancestor[Rv], and write that value into res at position idx.
   - That completes dfs(u). When you finish the last line of dfs(root), you’re done with all nodes.

10. Once dfs(root) is fully done, you stop. You haven’t missed any child or any query, because at the moment both vis[u] and vis[v] are TRUE you answered every relevant query exactly once. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things:

1. res – a list of the same length as B. Each entry in res corresponds to one query pair from B (in the same order). The number you see at position idx is exactly the value you wrote into res[idx] during the dfs step when that query was answered.

2. stats – a small dictionary with three numbers:
   • "find_calls": how many times you ran the find operation altogether.  
   • "union_calls": how many times you ran the union operation.  
   • "answered_queries": how many queries from B you actually answered (each time you wrote into res you bumped this by 1).

INPUTS: You start with three things: an integer n, an integer m, and a list called lst where each item is a two-integer pair (i, j). 

LOGICS: What youre going to do is set up a way to count and organize all those pairs step by step. First, pick a symbol INF and treat it in your head or on paper as an infinitely large placeholder. Next, write down two counters named x and y, and set both of them to zero. These will track how many times you inspect pairs in two different helper processes.

Now you need to build a structure called A. Start by creating an empty list and then, one at a time, add an empty sublist until you have exactly n sublists inside A (so A[0] through A[n-1] all exist). Once youve done that, go through your lst one pair at a time. For each pair, look at the two numbers i and j. If i is at least 0 and less than n, and j is at least 0 and less than m, then append j to the sublist A[i]. If either i or j falls outside those bounds, ignore that pair and move on to the next one. At this point youll have A filled with only the in-bounds j’s grouped by their i’s.

After A is ready, set up three more lists in a row: U of length n, V of length m, and D of length n. Fill every slot in U with -1, every slot in V with -1, and every slot in D with 0. That gives you your starting state.

What you do next is define two helper procedures, which well call b and d. These arent functions you run in code—theyre processes you follow by hand.

Helper b:
• Begin by writing down an empty queue. You can represent it as a list where you add items at the end and remove them from the front.  
• Next, go through each index i from 0 up to n–1. If U[i] is -1, set D[i] to 0 and enqueue i. If U[i] is not -1, set D[i] to INF.  
• Write down a flag called found and set it to False.  
• Now, repeat the following until your queue is empty:  
  – Dequeue an index i from the front.  
  – For each j in the list A[i], do:  
    · Add 1 to your counter x (this marks that youve inspected this j during b).  
    · Look at V[j] and call that number w.  
    · If w is not -1 and D[w] is INF, then set D[w] to D[i] + 1 and enqueue w.  
    · Else if w is -1, set found to True (but keep checking other j’s and queue items).  
• When the queue finally empties out, b ends by returning the value of found (True or False).

Helper d(i):
• You run this on a particular index i whenever you want to try to match i.  
• For each j in A[i], do:  
  – Add 1 to your counter y (this marks that youve inspected j during d).  
  – Let w = V[j].  
  – If w is -1, you can match right away: set U[i] = j and V[j] = i, then return True immediately.  
  – Otherwise, if w is not -1 and D[w] equals D[i] + 1, then recursively run d on w. If that recursive call returns True, set U[i] = j and V[j] = i, then return True.  
• If you finish the loop without returning True, set D[i] = INF and return False.

Main flow:
1. Write down a counter res and set it to 0.  
2. Now enter a loop where you first run helper b.  
3. If b returned True, then go through each i from 0 up to n–1. Whenever you find that U[i] is still -1, run d(i). If that call returns True, add 1 to res.  
4. After you finish checking all i in that round, go back and run b again.  
5. Keep repeating steps 2–4 until b returns False.  
6. At that point, you stop. res holds your final match count, and x and y have been accumulating all your inspections. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, youll end up with two things: first, the number res, and second, a small dictionary with two entries. The entry named "bfs_edge_checks" holds the value of x, which is the total times you inspected a j during the b helper. The entry named "dfs_edge_checks" holds the value of y, which is the total times you inspected a j during the d helper. Combined, your final output is (res, {"bfs_edge_checks": x, "dfs_edge_checks": y}).

INPUTS: An integer n and a string s that contains exactly n characters. 

LOGICS: First, you start by figuring out a helper value called val. The way you do that is take your integer n, add 1 to it, and store the result in val. Next, you need to set up a list named A that has exactly n spots, and in every one of those spots you put val. So right away A looks like [val, val, ..., val] with n entries.  Then you're going to scan through each position x from 0 up to n−1. At each step, look at s[x]. If that character exactly equals a, then you replace A[x] with the number x. If s[x] is anything else, you leave A[x] alone as val. Do that for all x so that A now records the index for any entry that was a, and val for every other entry.  Once that’s done, you want to find an initial ans value. To do this, go back through each character in s, turn it into a number by subtracting ord('a'), and pick the maximum of those results. Store that maximum in a variable named ans.  Next, prepare for the main iterative process by creating a second list called B of length n and filling all its entries with val. Also set three counters to zero: levels, match_count, and merge_count.  Now you enter a loop where you let y run from 1 up to 25 inclusive. Each value of y stands for the letter that’s y positions after a. Inside this loop, first make a list C of length n+1, and fill every spot in C with val. Then build C by running x backward from n−1 down to 0: at each x set C[x] = the smaller of C[x+1] and A[x]. After this reverse pass, each C[x] holds the smallest A value you’ve seen from index x onward.  After that setup, reset a flag called any_valid to False and compute the specific letter you’re targeting as str2 = chr(ord('a') + y). Now go forward through x from 0 to n−1. For each x do the following in order: first, check if s[x] equals str2. If it does, set a temporary variable best = x and add 1 to match_count. If it doesn’t, set best = val. Next, look at m = A[x]. If m is less than n−1, compute cand = C[m+1]; if cand is smaller than best, then set best = cand and add 1 to merge_count. Then write B[x] = best. If best is less than val, mark any_valid = True.  Once you’ve processed every x in B, check if any_valid stayed False. If it did, that means nothing got updated below val, so you break out of the y-loop entirely. If any_valid is True, add 1 to levels, then compare ans and y: if ans is smaller than y, set ans = y. Then swap A and B by doing A = B, followed by resetting B to a fresh list of length n all filled with val. Then continue to the next y.  When that y-loop finishes—either because y went all the way to 25 or because you broke early—you take the current ans, add 1 to it, and that is your first result. You also have your three counters levels, match_count, and merge_count ready to go as your second result in a dictionary. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things: a final number, which is the ans you’ve been updating plus one, and a dictionary with three entries: levels (counting how many y-iterations produced valid updates), match_count (counting how many times s[x] matched the current letter), and merge_count (counting how many times you picked a C[m+1] candidate over the direct match).

Next, you need to set up a list named A that has exactly n spots, and in every one of those spots you put val. So right away A looks like [val, val, ..., val] with n entries.  Then you're going to scan through each position x from 0 up to n−1. At each step, look at s[x]. If that character exactly equals a, then you replace A[x] with the number x. If s[x] is anything else, you leave A[x] alone as val. Do that for all x so that A now records the index for any entry that was a, and val for every other entry.  Once that’s done, you want to find an initial ans value. To do this, go back through each character in s, turn it into a number by subtracting ord('a'), and pick the maximum of those results. Store that maximum in a variable named ans.  Next, prepare for the main iterative process by creating a second list called B of length n and filling all its entries with val. Also set three counters to zero: levels, match_count, and merge_count.  Now you enter a loop where you let y run from 1 up to 25 inclusive. Each value of y stands for the letter that’s y positions after a. Inside this loop, first make a list C of length n+1, and fill every spot in C with val. Then build C by running x backward from n−1 down to 0: at each x set C[x] = the smaller of C[x+1] and A[x]. After this reverse pass, each C[x] holds the smallest A value you’ve seen from index x onward.  After that setup, reset a flag called any_valid to False and compute the specific letter you’re targeting as str2 = chr(ord('a') + y). Now go forward through x from 0 to n−1. For each x do the following in order: first, check if s[x] equals str2. If it does, set a temporary variable best = x and add 1 to match_count. If it doesn’t, set best = val. Next, look at m = A[x]. If m is less than n−1, compute cand = C[m+1]; if cand is smaller than best, then set best = cand and add 1 to merge_count. Then write B[x] = best. If best is less than val, mark any_valid = True.  Once you’ve processed every x in B, check if any_valid stayed False. If it did, that means nothing got updated below val, so you break out of the y-loop entirely. If any_valid is True, add 1 to levels, then compare ans and y: if ans is smaller than y, set ans = y. Then swap A and B by doing A = B, followed by resetting B to a fresh list of length n all filled with val. Then continue to the next y.  When that y-loop finishes—either because y went all the way to 25 or because you broke early—you take the current ans, add 1 to it, and that is your first result. You also have your three counters levels, match_count, and merge_count ready to go as your second result in a dictionary. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things: a final number, which is the ans you’ve been updating plus one, and a dictionary with three entries: levels (counting how many y-iterations produced valid updates), match_count (counting how many times s[x] matched the current letter), and merge_count (counting how many times you picked a C[m+1] candidate over the direct match).

LOGICS: First, what you're going to do is set up a statistics dictionary 'd' with three counters: 'segments', 'compute_calls', and 'j_iters', all starting at zero. Next, you check the first condition: if 'n' is less than or equal to zero, you just return the input 'val' and the dictionary 'd' as-is. But if 'n' is positive, you move on.
Now you need to sort the list 'A' so that its entries are in non-decreasing order. Once you have that sorted list, start building a new list called 'arr'. At the very beginning, put the first element of the sorted list 'A' into 'arr'. Then, one by one for i running from 1 up to n-1, you subtract the previous entry A[i-1] from the current entry A[i], and append that difference to 'arr'. After you finish that loop, take 'val', subtract the last entry of 'A', and append that final piece to 'arr'. At this point 'arr' has length 'N', which is n + 1.
Next, determine how many segments you can have by taking m + 1 and then if that number is bigger than 'N', you cap it at 'N'. Store that result back into 'segments' and also write segments into d['segments']. Then check if 'segments' is greater than or equal to 'N'. If it is, you just return the maximum value you see in 'arr' along with your dictionary 'd'. No further work is needed.
But if 'segments' is strictly less than 'N', you carry on. What you do now is build a prefix sum list called 'prefix' of length N + 1. Start with prefix[0] = 0. Then for each index i from 1 to N inclusive, set prefix[i] to prefix[i-1] + arr[i-1]. That means prefix[i] always holds the sum of the first i entries of 'arr'.
After that, you create two more lists of length N + 1 called 'prev_dp' and 'cur_dp'. You copy the entire 'prefix' list into 'prev_dp'. For 'cur_dp', you fill every slot from 0 to N with an infinitely large number.
We also define a little helper called 'cost(i, j)'. Whenever you call cost with two indices i and j, you look at prefix[j] and subtract prefix[i] from it. That gives you the sum of arr starting at i up to but not including j.
The heart of the work is a recursive routine called 'compute'. It takes five numbers: the segment index k, a left bound, a right bound, an optimal-left bound optL, and an optimal-right bound optR. Every time you enter this 'compute' routine, add 1 to d['compute_calls']. If the left bound is bigger than the right bound, you just return immediately — there are no entries to handle. Otherwise you figure out a midpoint 'mid' by taking the integer division (left + right) // 2. You set cur_dp[mid] to infinity and keep a variable 'best' = -1.
Then you decide how far to try splitting the previous results. You let 'start' = the bigger of optL and k-1, and 'end' = the smaller of mid-1 and optR. Now you loop j from 'start' to 'end' inclusive. Each time through this loop, add 1 to d['j_iters'], then compute a candidate value 'v' as the bigger of prev_dp[j] and cost(j, mid). If that candidate 'v' is smaller than the current cur_dp[mid], you overwrite cur_dp[mid] with v and set best = j. After the loop, if best remains -1, you set best back to 'start' so you have a default.
The final step in this 'compute' call is to split your problem in two. You call compute again with the same k, new bounds left to mid-1, and optL stays the same while optR becomes best. Then you call compute a second time with k, bounds mid+1 to right, optL becomes best, and optR stays the same.
Once you have that compute routine in place, you run a loop for k from 2 up through 'segments'. For each k you call compute(k, k, N, k-1, N-1). When that call finishes, you swap the lists prev_dp and cur_dp, and then refill every entry in cur_dp with infinity again.
After you complete that loop for every k, you stop. At that point prev_dp[N] holds your final output number. You return that number along with the dictionary 'd' containing the counts you collected all along. 

OUTPUTS: You finish with two things: a single number (the value stored in prev_dp[N] after the loops) and the dictionary 'd'. In 'd', 'segments' shows how many segments got used, 'compute_calls' is how many times you invoked the recursive compute routine, and 'j_iters' is the total count of inner loop steps when you scanned j from start to end.

INPUTS: You have four inputs to work with: 1. n – a single integer (a whole number). 2. m – another integer (a whole number). 3. k – another integer (a whole number). 4. A – a two-dimensional list: it has n rows, and each row is itself a list of m items you can compare for equality (like numbers or text). 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is walk through each part exactly as if you were the computer, but all by hand.  

1. Start by creating three counters and set them all to zero:  
   • sim_checks = 0   (this will count each time you compare A[i][t] to A[j][t])  
   • dp_calls = 0     (this will count how many times you enter the dp helper)  
   • mask_checks = 0  (this will count how many subsets, or "masks," you test at the end)  

2. Next, build an n×n table called M.  
   • Lay it out as a grid with n rows and n columns.  
   • Put a 0 in every single cell of that grid for now.  

3. Now you’re going to fill in M with the number of matching positions between every pair of rows in A:  
   • For i from 0 up to n−1, do this:  
     – For j from i+1 up to n−1, do this:  
       a. Start a counter c at 0.  
       b. For t from 0 up to m−1, do:  
          * Add 1 to sim_checks.  
          * Compare A[i][t] and A[j][t]. If they’re equal, add 1 to c.  
       c. After you finish the loop over t, write c into M[i][j] and also into M[j][i].  
   • By the time those two loops finish, M[i][j] (and M[j][i]) holds exactly how many entries matched between row i and row j.  

4. Before you define your helper, set up an empty lookup called cache.  
   • Think of cache as an empty dictionary or table keyed by each mask x you’ll see in dp.  
   • At the very start, cache has no entries, so every dp(x) is new until you store it.  

5. Now define a helper process called dp that takes an integer x (your bitmask) and returns a number.  Here’s how it works, step by step, in conversational terms:  
   a. First thing inside dp, add 1 to dp_calls.  
   b. Check cache: if you already have a stored value for this exact x, just grab that value and return it right away.  
   c. If it wasn’t in cache, you’re about to compute it.  
   d. Figure out how many bits are set in x; call that count y.  
   e. If y == 0, that means no bits are active, so set result = 0.  
   f. Otherwise, if y is odd or y > 2*k, that’s an invalid selection, so set result = negative infinity.  
      • To handle "negative infinity" by hand, just pick a symbol like -∞ or any number you know will be lower than any real total you’ll compute, and treat it as smaller than any other sum.  
   g. If neither of those conditions held (so y is even and y ≤ 2*k and y > 0), do this:  
      i. Find the least significant 1 bit in x. You can do that by isolating `lowBit = x & -x` and then finding its position i0 by counting how many times you would shift right until you get to that bit (i0 is between 0 and n−1).  
      ii. Set best = negative infinity (your special symbol).  
      iii. Make z = x with bit i0 cleared (that is, z = x − 2^i0).  
      iv. While z is not zero, repeat:  
          • Find the least significant 1 bit in z the same way, call its index j0.  
          • Clear that bit from z (z = z − 2^j0).  
          • Compute a candidate value: look up M[i0][j0], then call dp on x with both bits i0 and j0 cleared (that’s x − 2^i0 − 2^j0). Add the two: val = M[i0][j0] + dp(x − 2^i0 − 2^j0).  
          • If val > best, then set best = val.  
      v. When the while loop finishes (z is zero), set result = best.  
   h. Now that you have result for this x, store it in cache under key x (cache[x] = result), and then return result.  
   • That way, if dp(x) ever comes up again, you’ll skip all the work and go straight to the stored value.  

6. With dp in hand, you’re ready to find the final answer:  
   a. Set ans = 0.  
   b. Compute full = 1 shifted left by n (that’s 2^n).  
   c. For each integer x from 0 up to full−1, do:  
      i. Add 1 to mask_checks.  
      ii. Count the bits set in x. If that count equals 2*k, then:  
          * Call v = dp(x).  
          * If v > ans, then set ans = v.  
   d. By the end of that loop, you will have tested every possible subset of indices of size 2*k and found the maximum total.  

7. At this point, you’ve done all the work, and you’re ready to report your results. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have:  
1. ans – a single number, which is the largest total you found by pairing up exactly 2*k indices.  
2. stats – a dictionary with three entries:  
   • char_comparisons: the final value of sim_checks (that’s how many times you compared items in A).  
   • dp_calls: the final value of dp_calls (how many times you entered dp, even if it returned a cached result).  
   • masks_tested: the final value of mask_checks (how many bitmasks x you examined in the last loop).

     – For j from i+1 up to n−1, do this:  
       a. Start a counter c at 0.  
       b. For t from 0 up to m−1, do:  
          * Add 1 to sim_checks.  
          * Compare A[i][t] and A[j][t]. If they’re equal, add 1 to c.  
       c. After you finish the loop over t, write c into M[i][j] and also into M[j][i].  
   • By the time those two loops finish, M[i][j] (and M[j][i]) holds exactly how many entries matched between row i and row j.  

4. Before you define your helper, set up an empty lookup called cache.  
   • Think of cache as an empty dictionary or table keyed by each mask x you’ll see in dp.  
   • At the very start, cache has no entries, so every dp(x) is new until you store it.

   a. First thing inside dp, add 1 to dp_calls.  
   b. Check cache: if you already have a stored value for this exact x, just grab that value and return it right away.  
   c. If it wasn’t in cache, you’re about to compute it.  
   d. Figure out how many bits are set in x; call that count y.  
   e. If y == 0, that means no bits are active, so set result = 0.  
   f. Otherwise, if y is odd or y > 2*k, that’s an invalid selection, so set result = negative infinity.  
      • To handle "negative infinity" by hand, just pick a symbol like -∞ or any number you know will be lower than any real total you’ll compute, and treat it as smaller than any other sum.

          * Call v = dp(x).  
          * If v > ans, then set ans = v.  
   d. By the end of that loop, you will have tested every possible subset of indices of size 2*k and found the maximum total.

   • dp_calls: the final value of dp_calls (how many times you entered dp, even if it returned a cached result).  
   • masks_tested: the final value of mask_checks (how many bitmasks x you examined in the last loop).

def f(n, k, lst):
    st = set()
    for a, b, _ in lst:
        st.add(a)
        st.add(b + 1)
    arr = sorted(st)
    d = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(arr)}
    m = len(arr)
    if m <= 1:
        return (0, {"update_calls": 0, "push_calls": 0, "pull_calls": 0})
    x = m - 1
    size = 4 * x + 5
    A = [0] * size
    B = [0] * size
    C = [0] * size
    D = [0] * size
    E = [0] * size
    F = [0] * size
    c_u = 0
    c_pu = 0
    c_pl = 0
    def build(node, l, r):
        if l == r:
            F[node] = arr[l + 1] - arr[l]
            return
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        build(lc, l, mid)
        build(rc, mid + 1, r)
        F[node] = F[lc] + F[rc]
    def apply(node, val):
        A[node] += val
        B[node] += val
    def push(node):
        nonlocal c_pu
        c_pu += 1
        if B[node] != 0:
            v = B[node]
            lc = node * 2
            rc = node * 2 + 1
            apply(lc, v)
            apply(rc, v)
            B[node] = 0
    def pull(node):
        nonlocal c_pl
        c_pl += 1
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        A[node] = A[lc] if A[lc] < A[rc] else A[rc]
        if A[lc] >= k:
            C[node] = F[lc] + C[rc]
        else:
            C[node] = C[lc]
        if A[rc] >= k:
            D[node] = F[rc] + D[lc]
        else:
            D[node] = D[rc]
        v1 = E[lc]
        v2 = E[rc]
        v3 = D[lc] + C[rc]
        t = v1 if v1 > v2 else v2
        E[node] = t if t > v3 else v3
    def update(node, l, r, ql, qr):
        nonlocal c_u
        c_u += 1
        if ql > r or qr < l:
            return
        if ql <= l and r <= qr:
            apply(node, 1)
            return
        push(node)
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        if ql <= mid:
            update(lc, l, mid, ql, qr)
        if qr > mid:
            update(rc, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
        pull(node)
    build(1, 0, x - 1)
    lst.sort(key=lambda t: t[2])
    best = 0
    for a, b, w in lst:
        Lc = d[a]
        Rc = d[b + 1] - 1
        if Lc <= Rc:
            update(1, 0, x - 1, Lc, Rc)
        cur = E[1] * w
        if cur > best:
            best = cur
    return (best, {"update_calls": c_u, "push_calls": c_pu, "pull_calls": c_pl})

What you do next is define a helper called build(node, l, r):
- If l == r, you’re at a leaf segment. Look up arr[l+1] - arr[l], store that difference in F[node], and return.
- Otherwise, compute mid = (l + r) // 2. Let lc = node * 2, rc = node * 2 + 1. First call build(lc, l, mid), then build(rc, mid + 1, r). After both calls finish, set F[node] = F[lc] + F[rc], then return.

Then define apply(node, val):
- Add val to A[node]
- Add val to B[node]

Next, define push(node):
- Increment c_pu by 1
- If B[node] != 0, let v = B[node], set lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1, then call apply(lc, v) and apply(rc, v), and finally set B[node] = 0.

After that, define pull(node):
- Increment c_pl by 1
- Let lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1
- Set A[node] = the smaller of A[lc] and A[rc]
- For C[node]: if A[lc] >= k, set C[node] = F[lc] + C[rc]; otherwise set C[node] = C[lc]
- For D[node]: if A[rc] >= k, set D[node] = F[rc] + D[lc]; otherwise set D[node] = D[rc]
- Compute v1 = E[lc], v2 = E[rc], v3 = D[lc] + C[rc]
- Set E[node] to the largest of v1, v2, and v3

Then define update(node, l, r, ql, qr):
- Increment c_u by 1
- If ql > r or qr < l, there’s no overlap—just return
- If ql <= l and r <= qr, the entire segment is covered: call apply(node, 1) and return
- Otherwise you have a partial overlap:
  - First call push(node)
  - Compute mid = (l + r) // 2, lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1
  - If ql <= mid, call update(lc, l, mid, ql, qr)
  - If qr > mid, call update(rc, mid+1, r, ql, qr)
  - After those calls, call pull(node) and then return

At this point you’ve defined all your helpers. Now call build(1, 0, x - 1) to fill F.

Next, sort lst in ascending order by the third value w.

Initialize a variable best to 0.

Now go through each triple (a, b, w) in the sorted list:
- Look up Lc = d[a]
- Look up Rc = d[b + 1] - 1
- If Lc <= Rc, call update(1, 0, x - 1, Lc, Rc)
- After that, take E[1], multiply it by w to get cur
- If cur > best, set best = cur

Once you’ve processed every item, you’re done with the main processing flow. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll return a pair. The first element is best, a single number. The second element is a dictionary with three entries: update_calls (the final value of c_u), push_calls (the final value of c_pu), and pull_calls (the final value of c_pl). These three numbers tell you how many times you ran the update logic, how many times you pushed pending updates down to children, and how many times you pulled or recomputed values back up.

def f(n, k, lst):
    st = set()
    for a, b, _ in lst:
        st.add(a)
        st.add(b + 1)
    arr = sorted(st)
    d = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(arr)}
    m = len(arr)
    if m <= 1:
        return (0, {"update_calls": 0, "push_calls": 0, "pull_calls": 0})
    x = m - 1
    size = 4 * x + 5
    A = [0] * size
    B = [0] * size
    C = [0] * size
    D = [0] * size
    E = [0] * size
    F = [0] * size
    c_u = 0
    c_pu = 0
    c_pl = 0
    def build(node, l, r):
        if l == r:
            F[node] = arr[l + 1] - arr[l]
            return
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        build(lc, l, mid)
        build(rc, mid + 1, r)
        F[node] = F[lc] + F[rc]
    def apply(node, val):
        A[node] += val
        B[node] += val
    def push(node):
        nonlocal c_pu
        c_pu += 1
        if B[node] != 0:
            v = B[node]
            lc = node * 2
            rc = node * 2 + 1
            apply(lc, v)
            apply(rc, v)
            B[node] = 0
    def pull(node):
        nonlocal c_pl
        c_pl += 1
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        A[node] = A[lc] if A[lc] < A[rc] else A[rc]
        if A[lc] >= k:
            C[node] = F[lc] + C[rc]
        else:
            C[node] = C[lc]
        if A[rc] >= k:
            D[node] = F[rc] + D[lc]
        else:
            D[node] = D[rc]
        v1 = E[lc]
        v2 = E[rc]
        v3 = D[lc] + C[rc]
        t = v1 if v1 > v2 else v2
        E[node] = t if t > v3 else v3
    def update(node, l, r, ql, qr):
        nonlocal c_u
        c_u += 1
        if ql > r or qr < l:
            return
        if ql <= l and r <= qr:
            apply(node, 1)
            return
        push(node)
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        if ql <= mid:
            update(lc, l, mid, ql, qr)
        if qr > mid:
            update(rc, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
        pull(node)
    build(1, 0, x - 1)
    lst.sort(key=lambda t: t[2])
    best = 0
    for a, b, w in lst:
        Lc = d[a]
        Rc = d[b + 1] - 1
        if Lc <= Rc:
            update(1, 0, x - 1, Lc, Rc)
        cur = E[1] * w
        if cur > best:
            best = cur
    return (best, {"update_calls": c_u, "push_calls": c_pu, "pull_calls": c_pl})

INPUTS: You have two integers, n and k, and a list called lst. Each item in lst is a triple of integers (a, b, w). 

LOGICS: Start by creating an empty set called st.

Next, go through each item in lst. For each triple, take the first number a and put it into st, then take the second number b and put b+1 into st as well.

After you've done that for every item, gather all numbers from st, sort them into a list called arr.

Now build a dictionary called d: for each position i in arr, set d[arr[i]] = i.

Let m be the length of arr. If m is 1 or less, you have no ranges to handle, so you immediately return (0, {"update_calls": 0, "push_calls": 0, "pull_calls": 0}).

Otherwise, compute x = m - 1, then compute size = 4 * x + 5.

Create six arrays—A, B, C, D, E, F—each of length size, and fill them with zeros.
Also set three counters c_u, c_pu, c_pl all to zero. These will track how many times you invoke update, push, and pull.

What you do next is define a helper called build(node, l, r):
- If l == r, you’re at a leaf segment. Look up arr[l+1] - arr[l], store that difference in F[node], and return.
- Otherwise, compute mid = (l + r) // 2. Let lc = node * 2, rc = node * 2 + 1. First call build(lc, l, mid), then build(rc, mid + 1, r). After both calls finish, set F[node] = F[lc] + F[rc], then return.

Then define apply(node, val):
- Add val to A[node]
- Add val to B[node]

Next, define push(node):
- Increment c_pu by 1
- If B[node] != 0, let v = B[node], set lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1, then call apply(lc, v) and apply(rc, v), and finally set B[node] = 0.

After that, define pull(node):
- Increment c_pl by 1
- Let lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1
- Set A[node] = the smaller of A[lc] and A[rc]
- For C[node]: if A[lc] >= k, set C[node] = F[lc] + C[rc]; otherwise set C[node] = C[lc]
- For D[node]: if A[rc] >= k, set D[node] = F[rc] + D[lc]; otherwise set D[node] = D[rc]
- Compute v1 = E[lc], v2 = E[rc], v3 = D[lc] + C[rc]
- Set E[node] to the largest of v1, v2, and v3

Then define update(node, l, r, ql, qr):
- Increment c_u by 1
- If ql > r or qr < l, there’s no overlap—just return
- If ql <= l and r <= qr, the entire segment is covered: call apply(node, 1) and return
- Otherwise you have a partial overlap:
  - First call push(node)
  - Compute mid = (l + r) // 2, lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1
  - If ql <= mid, call update(lc, l, mid, ql, qr)
  - If qr > mid, call update(rc, mid+1, r, ql, qr)
  - After those calls, call pull(node) and then return

At this point you’ve defined all your helpers. Now call build(1, 0, x - 1) to fill F.

Next, sort lst in ascending order by the third value w.

Initialize a variable best to 0.

Now go through each triple (a, b, w) in the sorted list:
- Look up Lc = d[a]
- Look up Rc = d[b + 1] - 1
- If Lc <= Rc, call update(1, 0, x - 1, Lc, Rc)
- After that, take E[1], multiply it by w to get cur
- If cur > best, set best = cur

Once you’ve processed every item, you’re done with the main processing flow. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll return a pair. The first element is best, a single number. The second element is a dictionary with three entries: update_calls (the final value of c_u), push_calls (the final value of c_pu), and pull_calls (the final value of c_pl). These three numbers tell you how many times you ran the update logic, how many times you pushed pending updates down to children, and how many times you pulled or recomputed values back up.

def f(n, k, lst):
    st = set()
    for a, b, _ in lst:
        st.add(a)
        st.add(b + 1)
    arr = sorted(st)
    d = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(arr)}
    m = len(arr)
    if m <= 1:
        return (0, {"update_calls": 0, "push_calls": 0, "pull_calls": 0})
    x = m - 1
    size = 4 * x + 5
    A = [0] * size
    B = [0] * size
    C = [0] * size
    D = [0] * size
    E = [0] * size
    F = [0] * size
    c_u = 0
    c_pu = 0
    c_pl = 0
    def build(node, l, r):
        if l == r:
            F[node] = arr[l + 1] - arr[l]
            return
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        build(lc, l, mid)
        build(rc, mid + 1, r)
        F[node] = F[lc] + F[rc]
    def apply(node, val):
        A[node] += val
        B[node] += val
    def push(node):
        nonlocal c_pu
        c_pu += 1
        if B[node] != 0:
            v = B[node]
            lc = node * 2
            rc = node * 2 + 1
            apply(lc, v)
            apply(rc, v)
            B[node] = 0
    def pull(node):
        nonlocal c_pl
        c_pl += 1
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        A[node] = A[lc] if A[lc] < A[rc] else A[rc]
        if A[lc] >= k:
            C[node] = F[lc] + C[rc]
        else:
            C[node] = C[lc]
        if A[rc] >= k:
            D[node] = F[rc] + D[lc]
        else:
            D[node] = D[rc]
        v1 = E[lc]
        v2 = E[rc]
        v3 = D[lc] + C[rc]
        t = v1 if v1 > v2 else v2
        E[node] = t if t > v3 else v3
    def update(node, l, r, ql, qr):
        nonlocal c_u
        c_u += 1
        if ql > r or qr < l:
            return
        if ql <= l and r <= qr:
            apply(node, 1)
            return
        push(node)
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        if ql <= mid:
            update(lc, l, mid, ql, qr)
        if qr > mid:
            update(rc, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
        pull(node)
    build(1, 0, x - 1)
    lst.sort(key=lambda t: t[2])
    best = 0
    for a, b, w in lst:
        Lc = d[a]
        Rc = d[b + 1] - 1
        if Lc <= Rc:
            update(1, 0, x - 1, Lc, Rc)
        cur = E[1] * w
        if cur > best:
            best = cur
    return (best, {"update_calls": c_u, "push_calls": c_pu, "pull_calls": c_pl})
