INPUTS: You have one input, a list called A that holds numbers. That's the only data you start with. 

LOGICS: What you're going to do is start by letting n be the length of the list A and then figure out m by starting with 1 and doubling it until m is at least n+2. Next you create two arrays, tree1 and tree2, each of size 2*m. You fill tree1 with negative infinity and tree2 with zeros. Then you set three counters x, y, z to zero for counting calls and pops. Now you prepare a little helper named psh that you can call whenever you want to push down any pending updates stored in tree2. The way this works is at an index idx, if tree2[idx] is not zero and idx is less than m, you add that tree2[idx] value to both children at positions idx*2 and idx*2+1 in both tree2 and tree1, and then reset tree2[idx] back to zero. Next you also set up another helper called r_add for range addition. Every time you enter r_add you add 1 to x. Then you compare your current segment boundaries l and r to your query boundaries ql and qr. If they do not overlap at all, you return immediately. If the segment [l, r] is completely inside [ql, qr], you add the given val to tree2[idx] and tree1[idx] and return. Otherwise you call psh(idx) to push any pending updates, compute mid as the integer division of (l+r) by 2, recursively call r_add on the left child (idx*2, l to mid) and on the right child (idx*2+1, mid+1 to r), and after both calls update tree1[idx] to the maximum of its two children. You similarly prepare a helper named u_point to set a single position pos to a new value val. If l equals r, you are at the leaf, so you set tree1[idx] to val and tree2[idx] to zero and return. Otherwise you call psh(idx), compute mid, go left or right depending on whether pos is at or below mid, update that leaf, and then set tree1[idx] to the maximum of the two children on your way back up. Then you define q_max for querying a maximum. Each time you enter q_max you add 1 to y. If there is no overlap between [l, r] and [ql, qr] you return negative infinity. If [l, r] is fully inside [ql, qr] you return tree1[idx]. Otherwise you call psh(idx), compute mid, and return the larger of q_max on the left child and q_max on the right child. At this point you make an array dp of length n+1 initialized to zeros and an empty stack st. Then you loop i from 1 to n. In each pass do the following in order: call u_point(1,1,m,i, dp[i-1] minus A[i-1]) to set that position; then call r_add(1,1,m,1,i,A[i-1]) to add A[i-1] across the range from 1 to i; set a local variable l0 to i; then while the stack is not empty and the value at the top of the stack is less than A[i-1], pop the top element into (prev_val, prev_l), add 1 to z, call r_add(1,1,m,prev_l, l0-1, negative of (A[i-1] minus prev_val)) to adjust that previous interval, and set l0 to prev_l; when that loop ends push the pair (A[i-1], l0) onto the stack; finally set dp[i] by calling q_max(1,1,m,1,i). At this point you have completed the loop over all positions and you're done with the step-by-step processing. 

OUTPUTS: At the end you return dp[n] as the main result. You also produce a dictionary with three counts: 'range_add_calls' is x (how many times you entered the range-add procedure), 'query_max_calls' is y (how many times you entered the max-query procedure), and 'stack_pop_count' is z (how many times you popped from the stack).

description:
INPUTS: You have one input, a list called A that holds numbers. That's the only data you start with. 

LOGICS: What you're going to do is start by letting n be the length of the list A and then figure out m by starting with 1 and doubling it until m is at least n+2. Next you create two arrays, tree1 and tree2, each of size 2*m. You fill tree1 with negative infinity and tree2 with zeros. Then you set three counters x, y, z to zero for counting calls and pops. Now you prepare a little helper named psh that you can call whenever you want to push down any pending updates stored in tree2. The way this works is at an index idx, if tree2[idx] is not zero and idx is less than m, you add that tree2[idx] value to both children at positions idx*2 and idx*2+1 in both tree2 and tree1, and then reset tree2[idx] back to zero. Next you also set up another helper called r_add for range addition. Every time you enter r_add you add 1 to x. Then you compare your current segment boundaries l and r to your query boundaries ql and qr. If they do not overlap at all, you return immediately. If the segment [l, r] is completely inside [ql, qr], you add the given val to tree2[idx] and tree1[idx] and return. Otherwise you call psh(idx) to push any pending updates, compute mid as the integer division of (l+r) by 2, recursively call r_add on the left child (idx*2, l to mid) and on the right child (idx*2+1, mid+1 to r), and after both calls update tree1[idx] to the maximum of its two children. You similarly prepare a helper named u_point to set a single position pos to a new value val. If l equals r, you are at the leaf, so you set tree1[idx] to val and tree2[idx] to zero and return. Otherwise you call psh(idx), compute mid, go left or right depending on whether pos is at or below mid, update that leaf, and then set tree1[idx] to the maximum of the two children on your way back up. Then you define q_max for querying a maximum. Each time you enter q_max you add 1 to y. If there is no overlap between [l, r] and [ql, qr] you return negative infinity. If [l, r] is fully inside [ql, qr] you return tree1[idx]. Otherwise you call psh(idx), compute mid, and return the larger of q_max on the left child and q_max on the right child. At this point you make an array dp of length n+1 initialized to zeros and an empty stack st. Then you loop i from 1 to n. In each pass do the following in order: call u_point(1,1,m,i, dp[i-1] minus A[i-1]) to set that position; then call r_add(1,1,m,1,i,A[i-1]) to add A[i-1] across the range from 1 to i; set a local variable l0 to i; then while the stack is not empty and the value at the top of the stack is less than A[i-1], pop the top element into (prev_val, prev_l), add 1 to z, call r_add(1,1,m,prev_l, l0-1, negative of (A[i-1] minus prev_val)) to adjust that previous interval, and set l0 to prev_l; when that loop ends push the pair (A[i-1], l0) onto the stack; finally set dp[i] by calling q_max(1,1,m,1,i). At this point you have completed the loop over all positions and you're done with the step-by-step processing. 

OUTPUTS: At the end you return dp[n] as the main result. You also produce a dictionary with three counts: 'range_add_calls' is x (how many times you entered the range-add procedure), 'query_max_calls' is y (how many times you entered the max-query procedure), and 'stack_pop_count' is z (how many times you popped from the stack).

Now you prepare a little helper named psh that you can call whenever you want to push down any pending updates stored in tree2. The way this works is at an index idx, if tree2[idx] is not zero and idx is less than m, you add that tree2[idx] value to both children at positions idx*2 and idx*2+1 in both tree2 and tree1, and then reset tree2[idx] back to zero. Next you also set up another helper called r_add for range addition. Every time you enter r_add you add 1 to x. Then you compare your current segment boundaries l and r to your query boundaries ql and qr. If they do not overlap at all, you return immediately. If the segment [l, r] is completely inside [ql, qr], you add the given val to tree2[idx] and tree1[idx] and return. Otherwise you call psh(idx) to push any pending updates, compute mid as the integer division of (l+r) by 2, recursively call r_add on the left child (idx*2, l to mid) and on the right child (idx*2+1, mid+1 to r), and after both calls update tree1[idx] to the maximum of its two children. You similarly prepare a helper named u_point to set a single position pos to a new value val. If l equals r, you are at the leaf, so you set tree1[idx] to val and tree2[idx] to zero and return. Otherwise you call psh(idx), compute mid, go left or right depending on whether pos is at or below mid, update that leaf, and then set tree1[idx] to the maximum of the two children on your way back up. Then you define q_max for querying a maximum. Each time you enter q_max you add 1 to y. If there is no overlap between [l, r] and [ql, qr] you return negative infinity. If [l, r] is fully inside [ql, qr] you return tree1[idx]. Otherwise you call psh(idx), compute mid, and return the larger of q_max on the left child and q_max on the right child. At this point you make an array dp of length n+1 initialized to zeros and an empty stack st. Then you loop i from 1 to n. In each pass do the following in order: call u_point(1,1,m,i, dp[i-1] minus A[i-1]) to set that position; then call r_add(1,1,m,1,i,A[i-1]) to add A[i-1] across the range from 1 to i; set a local variable l0 to i; then while the stack is not empty and the value at the top of the stack is less than A[i-1], pop the top element into (prev_val, prev_l), add 1 to z, call r_add(1,1,m,prev_l, l0-1, negative of (A[i-1] minus prev_val)) to adjust that previous interval, and set l0 to prev_l; when that loop ends push the pair (A[i-1], l0) onto the stack; finally set dp[i] by calling q_max(1,1,m,1,i). INPUTS: You have one input, a list called A that holds numbers. That's the only data you start with. 

LOGICS: What you're going to do is start by letting n be the length of the list A and then figure out m by starting with 1 and doubling it until m is at least n+2. Next you create two arrays, tree1 and tree2, each of size 2*m. You fill tree1 with negative infinity and tree2 with zeros. Then you set three counters x, y, z to zero for counting calls and pops. Now you prepare a little helper named psh that you can call whenever you want to push down any pending updates stored in tree2. The way this works is at an index idx, if tree2[idx] is not zero and idx is less than m, you add that tree2[idx] value to both children at positions idx*2 and idx*2+1 in both tree2 and tree1, and then reset tree2[idx] back to zero. Next you also set up another helper called r_add for range addition. Every time you enter r_add you add 1 to x. Then you compare your current segment boundaries l and r to your query boundaries ql and qr. If they do not overlap at all, you return immediately. If the segment [l, r] is completely inside [ql, qr], you add the given val to tree2[idx] and tree1[idx] and return. Otherwise you call psh(idx) to push any pending updates, compute mid as the integer division of (l+r) by 2, recursively call r_add on the left child (idx*2, l to mid) and on the right child (idx*2+1, mid+1 to r), and after both calls update tree1[idx] to the maximum of its two children. You similarly prepare a helper named u_point to set a single position pos to a new value val. If l equals r, you are at the leaf, so you set tree1[idx] to val and tree2[idx] to zero and return. Otherwise you call psh(idx), compute mid, go left or right depending on whether pos is at or below mid, update that leaf, and then set tree1[idx] to the maximum of the two children on your way back up. Then you define q_max for querying a maximum. Each time you enter q_max you add 1 to y. If there is no overlap between [l, r] and [ql, qr] you return negative infinity. If [l, r] is fully inside [ql, qr] you return tree1[idx]. Otherwise you call psh(idx), compute mid, and return the larger of q_max on the left child and q_max on the right child. At this point you make an array dp of length n+1 initialized to zeros and an empty stack st. Then you loop i from 1 to n. In each pass do the following in order: call u_point(1,1,m,i, dp[i-1] minus A[i-1]) to set that position; then call r_add(1,1,m,1,i,A[i-1]) to add A[i-1] across the range from 1 to i; set a local variable l0 to i; then while the stack is not empty and the value at the top of the stack is less than A[i-1], pop the top element into (prev_val, prev_l), add 1 to z, call r_add(1,1,m,prev_l, l0-1, negative of (A[i-1] minus prev_val)) to adjust that previous interval, and set l0 to prev_l; when that loop ends push the pair (A[i-1], l0) onto the stack; finally set dp[i] by calling q_max(1,1,m,1,i). At this point you have completed the loop over all positions and you're done with the step-by-step processing. 

OUTPUTS: At the end you return dp[n] as the main result. You also produce a dictionary with three counts: 'range_add_calls' is x (how many times you entered the range-add procedure), 'query_max_calls' is y (how many times you entered the max-query procedure), and 'stack_pop_count' is z (how many times you popped from the stack).

INPUTS: n, m, and k are integers. lst is a list of k integers. arr is a list of m pairs of integers. 

LOGICS: Start by setting up a stats dictionary with keys red_enqueues, reach_enqueues, and probe_calls all at zero. Next you need to create a list A containing n empty lists. The way this works is each index in A will hold the neighbors for that index. Then go through each pair in arr. For each one, take the two numbers and subtract one from each to convert from one-based to zero-based indexing; call the first result x and the second y. Then append y to the list at A[x] and append x to A[y]. At this point A holds the adjacency structure. Now create a list d of length n and fill every entry with a large number so big it represents infinity. Next, set up an empty queue Q that you will use in a first search. Take each number s from lst, subtract one to get idx, and if d[idx] is greater than zero, set d[idx] to zero and add idx to the end of Q. That seeds your starting points. Then repeat the following until Q is empty: remove the first element of Q, call it u. Look at every neighbor v in A[u]; if d[v] is greater than d[u] plus one, then set d[v] to d[u] plus one, add v to the end of Q, and increase stats red_enqueues by one. After you finish that you have computed a distance array d. Next you will compute another distance array called dist: make a list of length n filled with infinity, then set dist at index zero to zero. Create a new empty queue Q and add zero to it. Now repeat until Q empties: remove the first element, call it u. For each neighbor v in A[u], if dist[v] is greater than dist[u] plus one, then set dist[v] to dist[u] plus one, add v to the end of Q, and increase stats reach_enqueues by one. Once that finishes check if dist at index n minus one is still infinity. If it is, you stop here and return negative one with the stats you have. If not, you proceed to define a helper procedure can that takes a parameter D. Inside can, first check if D is at least d at zero; if so, return false. Otherwise create two new lists of length n, vis filled with false and depth filled with zero. Then set up a queue Q2 containing zero and mark vis at zero as true. Repeat until Q2 empties: remove the first item, call it u2. If u2 equals n minus one, return true. Otherwise for each neighbor v2 in A[u2], check if vis[v2] is false and D plus depth at u2 plus one is less than d[v2]. If both are true, mark vis[v2] as true, set depth[v2] to depth[u2] plus one, and add v2 to the end of Q2. After that loop ends without returning true, return false. With that helper in place, start a binary search by setting lo to zero, hi to n, and ans to minus one. Then while lo is less than or equal to hi, compute mid as the floor of lo plus hi divided by two, add one to stats probe_calls, and call can(mid). If can(mid) returns true, set ans to mid and set lo to mid plus one. Otherwise set hi to mid minus one. Continue this until lo exceeds hi, then return ans and the stats dictionary. 

OUTPUTS: You return ans and stats. ans is your final integer result which will be minus one if the last index was unreachable or otherwise the highest integer D that satisfied the feasibility check. stats is a dictionary with three counts: red_enqueues shows how many times you added a node in the first distance filling search, reach_enqueues shows how many times you added a node in the second reachability search, and probe_calls shows how many times you tested a D value with the helper during the binary search.

INPUTS: n, m, and k are integers. lst is a list of k integers. arr is a list of m pairs of integers. 

LOGICS: Start by setting up a stats dictionary with keys red_enqueues, reach_enqueues, and probe_calls all at zero. Next you need to create a list A containing n empty lists. The way this works is each index in A will hold the neighbors for that index. Then go through each pair in arr. For each one, take the two numbers and subtract one from each to convert from one-based to zero-based indexing; call the first result x and the second y. Then append y to the list at A[x] and append x to A[y]. At this point A holds the adjacency structure. Now create a list d of length n and fill every entry with a large number so big it represents infinity. Next, set up an empty queue Q that you will use in a first search. Take each number s from lst, subtract one to get idx, and if d[idx] is greater than zero, set d[idx] to zero and add idx to the end of Q. That seeds your starting points. Then repeat the following until Q is empty: remove the first element of Q, call it u. Look at every neighbor v in A[u]; if d[v] is greater than d[u] plus one, then set d[v] to d[u] plus one, add v to the end of Q, and increase stats red_enqueues by one. After you finish that you have computed a distance array d. Next you will compute another distance array called dist: make a list of length n filled with infinity, then set dist at index zero to zero. Create a new empty queue Q and add zero to it. Now repeat until Q empties: remove the first element, call it u. For each neighbor v in A[u], if dist[v] is greater than dist[u] plus one, then set dist[v] to dist[u] plus one, add v to the end of Q, and increase stats reach_enqueues by one. Once that finishes check if dist at index n minus one is still infinity. If it is, you stop here and return negative one with the stats you have. If not, you proceed to define a helper procedure can that takes a parameter D. Inside can, first check if D is at least d at zero; if so, return false. Otherwise create two new lists of length n, vis filled with false and depth filled with zero. Then set up a queue Q2 containing zero and mark vis at zero as true. Repeat until Q2 empties: remove the first item, call it u2. If u2 equals n minus one, return true. Otherwise for each neighbor v2 in A[u2], check if vis[v2] is false and D plus depth at u2 plus one is less than d[v2]. If both are true, mark vis[v2] as true, set depth[v2] to depth[u2] plus one, and add v2 to the end of Q2. After that loop ends without returning true, return false. With that helper in place, start a binary search by setting lo to zero, hi to n, and ans to minus one. Then while lo is less than or equal to hi, compute mid as the floor of lo plus hi divided by two, add one to stats probe_calls, and call can(mid). If can(mid) returns true, set ans to mid and set lo to mid plus one. Otherwise set hi to mid minus one. Continue this until lo exceeds hi, then return ans and the stats dictionary. 

OUTPUTS: You return ans and stats. ans is your final integer result which will be minus one if the last index was unreachable or otherwise the highest integer D that satisfied the feasibility check. stats is a dictionary with three counts: red_enqueues shows how many times you added a node in the first distance filling search, reach_enqueues shows how many times you added a node in the second reachability search, and probe_calls shows how many times you tested a D value with the helper during the binary search.

Now create a list d of length n and fill every entry with a large number so big it represents infinity. Next, set up an empty queue Q that you will use in a first search. Then repeat the following until Q is empty: remove the first element of Q, call it u. Look at every neighbor v in A[u]; if d[v] is greater than d[u] plus one, then set d[v] to d[u] plus one, add v to the end of Q, and increase stats red_enqueues by one. After you finish that you have computed a distance array d. Next you will compute another distance array called dist: make a list of length n filled with infinity, then set dist at index zero to zero. Create a new empty queue Q and add zero to it. Now repeat until Q empties: remove the first element, call it u. For each neighbor v in A[u], if dist[v] is greater than dist[u] plus one, then set dist[v] to dist[u] plus one, add v to the end of Q, and increase stats reach_enqueues by one. Once that finishes check if dist at index n minus one is still infinity. If it is, you stop here and return negative one with the stats you have. If not, you proceed to define a helper procedure can that takes a parameter D. Inside can, first check if D is at least d at zero; if so, return false. With that helper in place, start a binary search by setting lo to zero, hi to n, and ans to minus one. INPUTS: You’re working with two pieces of data: first, an integer n, and second, a list L that contains m pairs of numbers (we’ll call each pair (x, y)). You can think of L as having length m, and each entry holds two numbers. 

LOGICS: Okay, here’s what you do step by step:

1. Set up three counters and name them exactly initial_edges, artificial_edges, and edge_traversals. Give each one the starting value 0.

2. Build an adjacency structure called A. To do that, create a list with n+1 empty sublists inside it. So A is a list whose entries A[0], A[1], …, A[n] are all empty lists right now.

3. Figure out m by counting how many pairs are in your list L.

4. Now go through each pair in L one at a time, and keep track of which number you’re on by using a counter val that starts at 1 and increments by 1 after each pair:
   - When you look at the val-th pair, call its two values x and y.
   - Add 1 to your counter initial_edges.
   - In the sublist A[x], append the tuple (y, val).
   - In the sublist A[y], append the tuple (x, val).
   - Then move on to the next pair and increase val by 1.

5. After you finish that loop, set up a new counter z and give it the value m + 1.

6. Next, you’re going to scan nodes numbered 1 through n in order. For each node number x:
   - Count how many items are currently in A[x].
   - If that count is odd (meaning there’s a remainder of 1 when you divide by 2), then:
     a. Add 1 to artificial_edges.
     b. In A[x], append the tuple (0, z).
     c. In A[0], append the tuple (x, z).
     d. Increase z by 1.
   - If the count is even, do nothing and move on to the next x.

7. Now you’ve finished adding any artificial connections. Time to prepare for the traversal:
   - Make a list vis of length z (so from index 0 up to z–1), and fill it with False.
   - Make a list B that has m+1 slots (indexes 0 through m), all set to None at first.
   - Make a list P of length n+1 (indexes 0 through n), all set to 0 at first.

8. You’re going to do a walk over these lists using a stack. For each starting point s from 0 up to n:
   - Check if P[s] is still less than the number of entries in A[s]. If it isn’t (meaning P[s] == len(A[s])), skip this s and move on.
   - If it is less, start with a stack containing just [s].
   - While the stack is not empty, repeat:
     a. Look at the top item on the stack and call it x.
     b. Now skip over any edges at A[x] that have already been visited. You do that by checking the current pointer P[x], looking at the tuple A[x][P[x]] which is (neighbor, edgeNumber), and if vis[edgeNumber] is True, add 1 to P[x] and check again. Keep doing that until you either find an unvisited edge or you run out of edges in A[x].
     c. If P[x] is now equal to the length of A[x], it means there are no more unused edges at x, so pop x off the stack and go back to the top of the while-loop.
     d. Otherwise, you have found an unused edge. Call that tuple (y, val2) = A[x][P[x]].
        i. Mark that edge as visited by setting vis[val2] = True.
       ii. Add 1 to edge_traversals.
      iii. Push y onto the stack.
       iv. Add 1 to P[x] to record that you consumed that entry.
        v. If val2 is less than or equal to m (meaning it’s one of your original pairs, not an artificial one), then record the direction by setting B[val2] = (x, y).
     e. Go back to step a with the updated stack.
   - When the stack empties, you’ve finished exploring from s. Move on to the next s until you’ve done all from 0 to n.

9. After all of that, you have filled in B for each original edge index from 1 to m, and you have updated your three counters along the way.

10. Finally, collect the results. You’ll return a list made of B[1], B[2], …, B[m] in that exact order, along with a dictionary that holds the final values of initial_edges, artificial_edges, and edge_traversals. 

OUTPUTS: When you’re done, you get two things:

1. A list of m pairs, where the i-th pair tells you (x, y) for the original i-th entry in L showing how that edge was traversed.
2. A dictionary with three numbers:
   – initial_edges: the total count of original pairs you processed (that ends up being m),
   – artificial_edges: how many extra connections you had to add because some nodes had an odd number of entries,
   – edge_traversals: the total number of times you marked an edge as visited during the stack-based walk.

1. Set up three counters and name them exactly initial_edges, artificial_edges, and edge_traversals. Give each one the starting value 0.

3. Figure out m by counting how many pairs are in your list L.

4. Now go through each pair in L one at a time, and keep track of which number you’re on by using a counter val that starts at 1 and increments by 1 after each pair:
   - When you look at the val-th pair, call its two values x and y.
   - Add 1 to your counter initial_edges.
   - In the sublist A[x], append the tuple (y, val).
   - In the sublist A[y], append the tuple (x, val).
   - Then move on to the next pair and increase val by 1.

5. After you finish that loop, set up a new counter z and give it the value m + 1.

6. Next, you’re going to scan nodes numbered 1 through n in order. For each node number x:
   - Count how many items are currently in A[x].

     a. Add 1 to artificial_edges.
     b. In A[x], append the tuple (0, z).
     c. In A[0], append the tuple (x, z).
     d. Increase z by 1.

def f(n, arr, A, B):
    from heapq import heapify, heappush, heappop
    L = sorted(range(n), key=lambda x: arr[x])
    P = [-1] * n
    N = [-1] * n
    for idx, i in enumerate(L):
        if idx > 0:
            P[i] = L[idx - 1]
        if idx < n - 1:
            N[i] = L[idx + 1]
    lst = A[:]
    pr = [-1] * n
    seen = [False] * n
    pq = [(lst[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    heapify(pq)
    total = 0
    out1 = []
    out2 = []
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    check_count = 0
    while pq:
        cost, i = heappop(pq)
        pop_count += 1
        if seen[i]:
            continue
        seen[i] = True
        total += cost
        if pr[i] == -1:
            out1.append(i + 1)
        else:
            out2.append((pr[i] + 1, i + 1))
        p = P[i]
        q = N[i]
        if p != -1:
            N[p] = q
        if q != -1:
            P[q] = p
        j = p
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = P[j]
            else:
                break
        j = q
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = N[j]
            else:
                break
    return ((total, out1, out2), {'heap_pushes': push_count, 'heap_pops': pop_count, 'neighbor_checks': check_count})

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is build a list called L that contains all the positions from 0 up to n−1, but sorted so that the position with the smallest arr value comes first and the largest comes last. To do that, just write down the numbers 0, 1, 2, …, n−1, then reorder them by looking at arr at each position and putting the smallest arr value’s index at the front, next smallest next, and so on.

Next, create two helper lists P and N, each of length n, and fill them both with −1. These will act like pointers in a doubly linked list. Now go through L in order: for each position idx in L, let i = L[idx]. If idx is greater than 0, set P[i] = L[idx−1]; that means i’s predecessor is the previous entry in L. If idx is less than n−1, set N[i] = L[idx+1]; that means i’s successor is the next entry in L.

Now copy your list A into a new list called lst (so you can change lst without touching A). Create another list pr of length n filled with −1; that will remember, for each position, which other position updated its cost. Also make a list seen of length n filled with False; that tracks which positions you’ve already taken out of your queue.

After that, build a list called pq of n pairs: for each position i from 0 to n−1, pair up (lst[i], i). Turn pq into a min-heap—this is your working priority queue. Then set up these counters: total = 0, out1 = empty list, out2 = empty list, push_count = 0, pop_count = 0, check_count = 0.

Now here’s the main loop: As long as pq is not empty, do the following steps:

  • Take the smallest pair out of pq (that’s a pop). You’ll get back two things: cost and an index i. As soon as you remove it, add 1 to pop_count.

  • If seen[i] is already True, just skip everything else in this loop and go back to popping the next pair—because you’ve already processed i before.

  • Otherwise, mark seen[i] = True, and add cost to total.

  • Look at pr[i]. If pr[i] is −1, that means nothing updated i’s cost, so append i+1 to out1. If pr[i] is some other position, append the pair (pr[i]+1, i+1) to out2. We add 1 to each index here just to shift from zero-based to one-based numbering in your final lists.

  • Next, you’re going to remove i from that linked-list structure: let p = P[i] and q = N[i]. If p is not −1, set N[p] = q (so p skips over i). If q is not −1, set P[q] = p.

  • Now you check neighbors on the left side. Set j = p. While j is not −1, do:
      – Add 1 to check_count.
      – Compute val = (B[i] + B[j]) × absolute value of (arr[i] − arr[j]).
      – If val is strictly less than lst[j], then:
          * Set lst[j] = val.
          * Set pr[j] = i.
          * Push the pair (val, j) onto pq, and add 1 to push_count.
          * Move j to P[j] (the next predecessor) and repeat the while.
        Otherwise (val ≥ lst[j]), break out of this while (you stop walking left).

  • After you finish the left side, do the same on the right side: set j = q. While j is not −1, do exactly the same steps (increment check_count, compute val, compare to lst[j], update lst, pr, push_count, and push onto pq if it’s lower, then move j to N[j]). If at any point val is not less, break out of that while.

  • Once both directions are handled, go back to the top of the big loop and pop the next item.

When pq finally empties out, you’ve built up total, out1, out2, and your three counters. Those are your final results. 

OUTPUTS: You’ll end up with two things: first, a triple (total, out1, out2). total is the sum of all the costs you actually accepted when you popped each new item for the first time. out1 is the list of 1-based positions that never had another position improving their cost (those with pr[i] = −1), and out2 is the list of ordered pairs (parent, child) in 1-based form showing which position improved which. Second, you get a small dictionary of statistics: 'heap_pushes' tells you how many times you pushed a new pair onto the heap, 'heap_pops' tells you how many times you removed a pair from the heap, and 'neighbor_checks' tells you how many times you computed that val and compared it to lst[j].

def f(n, arr, A, B):
    from heapq import heapify, heappush, heappop
    L = sorted(range(n), key=lambda x: arr[x])
    P = [-1] * n
    N = [-1] * n
    for idx, i in enumerate(L):
        if idx > 0:
            P[i] = L[idx - 1]
        if idx < n - 1:
            N[i] = L[idx + 1]
    lst = A[:]
    pr = [-1] * n
    seen = [False] * n
    pq = [(lst[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    heapify(pq)
    total = 0
    out1 = []
    out2 = []
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    check_count = 0
    while pq:
        cost, i = heappop(pq)
        pop_count += 1
        if seen[i]:
            continue
        seen[i] = True
        total += cost
        if pr[i] == -1:
            out1.append(i + 1)
        else:
            out2.append((pr[i] + 1, i + 1))
        p = P[i]
        q = N[i]
        if p != -1:
            N[p] = q
        if q != -1:
            P[q] = p
        j = p
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = P[j]
            else:
                break
        j = q
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = N[j]
            else:
                break
    return ((total, out1, out2), {'heap_pushes': push_count, 'heap_pops': pop_count, 'neighbor_checks': check_count})

INPUTS: You have four inputs: a number n, which tells you how many items you’re working with; a list called arr of length n that holds some numerical values; another list A of length n that holds a starting cost for each of those n items; and a third list B of length n that also holds a number for each item. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is build a list called L that contains all the positions from 0 up to n−1, but sorted so that the position with the smallest arr value comes first and the largest comes last. To do that, just write down the numbers 0, 1, 2, …, n−1, then reorder them by looking at arr at each position and putting the smallest arr value’s index at the front, next smallest next, and so on.

Next, create two helper lists P and N, each of length n, and fill them both with −1. These will act like pointers in a doubly linked list. Now go through L in order: for each position idx in L, let i = L[idx]. If idx is greater than 0, set P[i] = L[idx−1]; that means i’s predecessor is the previous entry in L. If idx is less than n−1, set N[i] = L[idx+1]; that means i’s successor is the next entry in L.

Now copy your list A into a new list called lst (so you can change lst without touching A). Create another list pr of length n filled with −1; that will remember, for each position, which other position updated its cost. Also make a list seen of length n filled with False; that tracks which positions you’ve already taken out of your queue.

After that, build a list called pq of n pairs: for each position i from 0 to n−1, pair up (lst[i], i). Turn pq into a min-heap—this is your working priority queue. Then set up these counters: total = 0, out1 = empty list, out2 = empty list, push_count = 0, pop_count = 0, check_count = 0.

Now here’s the main loop: As long as pq is not empty, do the following steps:

  • Take the smallest pair out of pq (that’s a pop). You’ll get back two things: cost and an index i. As soon as you remove it, add 1 to pop_count.

  • If seen[i] is already True, just skip everything else in this loop and go back to popping the next pair—because you’ve already processed i before.

  • Otherwise, mark seen[i] = True, and add cost to total.

  • Look at pr[i]. If pr[i] is −1, that means nothing updated i’s cost, so append i+1 to out1. If pr[i] is some other position, append the pair (pr[i]+1, i+1) to out2. We add 1 to each index here just to shift from zero-based to one-based numbering in your final lists.

  • Next, you’re going to remove i from that linked-list structure: let p = P[i] and q = N[i]. If p is not −1, set N[p] = q (so p skips over i). If q is not −1, set P[q] = p.

  • Now you check neighbors on the left side. Set j = p. While j is not −1, do:
      – Add 1 to check_count.
      – Compute val = (B[i] + B[j]) × absolute value of (arr[i] − arr[j]).
      – If val is strictly less than lst[j], then:
          * Set lst[j] = val.
          * Set pr[j] = i.
          * Push the pair (val, j) onto pq, and add 1 to push_count.
          * Move j to P[j] (the next predecessor) and repeat the while.
        Otherwise (val ≥ lst[j]), break out of this while (you stop walking left).

  • After you finish the left side, do the same on the right side: set j = q. While j is not −1, do exactly the same steps (increment check_count, compute val, compare to lst[j], update lst, pr, push_count, and push onto pq if it’s lower, then move j to N[j]). If at any point val is not less, break out of that while.

  • Once both directions are handled, go back to the top of the big loop and pop the next item.

When pq finally empties out, you’ve built up total, out1, out2, and your three counters. Those are your final results. 

OUTPUTS: You’ll end up with two things: first, a triple (total, out1, out2). total is the sum of all the costs you actually accepted when you popped each new item for the first time. out1 is the list of 1-based positions that never had another position improving their cost (those with pr[i] = −1), and out2 is the list of ordered pairs (parent, child) in 1-based form showing which position improved which. Second, you get a small dictionary of statistics: 'heap_pushes' tells you how many times you pushed a new pair onto the heap, 'heap_pops' tells you how many times you removed a pair from the heap, and 'neighbor_checks' tells you how many times you computed that val and compared it to lst[j].

def f(n, arr, A, B):
    from heapq import heapify, heappush, heappop
    L = sorted(range(n), key=lambda x: arr[x])
    P = [-1] * n
    N = [-1] * n
    for idx, i in enumerate(L):
        if idx > 0:
            P[i] = L[idx - 1]
        if idx < n - 1:
            N[i] = L[idx + 1]
    lst = A[:]
    pr = [-1] * n
    seen = [False] * n
    pq = [(lst[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    heapify(pq)
    total = 0
    out1 = []
    out2 = []
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    check_count = 0
    while pq:
        cost, i = heappop(pq)
        pop_count += 1
        if seen[i]:
            continue
        seen[i] = True
        total += cost
        if pr[i] == -1:
            out1.append(i + 1)
        else:
            out2.append((pr[i] + 1, i + 1))
        p = P[i]
        q = N[i]
        if p != -1:
            N[p] = q
        if q != -1:
            P[q] = p
        j = p
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = P[j]
            else:
                break
        j = q
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = N[j]
            else:
                break
    return ((total, out1, out2), {'heap_pushes': push_count, 'heap_pops': pop_count, 'neighbor_checks': check_count})

def f(n, arr, A, B):
    from heapq import heapify, heappush, heappop
    L = sorted(range(n), key=lambda x: arr[x])
    P = [-1] * n
    N = [-1] * n
    for idx, i in enumerate(L):
        if idx > 0:
            P[i] = L[idx - 1]
        if idx < n - 1:
            N[i] = L[idx + 1]
    lst = A[:]
    pr = [-1] * n
    seen = [False] * n
    pq = [(lst[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    heapify(pq)
    total = 0
    out1 = []
    out2 = []
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    check_count = 0
    while pq:
        cost, i = heappop(pq)
        pop_count += 1
        if seen[i]:
            continue
        seen[i] = True
        total += cost
        if pr[i] == -1:
            out1.append(i + 1)
        else:
            out2.append((pr[i] + 1, i + 1))
        p = P[i]
        q = N[i]
        if p != -1:
            N[p] = q
        if q != -1:
            P[q] = p
        j = p
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = P[j]
            else:
                break
        j = q
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = N[j]
            else:
                break
    return ((total, out1, out2), {'heap_pushes': push_count, 'heap_pops': pop_count, 'neighbor_checks': check_count})

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is build a list called L that contains all the positions from 0 up to n−1, but sorted so that the position with the smallest arr value comes first and the largest comes last. To do that, just write down the numbers 0, 1, 2, …, n−1, then reorder them by looking at arr at each position and putting the smallest arr value’s index at the front, next smallest next, and so on.

Next, create two helper lists P and N, each of length n, and fill them both with −1. These will act like pointers in a doubly linked list. Now go through L in order: for each position idx in L, let i = L[idx]. If idx is greater than 0, set P[i] = L[idx−1]; that means i’s predecessor is the previous entry in L. If idx is less than n−1, set N[i] = L[idx+1]; that means i’s successor is the next entry in L.

Now copy your list A into a new list called lst (so you can change lst without touching A). Create another list pr of length n filled with −1; that will remember, for each position, which other position updated its cost. Also make a list seen of length n filled with False; that tracks which positions you’ve already taken out of your queue.

After that, build a list called pq of n pairs: for each position i from 0 to n−1, pair up (lst[i], i). Turn pq into a min-heap—this is your working priority queue. Then set up these counters: total = 0, out1 = empty list, out2 = empty list, push_count = 0, pop_count = 0, check_count = 0.

Now here’s the main loop: As long as pq is not empty, do the following steps:

  • Take the smallest pair out of pq (that’s a pop). You’ll get back two things: cost and an index i. As soon as you remove it, add 1 to pop_count.

  • If seen[i] is already True, just skip everything else in this loop and go back to popping the next pair—because you’ve already processed i before.

  • Otherwise, mark seen[i] = True, and add cost to total.

  • Look at pr[i]. If pr[i] is −1, that means nothing updated i’s cost, so append i+1 to out1. If pr[i] is some other position, append the pair (pr[i]+1, i+1) to out2. We add 1 to each index here just to shift from zero-based to one-based numbering in your final lists.

  • Next, you’re going to remove i from that linked-list structure: let p = P[i] and q = N[i]. If p is not −1, set N[p] = q (so p skips over i). If q is not −1, set P[q] = p.

  • Now you check neighbors on the left side. Set j = p. While j is not −1, do:
      – Add 1 to check_count.
      – Compute val = (B[i] + B[j]) × absolute value of (arr[i] − arr[j]).
      – If val is strictly less than lst[j], then:
          * Set lst[j] = val.
          * Set pr[j] = i.
          * Push the pair (val, j) onto pq, and add 1 to push_count.
          * Move j to P[j] (the next predecessor) and repeat the while.
        Otherwise (val ≥ lst[j]), break out of this while (you stop walking left).

  • After you finish the left side, do the same on the right side: set j = q. While j is not −1, do exactly the same steps (increment check_count, compute val, compare to lst[j], update lst, pr, push_count, and push onto pq if it’s lower, then move j to N[j]). If at any point val is not less, break out of that while.

  • Once both directions are handled, go back to the top of the big loop and pop the next item.

When pq finally empties out, you’ve built up total, out1, out2, and your three counters. Those are your final results. 

OUTPUTS: You’ll end up with two things: first, a triple (total, out1, out2). total is the sum of all the costs you actually accepted when you popped each new item for the first time. out1 is the list of 1-based positions that never had another position improving their cost (those with pr[i] = −1), and out2 is the list of ordered pairs (parent, child) in 1-based form showing which position improved which. Second, you get a small dictionary of statistics: 'heap_pushes' tells you how many times you pushed a new pair onto the heap, 'heap_pops' tells you how many times you removed a pair from the heap, and 'neighbor_checks' tells you how many times you computed that val and compared it to lst[j].

INPUTS: You’ve got three pieces of data to work with: first, a single number called n; second, a list of pairs of numbers called lst (each pair written as (x, y)); and third, a plain list of numbers called arr. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is set up your workspace exactly as the code does and then follow every step by hand.  

1. Start by creating three counters: split_cnt = 0, merge_cnt = 0, and push_cnt = 0.  These will track how many times you run split, merge, and push.  
2. Make a variable named root and set it to None.  This will be the root of your tree.  

-- Building the initial tree from arr --  
3. Now you need to turn each number in arr into a Node and merge it into root in order.  So take the first number x in arr, then the next, and so on.  For each x:  
   a. Create a record called Node with these fields:  
      • val = x  
      • prio = pick a random integer once (for example, note down 8342753 or whatever you get) and record that exact number in your Node; you must use that same number whenever you compare this Node’s priority later.  
      • sz = 1  
      • left = None  
      • right = None  
      • rev = False  
   b. Now merge this new Node into your existing root by doing merge(root, Node).  Every time you begin a merge call (even if one of the arguments is None), immediately add 1 to merge_cnt.  

-- The merge operation, step by step --  
When you call merge(a, b):  
   1. You already bumped merge_cnt by 1.  
   2. If a is None, return b; if b is None, return a.  (Either way you still counted this merge call.)  
   3. Otherwise, compare a.prio and b.prio using the exact numbers you recorded.  
      - If a.prio < b.prio:  
        • Call push(a) before you do anything else.  That means add 1 to push_cnt, then check a.rev:  
          · If a.rev is True, swap a.left and a.right, then for each child that exists flip its rev flag (True becomes False, False becomes True), and then set a.rev = False.  
          · If a.rev is False, you still clear it by setting a.rev = False and you do the swap logic only if it was True, but you do count this push call regardless.  
        • After push(a), set a.right = merge(a.right, b).  Every recursive merge call also bumps merge_cnt at its start.  
        • Then recalculate a.sz = 1 + (size of a.left, zero if None) + (size of a.right, zero if None).  
        • Return a.  
      - If a.prio >= b.prio: do the same steps but on b:  
        • Call push(b) (add 1 to push_cnt, handle the swap and rev clearing unconditionally).  
        • Set b.left = merge(a, b.left).  
        • Recalculate b.sz = 1 + size(b.left) + size(b.right).  
        • Return b.  

Repeat those merge steps until every x in arr has been merged, so at the end of this loop root holds the full tree.  

-- Processing the reversals from lst in reverse order --  
4. Now you need to go through lst from the last pair to the first pair.  For each pair (x, y) in reversed(lst):  
   a. Compute x0 = x - 1 and y0 = y - 1, so you’re using zero-based positions.  
   b. First split: call split(root, x0).  
      • As soon as you call split, add 1 to split_cnt.  
      • If the node t you passed in is None, return (None, None).  Otherwise, at the top of split you must call push(t): add 1 to push_cnt, then if t.rev is True swap t.left and t.right, flip each child’s rev if it exists, and set t.rev = False (if it was already False you still clear it).  
      • Compute left_sz = size of t.left (zero if t.left is None).  
      • If left_sz >= k (here k is x0):  
         – Call split(t.left, k) (this bumps split_cnt and does a push on t.left), which returns (l, r).  
         – Then set t.left = r.  
         – Recalculate t.sz = 1 + size(t.left) + size(t.right).  
         – Return (l, t).  
      • Otherwise (left_sz < k):  
         – Call split(t.right, k - left_sz - 1).  
         – That returns (l, r).  
         – Set t.right = l.  
         – Recalculate t.sz = 1 + size(t.left) + size(t.right).  
         – Return (t, r).  
      • Collect the result of this first split as (a, br).  
   c. Second split: call split(br, y0 - x0 + 1).  Do exactly the same process: bump split_cnt, push on br, decide left_sz vs. the new k, split left or right recursively, update sizes.  Call the result (b, c).  
   d. If b is not None, toggle its rev flag by doing b.rev = not b.rev.  That means if it was False make it True, and vice versa.  
   e. Finally rebuild root by doing merge(a, b) (count 1 merge at its start) and then merge(that result, c) (another merge count).  Assign the final merged node back into root.  

Repeat that whole process for every pair in the reversed lst.  After you finish all of them, you have applied every reversal in exactly the right order.  

-- In-order traversal to collect the result --  
5. Now define a function inorder(t) that walks the tree in order and fills a list called result:  
   a. If t is None, just return.  
   b. At the top of inorder, call push(t): add 1 to push_cnt, then if t.rev is True swap t.left and t.right, flip each child’s rev if it exists, and set t.rev = False (if it was False you still clear it).  
   c. Call inorder(t.left).  
   d. Append t.val to result.  
   e. Call inorder(t.right).  
6. Start with result = an empty list.  Then call inorder(root).  When that finishes, result holds the final sequence of values, and you’ve also tallied every split, merge, and push along the way. 

OUTPUTS: When you’re done, you’ll have two things:  
1. result – a list of the numbers in the exact order you get when you walk the tree in-order after all those reversals.  
2. A small dictionary with three entries:  
   • 'split_calls': the final value of split_cnt (how many times you ran the split logic)  
   • 'merge_calls': the final value of merge_cnt (how many times you ran merge)  
   • 'push_calls': the final value of push_cnt (how many times you called push, at every split, merge, and in-order step)

      • right = None

   b. Now merge this new Node into your existing root by doing merge(root, Node).  Every time you begin a merge call (even if one of the arguments is None), immediately add 1 to merge_cnt.

   1. You already bumped merge_cnt by 1.  
   2. If a is None, return b; if b is None, return a.  (Either way you still counted this merge call.)  
   3. Otherwise, compare a.prio and b.prio using the exact numbers you recorded.  
      - If a.prio < b.prio:  
        • Call push(a) before you do anything else.  That means add 1 to push_cnt, then check a.rev:  
          · If a.rev is True, swap a.left and a.right, then for each child that exists flip its rev flag (True becomes False, False becomes True), and then set a.rev = False.  
          · If a.rev is False, you still clear it by setting a.rev = False and you do the swap logic only if it was True, but you do count this push call regardless.

        • Then recalculate a.sz = 1 + (size of a.left, zero if None) + (size of a.right, zero if None).  
        • Return a.

        • Call push(b) (add 1 to push_cnt, handle the swap and rev clearing unconditionally).  
        • Set b.left = merge(a, b.left).

         – Recalculate t.sz = 1 + size(t.left) + size(t.right).  
         – Return (l, t).  
      • Otherwise (left_sz < k):  
         – Call split(t.right, k - left_sz - 1).  
         – That returns (l, r).  
         – Set t.right = l.  
         – Recalculate t.sz = 1 + size(t.left) + size(t.right).  
         – Return (t, r).  
      • Collect the result of this first split as (a, br).  
   c. Second split: call split(br, y0 - x0 + 1).  Do exactly the same process: bump split_cnt, push on br, decide left_sz vs. the new k, split left or right recursively, update sizes.  Call the result (b, c).  
   d. If b is not None, toggle its rev flag by doing b.rev = not b.rev.  That means if it was False make it True, and vice versa.  
   e. Finally rebuild root by doing merge(a, b) (count 1 merge at its start) and then merge(that result, c) (another merge count).  Assign the final merged node back into root.  

Repeat that whole process for every pair in the reversed lst.  After you finish all of them, you have applied every reversal in exactly the right order.  

-- In-order traversal to collect the result --  
5. Now define a function inorder(t) that walks the tree in order and fills a list called result:  
   a. If t is None, just return.

   c. Call inorder(t.left).  
   d. Append t.val to result.  
   e. Call inorder(t.right).  
6. Start with result = an empty list.  Then call inorder(root).  When that finishes, result holds the final sequence of values, and you’ve also tallied every split, merge, and push along the way. 

OUTPUTS: When you’re done, you’ll have two things:  
1. result – a list of the numbers in the exact order you get when you walk the tree in-order after all those reversals.  
2. A small dictionary with three entries:  
   • 'split_calls': the final value of split_cnt (how many times you ran the split logic)  
   • 'merge_calls': the final value of merge_cnt (how many times you ran merge)  
   • 'push_calls': the final value of push_cnt (how many times you called push, at every split, merge, and in-order step)

INPUTS: You’ve got three pieces of data to work with: first, a single number called n; second, a list of pairs of numbers called lst (each pair written as (x, y)); and third, a plain list of numbers called arr. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is set up your workspace exactly as the code does and then follow every step by hand.  

1. Start by creating three counters: split_cnt = 0, merge_cnt = 0, and push_cnt = 0.  These will track how many times you run split, merge, and push.  
2. Make a variable named root and set it to None.  This will be the root of your tree.  

-- Building the initial tree from arr --  
3. Now you need to turn each number in arr into a Node and merge it into root in order.  So take the first number x in arr, then the next, and so on.  For each x:  
   a. Create a record called Node with these fields:  
      • val = x  
      • prio = pick a random integer once (for example, note down 8342753 or whatever you get) and record that exact number in your Node; you must use that same number whenever you compare this Node’s priority later.  
      • sz = 1  
      • left = None  
      • right = None  
      • rev = False  
   b. Now merge this new Node into your existing root by doing merge(root, Node).  Every time you begin a merge call (even if one of the arguments is None), immediately add 1 to merge_cnt.  

-- The merge operation, step by step --  
When you call merge(a, b):  
   1. You already bumped merge_cnt by 1.  
   2. If a is None, return b; if b is None, return a.  (Either way you still counted this merge call.)  
   3. Otherwise, compare a.prio and b.prio using the exact numbers you recorded.  
      - If a.prio < b.prio:  
        • Call push(a) before you do anything else.  That means add 1 to push_cnt, then check a.rev:  
          · If a.rev is True, swap a.left and a.right, then for each child that exists flip its rev flag (True becomes False, False becomes True), and then set a.rev = False.  
          · If a.rev is False, you still clear it by setting a.rev = False and you do the swap logic only if it was True, but you do count this push call regardless.  
        • After push(a), set a.right = merge(a.right, b).  Every recursive merge call also bumps merge_cnt at its start.  
        • Then recalculate a.sz = 1 + (size of a.left, zero if None) + (size of a.right, zero if None).  
        • Return a.  
      - If a.prio >= b.prio: do the same steps but on b:  
        • Call push(b) (add 1 to push_cnt, handle the swap and rev clearing unconditionally).  
        • Set b.left = merge(a, b.left).  
        • Recalculate b.sz = 1 + size(b.left) + size(b.right).  
        • Return b.  

Repeat those merge steps until every x in arr has been merged, so at the end of this loop root holds the full tree.  

-- Processing the reversals from lst in reverse order --  
4. Now you need to go through lst from the last pair to the first pair.  For each pair (x, y) in reversed(lst):  
   a. Compute x0 = x - 1 and y0 = y - 1, so you’re using zero-based positions.  
   b. First split: call split(root, x0).  
      • As soon as you call split, add 1 to split_cnt.  
      • If the node t you passed in is None, return (None, None).  Otherwise, at the top of split you must call push(t): add 1 to push_cnt, then if t.rev is True swap t.left and t.right, flip each child’s rev if it exists, and set t.rev = False (if it was already False you still clear it).  
      • Compute left_sz = size of t.left (zero if t.left is None).  
      • If left_sz >= k (here k is x0):  
         – Call split(t.left, k) (this bumps split_cnt and does a push on t.left), which returns (l, r).  
         – Then set t.left = r.  
         – Recalculate t.sz = 1 + size(t.left) + size(t.right).  
         – Return (l, t).  
      • Otherwise (left_sz < k):  
         – Call split(t.right, k - left_sz - 1).  
         – That returns (l, r).  
         – Set t.right = l.  
         – Recalculate t.sz = 1 + size(t.left) + size(t.right).  
         – Return (t, r).  
      • Collect the result of this first split as (a, br).  
   c. Second split: call split(br, y0 - x0 + 1).  Do exactly the same process: bump split_cnt, push on br, decide left_sz vs. the new k, split left or right recursively, update sizes.  Call the result (b, c).  
   d. If b is not None, toggle its rev flag by doing b.rev = not b.rev.  That means if it was False make it True, and vice versa.  
   e. Finally rebuild root by doing merge(a, b) (count 1 merge at its start) and then merge(that result, c) (another merge count).  Assign the final merged node back into root.  

Repeat that whole process for every pair in the reversed lst.  After you finish all of them, you have applied every reversal in exactly the right order.  

-- In-order traversal to collect the result --  
5. Now define a function inorder(t) that walks the tree in order and fills a list called result:  
   a. If t is None, just return.  
   b. At the top of inorder, call push(t): add 1 to push_cnt, then if t.rev is True swap t.left and t.right, flip each child’s rev if it exists, and set t.rev = False (if it was False you still clear it).  
   c. Call inorder(t.left).  
   d. Append t.val to result.  
   e. Call inorder(t.right).  
6. Start with result = an empty list.  Then call inorder(root).  When that finishes, result holds the final sequence of values, and you’ve also tallied every split, merge, and push along the way. 

OUTPUTS: When you’re done, you’ll have two things:  
1. result – a list of the numbers in the exact order you get when you walk the tree in-order after all those reversals.  
2. A small dictionary with three entries:  
   • 'split_calls': the final value of split_cnt (how many times you ran the split logic)  
   • 'merge_calls': the final value of merge_cnt (how many times you ran merge)  
   • 'push_calls': the final value of push_cnt (how many times you called push, at every split, merge, and in-order step)

INPUTS: You’ve got three pieces of data to work with: first, a single number called n; second, a list of pairs of numbers called lst (each pair written as (x, y)); and third, a plain list of numbers called arr. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is set up your workspace exactly as the code does and then follow every step by hand.  

1. Start by creating three counters: split_cnt = 0, merge_cnt = 0, and push_cnt = 0.  These will track how many times you run split, merge, and push.  
2. Make a variable named root and set it to None.  This will be the root of your tree.  

-- Building the initial tree from arr --  
3. Now you need to turn each number in arr into a Node and merge it into root in order.  So take the first number x in arr, then the next, and so on.  For each x:  
   a. Create a record called Node with these fields:  
      • val = x  
      • prio = pick a random integer once (for example, note down 8342753 or whatever you get) and record that exact number in your Node; you must use that same number whenever you compare this Node’s priority later.  
      • sz = 1  
      • left = None  
      • right = None  
      • rev = False  
   b. Now merge this new Node into your existing root by doing merge(root, Node).  Every time you begin a merge call (even if one of the arguments is None), immediately add 1 to merge_cnt.  

-- The merge operation, step by step --  
When you call merge(a, b):  
   1. You already bumped merge_cnt by 1.  
   2. If a is None, return b; if b is None, return a.  (Either way you still counted this merge call.)  
   3. Otherwise, compare a.prio and b.prio using the exact numbers you recorded.  
      - If a.prio < b.prio:  
        • Call push(a) before you do anything else.  That means add 1 to push_cnt, then check a.rev:  
          · If a.rev is True, swap a.left and a.right, then for each child that exists flip its rev flag (True becomes False, False becomes True), and then set a.rev = False.  
          · If a.rev is False, you still clear it by setting a.rev = False and you do the swap logic only if it was True, but you do count this push call regardless.  
        • After push(a), set a.right = merge(a.right, b).  Every recursive merge call also bumps merge_cnt at its start.

def f(x, lst):
    B = []
    nonone_window_iterations = 0
    pure_one_cases = 0
    one_block_segments = 0
    for d in lst:
        n = d['n']
        y = d['k']
        A = d['a']
        L = [i for i,v in enumerate(A) if v != 1]
        m = len(L)
        val = 0
        if m == 0:
            pure_one_cases += 1
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val = n * (n - 1) // 2
            else:
                val = n * (n + 1) // 2
            B.append(val)
            continue
        LOG = 60
        for i in range(m):
            p = 1
            s = 0
            for j in range(i, min(m, i + LOG)):
                nonone_window_iterations += 1
                idx = L[j]
                v = A[idx]
                p *= v
                s += v
                l = L[i] - (L[i - 1] if i > 0 else -1) - 1
                r = (L[j + 1] if j + 1 < m else n) - idx - 1
                req = (p + y) // y - s
                if req > l + r:
                    continue
                total = (l + 1) * (r + 1)
                if req <= 0:
                    val += total
                else:
                    bad = 0
                    ml = min(l, req - 1)
                    for uu in range(ml + 1):
                        rm = req - 1 - uu
                        bad += min(r, rm) + 1
                    val += total - bad
        pr = -1
        for idx in L:
            gap = idx - pr - 1
            if gap > 0:
                one_block_segments += 1
                if y == 1:
                    val += gap * (gap - 1) // 2
                else:
                    val += gap * (gap + 1) // 2
            pr = idx
        tail = n - L[-1] - 1
        if tail > 0:
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val += tail * (tail - 1) // 2
            else:
                val += tail * (tail + 1) // 2
        B.append(val)
    return B, {'nonone_window_iterations': nonone_window_iterations, 'pure_one_cases': pure_one_cases, 'one_block_segments': one_block_segments}

Each item is a small collection with three pieces: an integer called n, an integer called k (which we’ll refer to as y in our steps), and a list of integers called A. 

LOGICS: Start by creating an empty list called B. Then set three counters to zero: nonone_window_iterations, pure_one_cases, and one_block_segments.  

Now you need to go through each item in lst one by one. For each item (we’ll call it d):  
1. Pull out n from d under the label 'n'.  
2. Pull out y from d under the label 'k'.  
3. Pull out the list A from d under the label 'a'.  
4. Build a new list L to hold every index where A has a value not equal to 1. To do that, start with L empty, then for each index i from 0 up to the length of A minus one, if A[i] ≠ 1, put i into L.  
5. Let m be the number of entries in L (that is, the length of L).  
6. Initialize a running total called val to zero for this item.  

At this point check if m is zero (which means A was all ones):  
- If m == 0, add 1 to pure_one_cases and add 1 to one_block_segments.  
- Then check y:  
  • If y == 1, compute val = n * (n - 1) // 2.  
  • Otherwise compute val = n * (n + 1) // 2.  
- Append val to B, and then skip ahead to the next item in lst.  

If m > 0, you still need to handle blocks that include at least one non-1. Do this in two nested loops:  
1. Set a constant LOG to 60.  
2. For i from 0 to m - 1 do:  
   a. Set p = 1 and s = 0.  
   b. For j from i up to the smaller of (m - 1) and (i + LOG - 1) do:  
      i.   Add 1 to nonone_window_iterations.  
      ii.  Let idx = L[j].  
      iii. Let v = A[idx].  
      iv.  Multiply p by v, and add v to s.  
      v.   Compute l = L[i] minus (L[i - 1] if i > 0 else -1) minus 1.  
      vi.  Compute r = (L[j + 1] if j + 1 < m else n) minus idx minus 1.  
      vii. Compute req = (p + y) // y minus s.  
      viii.If req > l + r, then there’s no valid segment here, so go straight to the next j.  
      ix.  Otherwise compute total = (l + 1) * (r + 1).  
      x.   If req <= 0, add total to val.  
      xi.  If req > 0, you have to subtract the bad ones:  
             - Set bad = 0.  
             - Let limit = the smaller of l and (req - 1).  
             - For uu from 0 to limit do:  
                 * Compute rm = (req - 1) minus uu.  
                 * Add (min(r, rm) + 1) to bad.  
             - After that loop, add (total - bad) to val.  
   c. End of j loop.  
3. End of i loop.  

At this point you’ve counted every segment that contains at least one non-1. Next you need to count the pure-one runs that surround those non-1 blocks:  
1. Set pr = -1 (this marks the position before the array starts).  
2. For each idx in L do:  
   a. Compute gap = idx - pr - 1.  
   b. If gap > 0, you found a block of ones of length gap.  
      i.   Add 1 to one_block_segments.  
      ii.  If y == 1, add gap * (gap - 1) // 2 to val; otherwise add gap * (gap + 1) // 2 to val.  
   c. Set pr = idx.  
3. After you finish that, compute tail = n - L[-1] - 1 (the ones after the last non-1).  
   a. If tail > 0, add 1 to one_block_segments.  
   b. If y == 1, add tail * (tail - 1) // 2 to val; otherwise add tail * (tail + 1) // 2 to val.  

Now you’ve fully processed this item. Append the final val into B. Then move on to the next item in lst.  

Once you’ve gone through every item in lst, you’re done with the main work. 

OUTPUTS: When all items are processed, you end up with two things:  
1. B – a list of one computed val for each entry in lst, in the same order you processed them.  
2. A dictionary of three statistics:  
   • nonone_window_iterations: the total number of times you entered the inner j-loop over windows of non-ones.  
   • pure_one_cases: how many times you hit m == 0 (meaning the list A was all ones).  
   • one_block_segments: how many separate runs of consecutive ones you counted across all the data.

def f(x, lst):
    B = []
    nonone_window_iterations = 0
    pure_one_cases = 0
    one_block_segments = 0
    for d in lst:
        n = d['n']
        y = d['k']
        A = d['a']
        L = [i for i,v in enumerate(A) if v != 1]
        m = len(L)
        val = 0
        if m == 0:
            pure_one_cases += 1
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val = n * (n - 1) // 2
            else:
                val = n * (n + 1) // 2
            B.append(val)
            continue
        LOG = 60
        for i in range(m):
            p = 1
            s = 0
            for j in range(i, min(m, i + LOG)):
                nonone_window_iterations += 1
                idx = L[j]
                v = A[idx]
                p *= v
                s += v
                l = L[i] - (L[i - 1] if i > 0 else -1) - 1
                r = (L[j + 1] if j + 1 < m else n) - idx - 1
                req = (p + y) // y - s
                if req > l + r:
                    continue
                total = (l + 1) * (r + 1)
                if req <= 0:
                    val += total
                else:
                    bad = 0
                    ml = min(l, req - 1)
                    for uu in range(ml + 1):
                        rm = req - 1 - uu
                        bad += min(r, rm) + 1
                    val += total - bad
        pr = -1
        for idx in L:
            gap = idx - pr - 1
            if gap > 0:
                one_block_segments += 1
                if y == 1:
                    val += gap * (gap - 1) // 2
                else:
                    val += gap * (gap + 1) // 2
            pr = idx
        tail = n - L[-1] - 1
        if tail > 0:
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val += tail * (tail - 1) // 2
            else:
                val += tail * (tail + 1) // 2
        B.append(val)
    return B, {'nonone_window_iterations': nonone_window_iterations, 'pure_one_cases': pure_one_cases, 'one_block_segments': one_block_segments}

def f(x, lst):
    B = []
    nonone_window_iterations = 0
    pure_one_cases = 0
    one_block_segments = 0
    for d in lst:
        n = d['n']
        y = d['k']
        A = d['a']
        L = [i for i,v in enumerate(A) if v != 1]
        m = len(L)
        val = 0
        if m == 0:
            pure_one_cases += 1
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val = n * (n - 1) // 2
            else:
                val = n * (n + 1) // 2
            B.append(val)
            continue
        LOG = 60
        for i in range(m):
            p = 1
            s = 0
            for j in range(i, min(m, i + LOG)):
                nonone_window_iterations += 1
                idx = L[j]
                v = A[idx]
                p *= v
                s += v
                l = L[i] - (L[i - 1] if i > 0 else -1) - 1
                r = (L[j + 1] if j + 1 < m else n) - idx - 1
                req = (p + y) // y - s
                if req > l + r:
                    continue
                total = (l + 1) * (r + 1)
                if req <= 0:
                    val += total
                else:
                    bad = 0
                    ml = min(l, req - 1)
                    for uu in range(ml + 1):
                        rm = req - 1 - uu
                        bad += min(r, rm) + 1
                    val += total - bad
        pr = -1
        for idx in L:
            gap = idx - pr - 1
            if gap > 0:
                one_block_segments += 1
                if y == 1:
                    val += gap * (gap - 1) // 2
                else:
                    val += gap * (gap + 1) // 2
            pr = idx
        tail = n - L[-1] - 1
        if tail > 0:
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val += tail * (tail - 1) // 2
            else:
                val += tail * (tail + 1) // 2
        B.append(val)
    return B, {'nonone_window_iterations': nonone_window_iterations, 'pure_one_cases': pure_one_cases, 'one_block_segments': one_block_segments}

def f(x, lst):
    B = []
    nonone_window_iterations = 0
    pure_one_cases = 0
    one_block_segments = 0
    for d in lst:
        n = d['n']
        y = d['k']
        A = d['a']
        L = [i for i,v in enumerate(A) if v != 1]
        m = len(L)
        val = 0
        if m == 0:
            pure_one_cases += 1
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val = n * (n - 1) // 2
            else:
                val = n * (n + 1) // 2
            B.append(val)
            continue
        LOG = 60
        for i in range(m):
            p = 1
            s = 0
            for j in range(i, min(m, i + LOG)):
                nonone_window_iterations += 1
                idx = L[j]
                v = A[idx]
                p *= v
                s += v
                l = L[i] - (L[i - 1] if i > 0 else -1) - 1
                r = (L[j + 1] if j + 1 < m else n) - idx - 1
                req = (p + y) // y - s
                if req > l + r:
                    continue
                total = (l + 1) * (r + 1)
                if req <= 0:
                    val += total
                else:
                    bad = 0
                    ml = min(l, req - 1)
                    for uu in range(ml + 1):
                        rm = req - 1 - uu
                        bad += min(r, rm) + 1
                    val += total - bad
        pr = -1
        for idx in L:
            gap = idx - pr - 1
            if gap > 0:
                one_block_segments += 1
                if y == 1:
                    val += gap * (gap - 1) // 2
                else:
                    val += gap * (gap + 1) // 2
            pr = idx
        tail = n - L[-1] - 1
        if tail > 0:
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val += tail * (tail - 1) // 2
            else:
                val += tail * (tail + 1) // 2
        B.append(val)
    return B, {'nonone_window_iterations': nonone_window_iterations, 'pure_one_cases': pure_one_cases, 'one_block_segments': one_block_segments}

INPUTS: You have two inputs: A, which is a list of pairs of numbers (each pair has exactly two numeric entries, call them x and y), and k, which is a single integer. 

LOGICS: First thing you do is check if k is less than 3 or if the length of A (call that n) is less than k. If either of those checks is true, you stop right there and your result is 0.0 plus a dictionary with three zeros for cross_ops, dp_ops, and close_ops. Otherwise, you carry on. Next, set n equal to the number of pairs in A. Then you build a new list called B, also of length n: go through each pair in A, call the two numbers x and y, compute the arctan2 of y and x, and store that angle in B at the same position. After you have B, create a list called arr that just contains the indices from 0 up to n–1, but sorted so that B[arr[0]] is the smallest angle, B[arr[1]] the next smallest, and so on. Now make a list C by taking the elements of A in the order given by arr (so C[i] = A[arr[i]]). Then build D by sticking two copies of C back-to-back (so D has length m = 2·n). At this point, create an m×m table called M and fill every entry with 0. Also set three counters, c1, c2, and c3, all to zero. Now fill in M’s upper triangle: for i from 0 to m−1, let (x1,y1) = D[i]; then for j from i+1 to m−1, let (x2,y2) = D[j], compute a value by doing x1×y2 minus y1×x2, store that result in M[i][j], and add 1 to c1. After those loops finish, set a variable val_max to 0. Now you begin a sliding‐window phase: for each start index s from 0 to n−1, compute end = s + n. Create a list lst_prev of length m and fill every slot with negative infinity. Then for j from s+1 to end−1, set lst_prev[j] = M[s][j]. That seeds your first stage. Next you run through t from 2 up to k−1 inclusive: inside that, make a fresh list lst_cur of length m, again all negative infinity. Then for each j from s+1 to end−1, do this: set best to negative infinity, then for each l from s+1 to j−1 compute temp = lst_prev[l] + M[l][j], add 1 to c2, and if temp > best then update best = temp. When you’ve tried every l, store best into lst_cur[j]. After you’ve done every j, replace lst_prev with lst_cur and move to the next t. When you finish all t loops, set idx2 = s + n. Then for j from s+1 to end−1 compute temp = lst_prev[j] + M[j][idx2], add 1 to c3, and if temp > val_max then set val_max = temp. That completes one iteration of s. After you’ve done this for all s from 0 to n−1, you’re done with the main work. Finally, you return two things: the number val_max divided by 2.0, and a dictionary containing cross_ops = c1, dp_ops = c2, and close_ops = c3. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with a floating-point value equal to half of the largest accumulated total you found (that’s val_max/2.0), and a dictionary of three counts: cross_ops is how many times you filled in M in the first nested loops, dp_ops is how many pairwise sums and comparisons you performed inside the middle dynamic loops, and close_ops is how many final combination checks you did in the last step.
