INPUTS: You start with two integers and a grid of characters. n is the number of rows, m is the number of columns, and M is a list of n lists, each of length m, where each entry is a single character (either '*' or something else). 

LOGICS: First, what you're going to do is set up your workspace by creating four new n-by-m matrices filled with zeros, and you’ll call them M1, M2, M3, and M4. At the same time, make a stats dictionary with three counters—all set to zero—named 'dp_updates', 'center_evaluations', and 'verify_checks'.

Now you need to fill M1 and M2 in one sweep. So you go row by row: for each i from 0 up to n minus 1, and for each j from 0 up to m minus 1, check if M[i][j] is '*'. If it is, compute M1[i][j] by taking 1 plus the value at M1[i-1][j] if i is greater than 0, otherwise just use 1. As soon as you fill M1[i][j], add 1 to stats['dp_updates']. Then compute M2[i][j] by taking 1 plus M2[i][j-1] if j is greater than 0, otherwise 1, and again add 1 to stats['dp_updates'].

Once that top-left to bottom-right pass is done, you do a second pass backward to fill M3 and M4. Loop i from n minus 1 down to 0, and inside that loop j from m minus 1 down to 0. Whenever you see M[i][j] is '*', compute M3[i][j] as 1 plus M3[i+1][j] if i is less than n minus 1, otherwise 1, then add 1 to stats['dp_updates']. Next compute M4[i][j] as 1 plus M4[i][j+1] if j is less than m minus 1, otherwise 1, and add another 1 to stats['dp_updates'].

At this point you have four direction‐counts for every star. Now you want to find the best candidate center. So set max_val to 0 and x and y to -1. Then scan every cell again (i from 0 to n minus 1, j from 0 to m minus 1). If M[i][j] is '*', add 1 to stats['center_evaluations'], then look at the four numbers M1[i][j], M3[i][j], M2[i][j], and M4[i][j] and take the minimum—call that cur_val. If cur_val is bigger than max_val, update max_val to cur_val and record x = i, y = j.

After you finish that search, check if max_val is less than or equal to 1. If it is, you immediately stop and return 'NO' along with your stats, because you didn’t find a large enough shape.

If max_val is greater than 1, you build a boolean matrix B of size n by m all set to False. Then set B[x][y] = True. Compute r as max_val minus 1. For each k from 1 to r inclusive, set B[x-k][y] = True, B[x+k][y] = True, B[x][y-k] = True, and B[x][y+k] = True. That marks out a symmetric pattern around the chosen center.

Finally, you verify that every '*' in M falls onto a True spot in B. So you loop i and j over all positions again; whenever M[i][j] is '*', add 1 to stats['verify_checks'], then check if B[i][j] is True. If you ever find a '*' where B[i][j] is False, you return 'NO' and your stats. If you get through that entire check without failing, you return 'YES' and the stats. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two items: a string that is either 'YES' or 'NO', and the stats dictionary. In stats, 'dp_updates' is the total count of times you wrote into any of M1, M2, M3, or M4; 'center_evaluations' is the number of starred cells you tested as potential centers; and 'verify_checks' is the number of starred cells you rechecked against the final pattern.

At the same time, make a stats dictionary with three counters—all set to zero—named 'dp_updates', 'center_evaluations', and 'verify_checks'.

Now you need to fill M1 and M2 in one sweep. So you go row by row: for each i from 0 up to n minus 1, and for each j from 0 up to m minus 1, check if M[i][j] is '*'. If it is, compute M1[i][j] by taking 1 plus the value at M1[i-1][j] if i is greater than 0, otherwise just use 1. As soon as you fill M1[i][j], add 1 to stats['dp_updates']. Then compute M2[i][j] by taking 1 plus M2[i][j-1] if j is greater than 0, otherwise 1, and again add 1 to stats['dp_updates'].

Once that top-left to bottom-right pass is done, you do a second pass backward to fill M3 and M4. Loop i from n minus 1 down to 0, and inside that loop j from m minus 1 down to 0. Whenever you see M[i][j] is '*', compute M3[i][j] as 1 plus M3[i+1][j] if i is less than n minus 1, otherwise 1, then add 1 to stats['dp_updates']. Next compute M4[i][j] as 1 plus M4[i][j+1] if j is less than m minus 1, otherwise 1, and add another 1 to stats['dp_updates'].

At this point you have four direction‐counts for every star. Now you want to find the best candidate center. So set max_val to 0 and x and y to -1. Then scan every cell again (i from 0 to n minus 1, j from 0 to m minus 1). If M[i][j] is '*', add 1 to stats['center_evaluations'], then look at the four numbers M1[i][j], M3[i][j], M2[i][j], and M4[i][j] and take the minimum—call that cur_val. If cur_val is bigger than max_val, update max_val to cur_val and record x = i, y = j.

After you finish that search, check if max_val is less than or equal to 1. If it is, you immediately stop and return 'NO' along with your stats, because you didn’t find a large enough shape.

If max_val is greater than 1, you build a boolean matrix B of size n by m all set to False. Then set B[x][y] = True. Compute r as max_val minus 1. For each k from 1 to r inclusive, set B[x-k][y] = True, B[x+k][y] = True, B[x][y-k] = True, and B[x][y+k] = True. That marks out a symmetric pattern around the chosen center.

Finally, you verify that every '*' in M falls onto a True spot in B. So you loop i and j over all positions again; whenever M[i][j] is '*', add 1 to stats['verify_checks'], then check if B[i][j] is True. If you ever find a '*' where B[i][j] is False, you return 'NO' and your stats. If you get through that entire check without failing, you return 'YES' and the stats. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two items: a string that is either 'YES' or 'NO', and the stats dictionary. INPUTS: You’re working with a single variable called lst. lst is simply a list containing n text strings, and nothing else is given at the start. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is first set up three counters named char_count, sort_comp, and selections, all starting at zero. Next, figure out n by counting how many items are in lst. Then create a grid M with n rows and 5 columns, filling every cell with zero. Now you need to scan through every string in lst. For each string, keep track of its position x (from 0 up to n−1). Inside that string, look at each character c one by one: each time you see a character, add 1 to char_count. If that character falls between 'a' and 'e' (meaning it’s one of a, b, c, d, or e), then determine its column index by noting that 'a' corresponds to 0, 'b' to 1, 'c' to 2, 'd' to 3, and 'e' to 4, and add 1 to M[x][that index]. After you finish, M[x][0..4] holds how many a’s, b’s, c’s, d’s, and e’s each string had.  

At this point you define a helper process g that sorts a list of numbers in descending order while counting how many times you compare two numbers. Here’s how g works: if the incoming list arr has length 0 or 1, you just return it immediately. Otherwise find the midpoint m by taking the length of arr, dividing by two, and rounding down. Split arr into two parts— the first m items and the remaining items— then call g on each part to get two sorted sublists A and B. Now you merge A and B by setting two pointers x=0 and y=0 and building a new empty list C. While x is still inside A and y is still inside B, compare A[x] to B[y] and add 1 to sort_comp for that comparison. If A[x] is larger, append A[x] to C and bump x by 1; otherwise append B[y] and bump y by 1. Once one side runs out, append whatever is left of the other side onto C, and then return C.  

Now return to your main flow and set a variable res to zero. You’re going to do five passes, one for each column index y from 0 to 4. On each pass, build a fresh list called arr1: go through every string index x again, look up cnt = M[x][y], compute diff = cnt minus (the length of string x minus cnt), and append diff to arr1. That diff measures how many more of those target letters you had than all other letters combined. Next, call your helper g on arr1 to get a new list arr2 sorted in descending order; as you do, keep adding to sort_comp for each comparison. Then you run through arr2 in order, maintaining a running total val_sum starting at zero and a local count cnt1 also at zero. For each number val in arr2, check if val_sum + val would be positive. If it’s not (that is, if val_sum + val ≤ 0), you stop this loop immediately. Otherwise add val to val_sum, add 1 to cnt1, and also add 1 to the global counter selections. Keep going until you hit that break or exhaust arr2. When you’re done, compare cnt1 to res; if cnt1 is bigger, set res = cnt1. Then move on to the next column index y. After you’ve done all five, you finish with your final res plus your three counters. 

OUTPUTS: When you’re all done, you’ll output two things: first, a single number res, which is the largest count of items you managed to pick in any one of the five passes; and second, a small dictionary with three entries—“char_count” showing the total number of characters you looked at in the very first phase, “sort_comp” showing the total number of comparisons you made during every merge operation, and “selections” showing the total number of times you actually added a value to your running sums across all passes.

INPUTS: You’re working with a single variable called lst. lst is simply a list containing n text strings, and nothing else is given at the start. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is first set up three counters named char_count, sort_comp, and selections, all starting at zero. Next, figure out n by counting how many items are in lst. Then create a grid M with n rows and 5 columns, filling every cell with zero. Now you need to scan through every string in lst. For each string, keep track of its position x (from 0 up to n−1). Inside that string, look at each character c one by one: each time you see a character, add 1 to char_count. If that character falls between 'a' and 'e' (meaning it’s one of a, b, c, d, or e), then determine its column index by noting that 'a' corresponds to 0, 'b' to 1, 'c' to 2, 'd' to 3, and 'e' to 4, and add 1 to M[x][that index]. After you finish, M[x][0..4] holds how many a’s, b’s, c’s, d’s, and e’s each string had.  

At this point you define a helper process g that sorts a list of numbers in descending order while counting how many times you compare two numbers. Here’s how g works: if the incoming list arr has length 0 or 1, you just return it immediately. Otherwise find the midpoint m by taking the length of arr, dividing by two, and rounding down. Split arr into two parts— the first m items and the remaining items— then call g on each part to get two sorted sublists A and B. Now you merge A and B by setting two pointers x=0 and y=0 and building a new empty list C. While x is still inside A and y is still inside B, compare A[x] to B[y] and add 1 to sort_comp for that comparison. If A[x] is larger, append A[x] to C and bump x by 1; otherwise append B[y] and bump y by 1. Once one side runs out, append whatever is left of the other side onto C, and then return C.  

Now return to your main flow and set a variable res to zero. You’re going to do five passes, one for each column index y from 0 to 4. On each pass, build a fresh list called arr1: go through every string index x again, look up cnt = M[x][y], compute diff = cnt minus (the length of string x minus cnt), and append diff to arr1. That diff measures how many more of those target letters you had than all other letters combined. Next, call your helper g on arr1 to get a new list arr2 sorted in descending order; as you do, keep adding to sort_comp for each comparison. Then you run through arr2 in order, maintaining a running total val_sum starting at zero and a local count cnt1 also at zero. For each number val in arr2, check if val_sum + val would be positive. If it’s not (that is, if val_sum + val ≤ 0), you stop this loop immediately. Otherwise add val to val_sum, add 1 to cnt1, and also add 1 to the global counter selections. Keep going until you hit that break or exhaust arr2. When you’re done, compare cnt1 to res; if cnt1 is bigger, set res = cnt1. Then move on to the next column index y. After you’ve done all five, you finish with your final res plus your three counters. 

OUTPUTS: When you’re all done, you’ll output two things: first, a single number res, which is the largest count of items you managed to pick in any one of the five passes; and second, a small dictionary with three entries—“char_count” showing the total number of characters you looked at in the very first phase, “sort_comp” showing the total number of comparisons you made during every merge operation, and “selections” showing the total number of times you actually added a value to your running sums across all passes.

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is first set up three counters named char_count, sort_comp, and selections, all starting at zero. Next, figure out n by counting how many items are in lst. Then create a grid M with n rows and 5 columns, filling every cell with zero. Now you need to scan through every string in lst. For each string, keep track of its position x (from 0 up to n−1). Inside that string, look at each character c one by one: each time you see a character, add 1 to char_count. If that character falls between 'a' and 'e' (meaning it’s one of a, b, c, d, or e), then determine its column index by noting that 'a' corresponds to 0, 'b' to 1, 'c' to 2, 'd' to 3, and 'e' to 4, and add 1 to M[x][that index]. After you finish, M[x][0..4] holds how many a’s, b’s, c’s, d’s, and e’s each string had.  

At this point you define a helper process g that sorts a list of numbers in descending order while counting how many times you compare two numbers. Here’s how g works: if the incoming list arr has length 0 or 1, you just return it immediately. Otherwise find the midpoint m by taking the length of arr, dividing by two, and rounding down. Split arr into two parts— the first m items and the remaining items— then call g on each part to get two sorted sublists A and B. Now you merge A and B by setting two pointers x=0 and y=0 and building a new empty list C. While x is still inside A and y is still inside B, compare A[x] to B[y] and add 1 to sort_comp for that comparison. If A[x] is larger, append A[x] to C and bump x by 1; otherwise append B[y] and bump y by 1. Once one side runs out, append whatever is left of the other side onto C, and then return C.  

Now return to your main flow and set a variable res to zero. You’re going to do five passes, one for each column index y from 0 to 4. On each pass, build a fresh list called arr1: go through every string index x again, look up cnt = M[x][y], compute diff = cnt minus (the length of string x minus cnt), and append diff to arr1. That diff measures how many more of those target letters you had than all other letters combined. Next, call your helper g on arr1 to get a new list arr2 sorted in descending order; as you do, keep adding to sort_comp for each comparison. Then you run through arr2 in order, maintaining a running total val_sum starting at zero and a local count cnt1 also at zero. For each number val in arr2, check if val_sum + val would be positive. If it’s not (that is, if val_sum + val ≤ 0), you stop this loop immediately. Otherwise add val to val_sum, add 1 to cnt1, and also add 1 to the global counter selections. Keep going until you hit that break or exhaust arr2. When you’re done, compare cnt1 to res; if cnt1 is bigger, set res = cnt1. Then move on to the next column index y. After you’ve done all five, you finish with your final res plus your three counters. 

OUTPUTS: When you’re all done, you’ll output two things: first, a single number res, which is the largest count of items you managed to pick in any one of the five passes; and second, a small dictionary with three entries—“char_count” showing the total number of characters you looked at in the very first phase, “sort_comp” showing the total number of comparisons you made during every merge operation, and “selections” showing the total number of times you actually added a value to your running sums across all passes.

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

INPUTS: You have four inputs: a number called n, a number called t_lim, a list of numbers called L of length n, and another list of numbers called A of the same length. 

LOGICS: First, what you're going to do is pair up each item from list L with the corresponding item from list A to form a list called B. So if L has k items and A has k items, you’ll get k pairs like (L[0],A[0]), (L[1],A[1]), and so on. Next, add one more pair (0, 0) at the end of B. Now sort the entire list B in ascending order by the first number in each pair. After sorting, split B into two new lists: arr will hold the first numbers of each pair in order, and val will hold the second numbers. Count how many elements you now have in arr and call that m. Then scan arr from the start until you find the element equal to zero; record its index as s. Now create a list called ps of length m, initialized with zeros. Put val[0] into ps[0]. Also set a counter called prefix_sum_ops to 0. To fill the rest of ps, do this: for each index i from 1 up to m−1, set ps[i] to ps[i−1] plus val[i], and each time you do that addition add 1 to prefix_sum_ops. At this point ps holds the running totals of val. Next, introduce a symbol INF to stand for an infinitely large placeholder. Build a three-dimensional table dp with m rows and m columns, where each cell dp[i][j] itself holds two numbers. Initialize every dp[i][j][0] and dp[i][j][1] to INF. Then go to the cell at row s and column s and set dp[s][s][0] to 0 and dp[s][s][1] to 0. Also create three counters: ans = 0, reachable_states = 0, and dp_transitions = 0. Now you run the main loops. Loop a variable w from 0 up to m−1. Inside that, loop a variable i from (s−w) up through s. For each i compute j = i + w. If i is less than 0 or j is at least m, skip directly to the next i. Otherwise look at dp[i][j]: if both dp[i][j][0] and dp[i][j][1] are still INF, skip to the next i as well. If you didn’t skip, that means this state is reachable, so add 1 to reachable_states. Then compute total = ps[j] minus ps[i−1] if i>0, or just ps[j] if i==0. Next compute tL = dp[i][j][0] + absolute value of arr[i]. If tL ≤ t_lim, set ans to the larger of ans and total. Then compute tR = dp[i][j][1] + absolute value of arr[j]. If tR ≤ t_lim, set ans to the larger of ans and total. After these checks, try extending to the left: if i>0 then compute lm = the smaller of (dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i]−arr[i−1])) and (dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j]−arr[i−1])). If lm is less than dp[i−1][j][0], update dp[i−1][j][0] = lm and add 1 to dp_transitions. Then try extending to the right: if j<m−1 then compute rm = the smaller of (dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1]−arr[i])) and (dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1]−arr[j])). If rm is less than dp[i][j+1][1], update dp[i][j+1][1] = rm and add 1 to dp_transitions. That completes the inner loops. When all values of w, i, and j are covered, you stop. 

OUTPUTS: At the end you return two things. First, ans is the maximum total value you managed to gather under the t_lim threshold. Second, you return a dictionary with three statistics: prefix_sum_ops (the number of additions you did when building the ps list), reachable_states (the count of dp table entries you actually processed where at least one of the two values wasn’t INF), and dp_transitions (the number of times you found a smaller cost and updated an entry in the dp table).

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

INPUTS: You have a variable L, which is a list. Each item in L is itself a list (which might be empty), and each of those lists contains pairs of values. Each pair has two entries: the first is x and the second is y. 

LOGICS: Start by creating three number counters called union_calls, find_calls, and connectivity_checks, and set them all to zero. Also make an empty list called res. What you're going to do is go through each sublist in L one at a time, and for each one you'll check various conditions and then record True or False in res.

Now, take the first sublist in L and call it A. The way this works is: if A is completely empty (no pairs inside), then you immediately add True to res and move on to the next sublist in L.

If A is not empty, you need to build some working structures. Create:
  - a map called mp, where you'll store parent links for each item,
  - a map called mp2, which will track a rank number for each item,
  - a map called d, which will count how many times each item appears as the second entry in a pair,
  - a set called st, which will keep track of all the distinct items you see,
  - a flag called flag, and set it to False.

Next, go through each pair in A. For each pair, pull out x and y. Add x and y into the set st. If x is not yet a key in mp, put mp[x] = x; do the same for y. If x is not yet in mp2, set mp2[x] = 0; same for y. If x is not yet in d, set d[x] = 0; same for y.

What you do now is define two helper procedures in your head that you’ll apply by hand:
  1. find(a):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     - Look at mp[a]. If mp[a] equals a, that means it’s its own parent, so return a.
     - Otherwise, call find(mp[a]) to get the ultimate parent, then set mp[a] to that returned parent (path compression), and then return that parent.

  2. union(a, b):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     - Call find(a) and find(b) to get their roots ra and rb.
     - If ra and rb are the same, return False (they’re already connected).
     - Otherwise, compare mp2[ra] and mp2[rb]. If mp2[ra] < mp2[rb], set mp[ra] = rb. Otherwise, set mp[rb] = ra; and if mp2[ra] and mp2[rb] were equal before, add 1 to mp2[ra]. Then return True.

At this point, go back and do another pass over each pair x, y in A in order. For each pair:
  - Add 1 to d[y].
  - If d[y] ever becomes greater than 1, that means y showed up too many times as a second entry, so set flag = True and stop processing further pairs in A.
  - If that didn’t happen, call union(x, y). If union returns False, set flag = True and stop processing further pairs in A.

Once you've either finished all pairs or stopped early with flag = True, check flag. If flag is True, append False to res and move to the next A. If flag is still False, do these final checks:

  1. Count how many items in st have d[n] equal to 0. Call that root_count.
  2. Check two conditions: root_count must be exactly 1, and the number of pairs in A must equal the size of st minus 1. If either condition fails, set flag = True.
  3. If flag is still False, pick any item from st (for example the first one you see), call find on it to get a root, and then go through every item n in st:
     - Add 1 to connectivity_checks.
     - Call find(n). If that result does not match your chosen root, set flag = True and stop checking.

After that, append (not flag) to your res list—that will be True if none of the checks set flag to True, or False if any check did.

Repeat this entire process for each sublist A inside your original list L. When you’ve processed every A, you’ll have your res list and your three counters populated. 

OUTPUTS: When you're all done, you end up with two things:

1. res — a list of True/False values, one for each sublist in L, telling you whether each passed all the checks.
2. stats — a dictionary with three entries:
   • union_calls: the total number of times you performed the union procedure.
   • find_calls: the total number of times you ran the find procedure.
   • connectivity_checks: the total number of individual connectivity verifications you made when checking that every item shared the same root.

INPUTS: You have a variable L, which is a list. Each item in L is itself a list (which might be empty), and each of those lists contains pairs of values. Each pair has two entries: the first is x and the second is y. 

LOGICS: Start by creating three number counters called union_calls, find_calls, and connectivity_checks, and set them all to zero. Also make an empty list called res. What you're going to do is go through each sublist in L one at a time, and for each one you'll check various conditions and then record True or False in res.

Now, take the first sublist in L and call it A. The way this works is: if A is completely empty (no pairs inside), then you immediately add True to res and move on to the next sublist in L.

If A is not empty, you need to build some working structures. Create:
  - a map called mp, where you'll store parent links for each item,
  - a map called mp2, which will track a rank number for each item,
  - a map called d, which will count how many times each item appears as the second entry in a pair,
  - a set called st, which will keep track of all the distinct items you see,
  - a flag called flag, and set it to False.

Next, go through each pair in A. For each pair, pull out x and y. Add x and y into the set st. If x is not yet a key in mp, put mp[x] = x; do the same for y. If x is not yet in mp2, set mp2[x] = 0; same for y. If x is not yet in d, set d[x] = 0; same for y.

What you do now is define two helper procedures in your head that you’ll apply by hand:
  1. find(a):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     - Look at mp[a]. If mp[a] equals a, that means it’s its own parent, so return a.
     - Otherwise, call find(mp[a]) to get the ultimate parent, then set mp[a] to that returned parent (path compression), and then return that parent.

  2. union(a, b):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     - Call find(a) and find(b) to get their roots ra and rb.
     - If ra and rb are the same, return False (they’re already connected).
     - Otherwise, compare mp2[ra] and mp2[rb]. If mp2[ra] < mp2[rb], set mp[ra] = rb. Otherwise, set mp[rb] = ra; and if mp2[ra] and mp2[rb] were equal before, add 1 to mp2[ra]. Then return True.

At this point, go back and do another pass over each pair x, y in A in order. For each pair:
  - Add 1 to d[y].
  - If d[y] ever becomes greater than 1, that means y showed up too many times as a second entry, so set flag = True and stop processing further pairs in A.
  - If that didn’t happen, call union(x, y). If union returns False, set flag = True and stop processing further pairs in A.

Once you've either finished all pairs or stopped early with flag = True, check flag. If flag is True, append False to res and move to the next A. If flag is still False, do these final checks:

  1. Count how many items in st have d[n] equal to 0. Call that root_count.
  2. Check two conditions: root_count must be exactly 1, and the number of pairs in A must equal the size of st minus 1. If either condition fails, set flag = True.
  3. If flag is still False, pick any item from st (for example the first one you see), call find on it to get a root, and then go through every item n in st:
     - Add 1 to connectivity_checks.
     - Call find(n). If that result does not match your chosen root, set flag = True and stop checking.

After that, append (not flag) to your res list—that will be True if none of the checks set flag to True, or False if any check did.

Repeat this entire process for each sublist A inside your original list L. When you’ve processed every A, you’ll have your res list and your three counters populated. 

OUTPUTS: When you're all done, you end up with two things:

1. res — a list of True/False values, one for each sublist in L, telling you whether each passed all the checks.
2. stats — a dictionary with three entries:
   • union_calls: the total number of times you performed the union procedure.
   • find_calls: the total number of times you ran the find procedure.
   • connectivity_checks: the total number of individual connectivity verifications you made when checking that every item shared the same root.

  - a map called mp2, which will track a rank number for each item,

  - a set called st, which will keep track of all the distinct items you see,

What you're going to do is go through each sublist in L one at a time, and for each one you'll check various conditions and then record True or False in res.

Now, take the first sublist in L and call it A. The way this works is: if A is completely empty (no pairs inside), then you immediately add True to res and move on to the next sublist in L.

If A is not empty, you need to build some working structures. Create:
  - a map called mp, where you'll store parent links for each item,
  - a map called mp2, which will track a rank number for each item,
  - a map called d, which will count how many times each item appears as the second entry in a pair,
  - a set called st, which will keep track of all the distinct items you see,
  - a flag called flag, and set it to False.

Next, go through each pair in A. For each pair, pull out x and y. Add x and y into the set st. If x is not yet a key in mp, put mp[x] = x; do the same for y. If x is not yet in mp2, set mp2[x] = 0; same for y. If x is not yet in d, set d[x] = 0; same for y.

What you do now is define two helper procedures in your head that you’ll apply by hand:
  1. find(a):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     - Look at mp[a]. If mp[a] equals a, that means it’s its own parent, so return a.
     - Otherwise, call find(mp[a]) to get the ultimate parent, then set mp[a] to that returned parent (path compression), and then return that parent.

  2. union(a, b):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     - Call find(a) and find(b) to get their roots ra and rb.
     - If ra and rb are the same, return False (they’re already connected).
     - Otherwise, compare mp2[ra] and mp2[rb]. If mp2[ra] < mp2[rb], set mp[ra] = rb. Otherwise, set mp[rb] = ra; and if mp2[ra] and mp2[rb] were equal before, add 1 to mp2[ra]. Then return True.

INPUTS: You have a variable L, which is a list. Each item in L is itself a list (which might be empty), and each of those lists contains pairs of values. Each pair has two entries: the first is x and the second is y. 

LOGICS: Start by creating three number counters called union_calls, find_calls, and connectivity_checks, and set them all to zero. Also make an empty list called res. What you're going to do is go through each sublist in L one at a time, and for each one you'll check various conditions and then record True or False in res.

Now, take the first sublist in L and call it A. The way this works is: if A is completely empty (no pairs inside), then you immediately add True to res and move on to the next sublist in L.

If A is not empty, you need to build some working structures. Create:
  - a map called mp, where you'll store parent links for each item,
  - a map called mp2, which will track a rank number for each item,
  - a map called d, which will count how many times each item appears as the second entry in a pair,
  - a set called st, which will keep track of all the distinct items you see,
  - a flag called flag, and set it to False.

Next, go through each pair in A. For each pair, pull out x and y. Add x and y into the set st. If x is not yet a key in mp, put mp[x] = x; do the same for y. If x is not yet in mp2, set mp2[x] = 0; same for y. If x is not yet in d, set d[x] = 0; same for y.

What you do now is define two helper procedures in your head that you’ll apply by hand:
  1. find(a):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     - Look at mp[a]. If mp[a] equals a, that means it’s its own parent, so return a.
     - Otherwise, call find(mp[a]) to get the ultimate parent, then set mp[a] to that returned parent (path compression), and then return that parent.

  2. union(a, b):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     - Call find(a) and find(b) to get their roots ra and rb.
     - If ra and rb are the same, return False (they’re already connected).
     - Otherwise, compare mp2[ra] and mp2[rb]. If mp2[ra] < mp2[rb], set mp[ra] = rb. Otherwise, set mp[rb] = ra; and if mp2[ra] and mp2[rb] were equal before, add 1 to mp2[ra]. Then return True.

At this point, go back and do another pass over each pair x, y in A in order. For each pair:
  - Add 1 to d[y].
  - If d[y] ever becomes greater than 1, that means y showed up too many times as a second entry, so set flag = True and stop processing further pairs in A.
  - If that didn’t happen, call union(x, y). If union returns False, set flag = True and stop processing further pairs in A.

Once you've either finished all pairs or stopped early with flag = True, check flag. If flag is True, append False to res and move to the next A. If flag is still False, do these final checks:

  1. Count how many items in st have d[n] equal to 0. Call that root_count.
  2. Check two conditions: root_count must be exactly 1, and the number of pairs in A must equal the size of st minus 1. If either condition fails, set flag = True.
  3. If flag is still False, pick any item from st (for example the first one you see), call find on it to get a root, and then go through every item n in st:
     - Add 1 to connectivity_checks.
     - Call find(n). If that result does not match your chosen root, set flag = True and stop checking.

After that, append (not flag) to your res list—that will be True if none of the checks set flag to True, or False if any check did.

Repeat this entire process for each sublist A inside your original list L. When you’ve processed every A, you’ll have your res list and your three counters populated. 

OUTPUTS: When you're all done, you end up with two things:

1. res — a list of True/False values, one for each sublist in L, telling you whether each passed all the checks.
2. stats — a dictionary with three entries:
   • union_calls: the total number of times you performed the union procedure.
   • find_calls: the total number of times you ran the find procedure.
   • connectivity_checks: the total number of individual connectivity verifications you made when checking that every item shared the same root.

INPUTS: You have two integers: n (the number of rows) and m (the number of columns). Then you have grid, which is a list of n text strings; each string is exactly m characters long and consists only of the characters '0' and '1'. 

LOGICS: Okay, let’s walk through every step so you could literally do this by hand:

1. First off, fix your random number sequence by setting the seed to 0. That way, whenever you pick random numbers later, you’ll get the same sequence.

2. Now you need to build a list called L. What you do is go through each row of grid in order (from row 0 up to row n–1). For each row, scan its characters from column 0 to column m–1. Whenever you see a '1', note down that column index in a small list. After you’ve scanned the whole row, that small list holds exactly the positions of '1's in that row. Do this for every row and collect all those small lists into L. In the end, L is a list of n lists, and each inner list tells you which columns had '1's in that row.

3. Next, set up your working variables:
   – Make a string res of length m that’s all '0's (just write down m zeros in a row).
   – Set v = 0. This will track the size of the best pattern you’ve found so far.
   – Compute thr by taking n plus 1, then dividing by 2 using integer division (ignore any remainder).
   – Let t be the smaller of n and 15.
   – Initialize three counters c1, c2, c3 all to 0. You’ll use them to collect some statistics as you go.

4. Now you’re ready for the main loop. You’re going to repeat the following exactly t times:
   a. Pick a random integer x between 0 and n–1 (inclusive) using your seeded random generator.
   b. Look up P = L[x], and let k = the number of items in P.
   c. If k is not greater than v, skip the rest of this pass and move on to the next repetition.
   d. If k is greater than 20, also skip the rest of this pass and move on.
   e. If you didn’t skip, you’re processing this P as a pivot set, so add 1 to c1.
   f. Now build a map mp from integer masks to counts:
      • Start mp empty.
      • For each arr in L:
         – Convert arr into a set st (so you can check membership quickly).
         – Start an integer val = 0.
         – For each index i from 0 to k–1, look at the column y = P[i]. If y is in st, then set bit i of val by adding 2^i.
         – Once you’ve checked all i’s, increase mp[val] by 1 (if val wasn’t there before, set mp[val] = 1; otherwise add 1).
   g. After you’ve done that for every arr, compute size = 2^k, and make a list B of length size, all zeros.
   h. For each entry (mask, count) in mp, set B[mask] = count.
   i. Now perform the subset‐sum (zeta) pass:
      • For each i from 0 to k–1,
      •   for each s from 0 to size–1,
      •     if the i-th bit of s is 0 (that is, (s & (1<<i)) == 0), then add B[s | (1<<i)] into B[s] and add 1 to c2.
   j. At this point, B[s] tells you how many rows have at least the bits in s. Next, you scan s from 0 to size–1:
      • For each s, add 1 to c3.
      • If B[s] is at least thr, then count how many bits are set in s (call that pop).
      • If pop is greater than v, you’ve got a better pattern:
         – Set v = pop.
         – Make a fresh list C of length m filled with '0'.
         – For each i from 0 to k–1, if bit i of s is 1, set C[P[i]] = '1'.
         – Join C into a string and replace res with that string.
   That completes one of the t passes.

5. After you’ve repeated that entire sequence t times, you’re done with processing. 

OUTPUTS: When all that is finished, you end up with two things:

1. res: a text string of length m made up of '0's and '1's, reflecting the best pattern you found.
2. A dictionary of three counts:
   • 'pivots_processed': c1 — how many pivot lists P you actually processed (i.e. passed both k>v and k≤20 checks).
   • 'zeta_ops': c2 — how many times you performed that subset‐sum addition step in the zeta transform.
   • 'mask_checks': c3 — how many total mask patterns s you inspected in the final scan.

INPUTS: You have two integers: n (the number of rows) and m (the number of columns). Then you have grid, which is a list of n text strings; each string is exactly m characters long and consists only of the characters '0' and '1'. 

LOGICS: Okay, let’s walk through every step so you could literally do this by hand:

1. First off, fix your random number sequence by setting the seed to 0. That way, whenever you pick random numbers later, you’ll get the same sequence.

2. Now you need to build a list called L. What you do is go through each row of grid in order (from row 0 up to row n–1). For each row, scan its characters from column 0 to column m–1. Whenever you see a '1', note down that column index in a small list. After you’ve scanned the whole row, that small list holds exactly the positions of '1's in that row. Do this for every row and collect all those small lists into L. In the end, L is a list of n lists, and each inner list tells you which columns had '1's in that row.

3. Next, set up your working variables:
   – Make a string res of length m that’s all '0's (just write down m zeros in a row).
   – Set v = 0. This will track the size of the best pattern you’ve found so far.
   – Compute thr by taking n plus 1, then dividing by 2 using integer division (ignore any remainder).
   – Let t be the smaller of n and 15.
   – Initialize three counters c1, c2, c3 all to 0. You’ll use them to collect some statistics as you go.

4. Now you’re ready for the main loop. You’re going to repeat the following exactly t times:
   a. Pick a random integer x between 0 and n–1 (inclusive) using your seeded random generator.
   b. Look up P = L[x], and let k = the number of items in P.
   c. If k is not greater than v, skip the rest of this pass and move on to the next repetition.
   d. If k is greater than 20, also skip the rest of this pass and move on.
   e. If you didn’t skip, you’re processing this P as a pivot set, so add 1 to c1.
   f. Now build a map mp from integer masks to counts:
      • Start mp empty.
      • For each arr in L:
         – Convert arr into a set st (so you can check membership quickly).
         – Start an integer val = 0.
         – For each index i from 0 to k–1, look at the column y = P[i]. If y is in st, then set bit i of val by adding 2^i.
         – Once you’ve checked all i’s, increase mp[val] by 1 (if val wasn’t there before, set mp[val] = 1; otherwise add 1).
   g. After you’ve done that for every arr, compute size = 2^k, and make a list B of length size, all zeros.
   h. For each entry (mask, count) in mp, set B[mask] = count.
   i. Now perform the subset‐sum (zeta) pass:
      • For each i from 0 to k–1,
      •   for each s from 0 to size–1,
      •     if the i-th bit of s is 0 (that is, (s & (1<<i)) == 0), then add B[s | (1<<i)] into B[s] and add 1 to c2.
   j. At this point, B[s] tells you how many rows have at least the bits in s. Next, you scan s from 0 to size–1:
      • For each s, add 1 to c3.
      • If B[s] is at least thr, then count how many bits are set in s (call that pop).
      • If pop is greater than v, you’ve got a better pattern:
         – Set v = pop.
         – Make a fresh list C of length m filled with '0'.
         – For each i from 0 to k–1, if bit i of s is 1, set C[P[i]] = '1'.
         – Join C into a string and replace res with that string.
   That completes one of the t passes.

5. After you’ve repeated that entire sequence t times, you’re done with processing. 

OUTPUTS: When all that is finished, you end up with two things:

1. res: a text string of length m made up of '0's and '1's, reflecting the best pattern you found.
2. A dictionary of three counts:
   • 'pivots_processed': c1 — how many pivot lists P you actually processed (i.e. passed both k>v and k≤20 checks).
   • 'zeta_ops': c2 — how many times you performed that subset‐sum addition step in the zeta transform.
   • 'mask_checks': c3 — how many total mask patterns s you inspected in the final scan.

LOGICS: First thing you do is ignore whatever n was and set n equal to the number of pairs in L. Next, create two new lists called A and B, each of length n, and fill every slot with 0. Now you need to populate A and B in lockstep: go through each index i from 0 up to n–1, grab the pair (x, y) from L at position i, then compute x+y and put that into A[i], and compute x–y and put that into B[i].

At this point, set up an empty list called edges. You’ll be gathering triples into this as you go.

Now you’re going to make four passes, one for each d in 0, 1, 2, 3. On each pass:
  1. Start by making an empty list called tmp.
  2. For each index i from 0 to n–1, do this:
     • If d is even (that means 0 or 2), let X = A[i] and Y = B[i]. Otherwise (d is 1 or 3), let X = B[i] and Y = A[i].
     • Then, if d is 2 or 3 (i.e. d ≥ 2), replace X with –X.
     • Append the triple (X, Y, i) into tmp.
  3. Once tmp is full, sort it so that triples are in ascending order by X first, and when X values tie, by Y second.
  4. Walk through the sorted tmp list and build a new list called keys, where each entry is Y–X from that triple.
  5. Take the unique values in keys, sort them ascending to get a list uniq.
  6. Make a dictionary mp that maps each value in uniq to its index in uniq (so the smallest uniq value maps to 0, next to 1, and so on).
  7. Let m_val be the length of uniq. Now create two lists of length m_val+1:
     – BIT_val, and put the exact value –10**18 (that is, minus ten to the eighteenth power) in every slot.
     – BIT_id, and put –1 in every slot.
     These two lists together form a Fenwick tree (or BIT). The way this works is that when you see an index j, doing j & -j (a bitwise AND between j and its two’s-complement negative) gives you the size of the lowest set bit in j, which tells you how far to jump in the tree structure.
  8. Define an update procedure that takes (idx, val, pid):
     • Set j = idx + 1 (switching from 0-based to 1-based indexing).
     • While j ≤ m_val:
         – If val > BIT_val[j], then set BIT_val[j] = val and BIT_id[j] = pid.
         – Then set j = j + (j & -j), where (j & -j) picks out the lowest set bit of j so you know how far to move up the tree.
  9. Define a query procedure that takes idx:
     • Set j = idx + 1, best = –10**18, and bid = –1.
     • While j > 0:
         – If BIT_val[j] > best, then set best = BIT_val[j] and bid = BIT_id[j].
         – Then set j = j - (j & -j), subtracting the lowest set bit to move downward in the tree.
     • When j reaches 0, return the pair (best, bid).
 10. Now go through each triple (X, Y, pid) in the sorted tmp list:
     • Compute kkey = mp[Y - X].
     • Call query(kkey), which gives you (best_sum, best_pid).
     • If best_pid is not –1, that means you found a previous entry that can pair with this one:
         – Compute w = (X + Y) - best_sum.
         – Append the triple (pid, best_pid, w) to your edges list.
     • Whether you appended or not, call update(kkey, X + Y, pid) to record this entry in the Fenwick tree.

Repeat that entire sequence for d = 0, then d = 1, then d = 2, then d = 3. When you finish all four passes, edges is a long list of triples (a, b, w). Next, record candidate_edges = the length of edges, since that’s how many you gathered.

Now sort edges in ascending order by their third element w. You’re going to pick some of these edges to form a structure without cycles. To do that, set up a union-find (disjoint set) system:
  • Create a list parent of size n where parent[i] = i for each i from 0 to n–1.
  • Create a list rank of size n where every entry is 0.

Define a find(x) function as follows:
  – If parent[x] ≠ x, then set parent[x] = find(parent[x]) and return that value. Otherwise just return x.

Define a union(a, b) function:
  – Let ra = find(a) and rb = find(b).
  – If ra == rb, return False because they’re already in the same set.
  – Otherwise, compare rank[ra] and rank[rb]. If rank[ra] < rank[rb], set parent[ra] = rb. Else set parent[rb] = ra, and if rank[ra] == rank[rb], add 1 to rank[ra].
  – Return True to signal you merged two previously separate sets.

Now create an empty list called mst_weights and set edges_examined = 0. Walk through your sorted edges one by one, and for each triple (a, b, w):
  • Add 1 to edges_examined.
  • Call union(a, b). If it returns True, append w to mst_weights.
  • If the length of mst_weights reaches n–1, break out of the loop early because you’ve connected everything you can.

At this point you have up to n–1 weights in mst_weights. The last step is to pick your final result based on k:
  • If k ≥ n, just set result = 0.
  • Otherwise, sort mst_weights in ascending order, compute idx = (length of mst_weights) − k, and then set result = mst_weights[idx] // 2 (that is, integer divide that weight by 2).

Finally, you’re going to return two things: the number result, and a small dictionary with the two stats you collected (candidate_edges and edges_examined). 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you get back two values: 1) result, which is either 0 (if k ≥ n) or otherwise is one of the collected w values divided by two (using integer division) as determined by your k-based index rule; and 2) a dictionary with two counts – “candidate_edges” tells you how many edge triples you gathered across all four passes, and “edges_examined” tells you how many edges you actually looked at in the final union-find phase.

     – BIT_val, and put the exact value –10**18 (that is, minus ten to the eighteenth power) in every slot.
     – BIT_id, and put –1 in every slot.
     These two lists together form a Fenwick tree (or BIT). The way this works is that when you see an index j, doing j & -j (a bitwise AND between j and its two’s-complement negative) gives you the size of the lowest set bit in j, which tells you how far to jump in the tree structure.
  8. Define an update procedure that takes (idx, val, pid):

  9. Define a query procedure that takes idx:

     • If d is even (that means 0 or 2), let X = A[i] and Y = B[i]. Otherwise (d is 1 or 3), let X = B[i] and Y = A[i].
     • Then, if d is 2 or 3 (i.e. d ≥ 2), replace X with –X.
     • Append the triple (X, Y, i) into tmp.
  3. Once tmp is full, sort it so that triples are in ascending order by X first, and when X values tie, by Y second.
  4. Walk through the sorted tmp list and build a new list called keys, where each entry is Y–X from that triple.
  5. Take the unique values in keys, sort them ascending to get a list uniq.

     – BIT_val, and put the exact value –10**18 (that is, minus ten to the eighteenth power) in every slot.
     – BIT_id, and put –1 in every slot.
     These two lists together form a Fenwick tree (or BIT). The way this works is that when you see an index j, doing j & -j (a bitwise AND between j and its two’s-complement negative) gives you the size of the lowest set bit in j, which tells you how far to jump in the tree structure.
  8. Define an update procedure that takes (idx, val, pid):
     • Set j = idx + 1 (switching from 0-based to 1-based indexing).

         – If val > BIT_val[j], then set BIT_val[j] = val and BIT_id[j] = pid.
         – Then set j = j + (j & -j), where (j & -j) picks out the lowest set bit of j so you know how far to move up the tree.
  9. Define a query procedure that takes idx:
     • Set j = idx + 1, best = –10**18, and bid = –1.
     • While j > 0:
         – If BIT_val[j] > best, then set best = BIT_val[j] and bid = BIT_id[j].

LOGICS: First thing you do is ignore whatever n was and set n equal to the number of pairs in L. Next, create two new lists called A and B, each of length n, and fill every slot with 0. Now you need to populate A and B in lockstep: go through each index i from 0 up to n–1, grab the pair (x, y) from L at position i, then compute x+y and put that into A[i], and compute x–y and put that into B[i].

At this point, set up an empty list called edges. You’ll be gathering triples into this as you go.

Now you’re going to make four passes, one for each d in 0, 1, 2, 3. On each pass:
  1. Start by making an empty list called tmp.
  2. For each index i from 0 to n–1, do this:
     • If d is even (that means 0 or 2), let X = A[i] and Y = B[i]. Otherwise (d is 1 or 3), let X = B[i] and Y = A[i].
     • Then, if d is 2 or 3 (i.e. d ≥ 2), replace X with –X.
     • Append the triple (X, Y, i) into tmp.
  3. Once tmp is full, sort it so that triples are in ascending order by X first, and when X values tie, by Y second.
  4. Walk through the sorted tmp list and build a new list called keys, where each entry is Y–X from that triple.
  5. Take the unique values in keys, sort them ascending to get a list uniq.
  6. Make a dictionary mp that maps each value in uniq to its index in uniq (so the smallest uniq value maps to 0, next to 1, and so on).
  7. Let m_val be the length of uniq. Now create two lists of length m_val+1:
     – BIT_val, and put the exact value –10**18 (that is, minus ten to the eighteenth power) in every slot.
     – BIT_id, and put –1 in every slot.
     These two lists together form a Fenwick tree (or BIT). The way this works is that when you see an index j, doing j & -j (a bitwise AND between j and its two’s-complement negative) gives you the size of the lowest set bit in j, which tells you how far to jump in the tree structure.
  8. Define an update procedure that takes (idx, val, pid):
     • Set j = idx + 1 (switching from 0-based to 1-based indexing).
     • While j ≤ m_val:
         – If val > BIT_val[j], then set BIT_val[j] = val and BIT_id[j] = pid.
         – Then set j = j + (j & -j), where (j & -j) picks out the lowest set bit of j so you know how far to move up the tree.
  9. Define a query procedure that takes idx:
     • Set j = idx + 1, best = –10**18, and bid = –1.
     • While j > 0:
         – If BIT_val[j] > best, then set best = BIT_val[j] and bid = BIT_id[j].
         – Then set j = j - (j & -j), subtracting the lowest set bit to move downward in the tree.
     • When j reaches 0, return the pair (best, bid).
 10. Now go through each triple (X, Y, pid) in the sorted tmp list:
     • Compute kkey = mp[Y - X].
     • Call query(kkey), which gives you (best_sum, best_pid).
     • If best_pid is not –1, that means you found a previous entry that can pair with this one:
         – Compute w = (X + Y) - best_sum.
         – Append the triple (pid, best_pid, w) to your edges list.
     • Whether you appended or not, call update(kkey, X + Y, pid) to record this entry in the Fenwick tree.

Repeat that entire sequence for d = 0, then d = 1, then d = 2, then d = 3. When you finish all four passes, edges is a long list of triples (a, b, w). Next, record candidate_edges = the length of edges, since that’s how many you gathered.

Now sort edges in ascending order by their third element w. You’re going to pick some of these edges to form a structure without cycles. To do that, set up a union-find (disjoint set) system:
  • Create a list parent of size n where parent[i] = i for each i from 0 to n–1.
  • Create a list rank of size n where every entry is 0.

Define a find(x) function as follows:
  – If parent[x] ≠ x, then set parent[x] = find(parent[x]) and return that value. Otherwise just return x.

Define a union(a, b) function:
  – Let ra = find(a) and rb = find(b).
  – If ra == rb, return False because they’re already in the same set.
  – Otherwise, compare rank[ra] and rank[rb]. If rank[ra] < rank[rb], set parent[ra] = rb. Else set parent[rb] = ra, and if rank[ra] == rank[rb], add 1 to rank[ra].
  – Return True to signal you merged two previously separate sets.

Now create an empty list called mst_weights and set edges_examined = 0. Walk through your sorted edges one by one, and for each triple (a, b, w):
  • Add 1 to edges_examined.
  • Call union(a, b). If it returns True, append w to mst_weights.
  • If the length of mst_weights reaches n–1, break out of the loop early because you’ve connected everything you can.

At this point you have up to n–1 weights in mst_weights. The last step is to pick your final result based on k:
  • If k ≥ n, just set result = 0.
  • Otherwise, sort mst_weights in ascending order, compute idx = (length of mst_weights) − k, and then set result = mst_weights[idx] // 2 (that is, integer divide that weight by 2).

Finally, you’re going to return two things: the number result, and a small dictionary with the two stats you collected (candidate_edges and edges_examined). 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you get back two values: 1) result, which is either 0 (if k ≥ n) or otherwise is one of the collected w values divided by two (using integer division) as determined by your k-based index rule; and 2) a dictionary with two counts – “candidate_edges” tells you how many edge triples you gathered across all four passes, and “edges_examined” tells you how many edges you actually looked at in the final union-find phase.

INPUTS: You start with three pieces of data: an integer n (which you’ll immediately overwrite), an integer k, and a list L of n items where each item is itself a pair of integers (x, y). 

LOGICS: First thing you do is ignore whatever n was and set n equal to the number of pairs in L. Next, create two new lists called A and B, each of length n, and fill every slot with 0. Now you need to populate A and B in lockstep: go through each index i from 0 up to n–1, grab the pair (x, y) from L at position i, then compute x+y and put that into A[i], and compute x–y and put that into B[i].

At this point, set up an empty list called edges. You’ll be gathering triples into this as you go.

Now you’re going to make four passes, one for each d in 0, 1, 2, 3. On each pass:
  1. Start by making an empty list called tmp.
  2. For each index i from 0 to n–1, do this:
     • If d is even (that means 0 or 2), let X = A[i] and Y = B[i]. Otherwise (d is 1 or 3), let X = B[i] and Y = A[i].
     • Then, if d is 2 or 3 (i.e. d ≥ 2), replace X with –X.
     • Append the triple (X, Y, i) into tmp.
  3. Once tmp is full, sort it so that triples are in ascending order by X first, and when X values tie, by Y second.
  4. Walk through the sorted tmp list and build a new list called keys, where each entry is Y–X from that triple.
  5. Take the unique values in keys, sort them ascending to get a list uniq.
  6. Make a dictionary mp that maps each value in uniq to its index in uniq (so the smallest uniq value maps to 0, next to 1, and so on).
  7. Let m_val be the length of uniq. Now create two lists of length m_val+1:
     – BIT_val, and put the exact value –10**18 (that is, minus ten to the eighteenth power) in every slot.
     – BIT_id, and put –1 in every slot.
     These two lists together form a Fenwick tree (or BIT). The way this works is that when you see an index j, doing j & -j (a bitwise AND between j and its two’s-complement negative) gives you the size of the lowest set bit in j, which tells you how far to jump in the tree structure.
  8. Define an update procedure that takes (idx, val, pid):
     • Set j = idx + 1 (switching from 0-based to 1-based indexing).
     • While j ≤ m_val:
         – If val > BIT_val[j], then set BIT_val[j] = val and BIT_id[j] = pid.
         – Then set j = j + (j & -j), where (j & -j) picks out the lowest set bit of j so you know how far to move up the tree.
  9. Define a query procedure that takes idx:
     • Set j = idx + 1, best = –10**18, and bid = –1.
     • While j > 0:
         – If BIT_val[j] > best, then set best = BIT_val[j] and bid = BIT_id[j].
         – Then set j = j - (j & -j), subtracting the lowest set bit to move downward in the tree.
     • When j reaches 0, return the pair (best, bid).
 10. Now go through each triple (X, Y, pid) in the sorted tmp list:
     • Compute kkey = mp[Y - X].
     • Call query(kkey), which gives you (best_sum, best_pid).
     • If best_pid is not –1, that means you found a previous entry that can pair with this one:
         – Compute w = (X + Y) - best_sum.
         – Append the triple (pid, best_pid, w) to your edges list.
     • Whether you appended or not, call update(kkey, X + Y, pid) to record this entry in the Fenwick tree.

Repeat that entire sequence for d = 0, then d = 1, then d = 2, then d = 3. When you finish all four passes, edges is a long list of triples (a, b, w). Next, record candidate_edges = the length of edges, since that’s how many you gathered.

Now sort edges in ascending order by their third element w. You’re going to pick some of these edges to form a structure without cycles. To do that, set up a union-find (disjoint set) system:
  • Create a list parent of size n where parent[i] = i for each i from 0 to n–1.
  • Create a list rank of size n where every entry is 0.

Define a find(x) function as follows:
  – If parent[x] ≠ x, then set parent[x] = find(parent[x]) and return that value. Otherwise just return x.

Define a union(a, b) function:
  – Let ra = find(a) and rb = find(b).
  – If ra == rb, return False because they’re already in the same set.
  – Otherwise, compare rank[ra] and rank[rb]. If rank[ra] < rank[rb], set parent[ra] = rb. Else set parent[rb] = ra, and if rank[ra] == rank[rb], add 1 to rank[ra].
  – Return True to signal you merged two previously separate sets.

Now create an empty list called mst_weights and set edges_examined = 0. Walk through your sorted edges one by one, and for each triple (a, b, w):
  • Add 1 to edges_examined.
  • Call union(a, b). If it returns True, append w to mst_weights.
  • If the length of mst_weights reaches n–1, break out of the loop early because you’ve connected everything you can.

At this point you have up to n–1 weights in mst_weights. The last step is to pick your final result based on k:
  • If k ≥ n, just set result = 0.
  • Otherwise, sort mst_weights in ascending order, compute idx = (length of mst_weights) − k, and then set result = mst_weights[idx] // 2 (that is, integer divide that weight by 2).

Finally, you’re going to return two things: the number result, and a small dictionary with the two stats you collected (candidate_edges and edges_examined). 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you get back two values: 1) result, which is either 0 (if k ≥ n) or otherwise is one of the collected w values divided by two (using integer division) as determined by your k-based index rule; and 2) a dictionary with two counts – “candidate_edges” tells you how many edge triples you gathered across all four passes, and “edges_examined” tells you how many edges you actually looked at in the final union-find phase.

LOGICS: First thing you do is ignore whatever n was and set n equal to the number of pairs in L. Next, create two new lists called A and B, each of length n, and fill every slot with 0. Now you need to populate A and B in lockstep: go through each index i from 0 up to n–1, grab the pair (x, y) from L at position i, then compute x+y and put that into A[i], and compute x–y and put that into B[i].

At this point, set up an empty list called edges. You’ll be gathering triples into this as you go.

Now you’re going to make four passes, one for each d in 0, 1, 2, 3. On each pass:
  1. Start by making an empty list called tmp.
  2. For each index i from 0 to n–1, do this:
     • If d is even (that means 0 or 2), let X = A[i] and Y = B[i]. Otherwise (d is 1 or 3), let X = B[i] and Y = A[i].
     • Then, if d is 2 or 3 (i.e. d ≥ 2), replace X with –X.
     • Append the triple (X, Y, i) into tmp.
  3. Once tmp is full, sort it so that triples are in ascending order by X first, and when X values tie, by Y second.
  4. Walk through the sorted tmp list and build a new list called keys, where each entry is Y–X from that triple.
  5. Take the unique values in keys, sort them ascending to get a list uniq.
  6. Make a dictionary mp that maps each value in uniq to its index in uniq (so the smallest uniq value maps to 0, next to 1, and so on).
  7. Let m_val be the length of uniq. Now create two lists of length m_val+1:
     – BIT_val, and put the exact value –10**18 (that is, minus ten to the eighteenth power) in every slot.
     – BIT_id, and put –1 in every slot.
     These two lists together form a Fenwick tree (or BIT). The way this works is that when you see an index j, doing j & -j (a bitwise AND between j and its two’s-complement negative) gives you the size of the lowest set bit in j, which tells you how far to jump in the tree structure.
  8. Define an update procedure that takes (idx, val, pid):
     • Set j = idx + 1 (switching from 0-based to 1-based indexing).
     • While j ≤ m_val:
         – If val > BIT_val[j], then set BIT_val[j] = val and BIT_id[j] = pid.
         – Then set j = j + (j & -j), where (j & -j) picks out the lowest set bit of j so you know how far to move up the tree.
  9. Define a query procedure that takes idx:
     • Set j = idx + 1, best = –10**18, and bid = –1.
     • While j > 0:
         – If BIT_val[j] > best, then set best = BIT_val[j] and bid = BIT_id[j].
         – Then set j = j - (j & -j), subtracting the lowest set bit to move downward in the tree.
     • When j reaches 0, return the pair (best, bid).
 10. Now go through each triple (X, Y, pid) in the sorted tmp list:
     • Compute kkey = mp[Y - X].
     • Call query(kkey), which gives you (best_sum, best_pid).
     • If best_pid is not –1, that means you found a previous entry that can pair with this one:
         – Compute w = (X + Y) - best_sum.
         – Append the triple (pid, best_pid, w) to your edges list.
     • Whether you appended or not, call update(kkey, X + Y, pid) to record this entry in the Fenwick tree.

Repeat that entire sequence for d = 0, then d = 1, then d = 2, then d = 3. When you finish all four passes, edges is a long list of triples (a, b, w). Next, record candidate_edges = the length of edges, since that’s how many you gathered.

Now sort edges in ascending order by their third element w. You’re going to pick some of these edges to form a structure without cycles. To do that, set up a union-find (disjoint set) system:
  • Create a list parent of size n where parent[i] = i for each i from 0 to n–1.
  • Create a list rank of size n where every entry is 0.

Define a find(x) function as follows:
  – If parent[x] ≠ x, then set parent[x] = find(parent[x]) and return that value. Otherwise just return x.

Define a union(a, b) function:
  – Let ra = find(a) and rb = find(b).
  – If ra == rb, return False because they’re already in the same set.
  – Otherwise, compare rank[ra] and rank[rb]. If rank[ra] < rank[rb], set parent[ra] = rb. Else set parent[rb] = ra, and if rank[ra] == rank[rb], add 1 to rank[ra].
  – Return True to signal you merged two previously separate sets.

Now create an empty list called mst_weights and set edges_examined = 0. Walk through your sorted edges one by one, and for each triple (a, b, w):
  • Add 1 to edges_examined.
  • Call union(a, b). If it returns True, append w to mst_weights.
  • If the length of mst_weights reaches n–1, break out of the loop early because you’ve connected everything you can.

At this point you have up to n–1 weights in mst_weights. The last step is to pick your final result based on k:
  • If k ≥ n, just set result = 0.
  • Otherwise, sort mst_weights in ascending order, compute idx = (length of mst_weights) − k, and then set result = mst_weights[idx] // 2 (that is, integer divide that weight by 2).

Finally, you’re going to return two things: the number result, and a small dictionary with the two stats you collected (candidate_edges and edges_examined). 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you get back two values: 1) result, which is either 0 (if k ≥ n) or otherwise is one of the collected w values divided by two (using integer division) as determined by your k-based index rule; and 2) a dictionary with two counts – “candidate_edges” tells you how many edge triples you gathered across all four passes, and “edges_examined” tells you how many edges you actually looked at in the final union-find phase.

INPUTS: You have four inputs: n, m, k, and arr. n, m, and k are each single integers. arr is a list of m items, and each item is a pair of two integers (x, y). You can think of arr as just a collection of those integer pairs. 

LOGICS: What you're going to do is walk through this in several clear stages. First, set up a map called mp. For each integer i from 1 up to n, give mp[i] an empty set. Then create an array A with positions 0 through n, and fill them all with 0. Next, go through each pair (x, y) in arr one by one: add y into the set mp[x], add x into mp[y], then add 1 to A[x] and also add 1 to A[y]. After that, make an array B of length n+1 where every entry is False. Now you need a min-heap structure: build a list of pairs (A[i], i) for i from 1 to n, and organize that list so the smallest first element is always at the front (if there’s a tie on the first element, you can pick the smaller i first). Call that your heap. Also prepare an empty list called order, and set two counters cnt1 = 0 and cnt2 = 0. Now begin a loop: while the heap still has items, pop off the front pair and call it (val, x). The way this works is, if B[x] is already True or val doesn’t match the current A[x], you just skip this popped item and go back to popping the next one. Otherwise, if val is at least k, you break out of the loop entirely. If neither of those conditions holds, you gather a list lst of all the y values from mp[x] for which B[y] is still False. Then mark B[x] = True to record you’ve removed x, append the triple (x, val, lst) into your order list, and add 1 to cnt1. Next, go through each y in lst: subtract 1 from A[y], add 1 to cnt2, then push the new pair (A[y], y) back into your heap so it can re-sort itself for the next pop. Once that loop finishes (either the heap is empty or you hit a val ≥ k), build a list core of every index i from 1 to n for which B[i] is still False. If the size of core is at least k, set result to type 1 with core and skip ahead. If not, set result to None for now. At this point, initialize cnt3 = 0. If you don’t yet have a result, go back through each triple (x, val, lst) in the exact order you recorded them. For each one, check if val equals k−1. If it does, form a candidate list cand by writing x first and then all of lst. If cand has fewer than k items, move on to the next triple. Otherwise take the first k items of cand as a temporary clique. Now test every pair among those k items: for i from 0 to k−2 and for j from i+1 to k−1, each time add 1 to cnt3 and check whether the jth item is in mp of the ith item. If any check fails, quit those two loops early and mark ok = False. If all pairs pass, set result to type 2 with that clique, then break out of both loops. After you’ve tried all triples, if result is still None, set result to type -1 with an empty list. You’re done with the logic here. 

OUTPUTS: At the end you get two things: first, a result pair whose first element is 1, 2, or -1 and whose second element is either the core list, the clique list, or an empty list; second, a dictionary of three counts: peel_ops is cnt1 (the number of removal operations you did), deg_updates is cnt2 (the total times you decremented a neighbor’s count), and clique_checks is cnt3 (the total pairwise checks you ran in the clique search).
